blocks.text: Why I Started This Newsletter
Over the past few weeks, I’ve been spending a lot of time trying to understand what actually happens when large language models move from demos to real production systems.

Most discussions around LLMs focus on prompting, agents, or model capabilities. But once you start looking at how these systems are actually served at scale, a completely different set of problems appears.

How do these models fit into GPU memory? Why does latency increase with more users? What exactly is KV cache? Why do we need multiple GPUs? How do systems like tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism actually work?
I realized that many of these concepts are often explained in a very research-heavy or infrastructure-heavy way, which can make them difficult to approach if you are trying to build intuition first.
So I started writing a series of conversational articles where I try to simplify these ideas in the same way I’m learning them myself.

Initially, these articles were published individually on LinkedIn. But over time, I started seeing a lot of interest and engagement around these posts. That was honestly very motivating. It pushed me to keep learning more deeply and continue sharing what I was understanding along the way.
Since all of these articles are connected and build on top of one another, I wanted a single place where this learning journey could continue in a more structured way.
That’s why I’m starting this newsletter: Inside LLM Inference.
Going forward, this newsletter will become the home for all future articles in this series.
What We’ve Explored So Far
Article 1 — Understanding KV Cache
The first article focused on one of the most important optimizations in LLM inference: KV caching.
I explored:

why autoregressive generation is slow
why models repeatedly recompute previous tokens
how KV cache avoids redundant computation
and how this significantly improves token generation speed
This article was mainly about building the intuition behind why KV cache exists in the first place.
Understanding KV Cache
Article 2 — Memory Challenges in LLM Inference
Once KV cache enters the picture, memory becomes a much bigger problem than it initially appears.
In this article, I explored:

memory fragmentation
memory duplication
why GPU memory utilization becomes difficult
and how inference systems try to manage memory efficiently
This was the point where inference started feeling less like “just running a model” and more like a systems engineering problem.
Memory Challenges in LLM Inference
Article 3 — GPU Utilization and Batching
A powerful GPU does not automatically mean efficient inference.
This article focused on:

why token generation is sequential
why GPUs are often underutilized
how batching improves throughput
continuous batching
and the tradeoff between latency and throughput
This article connected the earlier memory discussions with actual serving efficiency.
GPU Utilization and Batching
Article 4 — Why We Need Multiple GPUs
At some point, a single GPU simply stops being enough.
This article explored two major problems:

the model is too large to fit into memory
the system cannot handle enough concurrent users
I also discussed:

what parameters and weights actually are
how model size translates into memory
why larger models require distributed systems
This article became the bridge into multi-GPU inference.
Why We Need Multiple GPUs
Article 5 — Understanding Tensor Parallelism
This article focused on one of the core techniques used when models become too large for a single GPU.
I explored:

what tensors actually are
how weights are stored as tensors
how tensors can be split across GPUs
how GPUs collaborate during computation
and the tradeoffs introduced by GPU communication
This was the first article where distributed inference concepts started becoming much more concrete.
Understanding Tensor Parallelism
Article 6 — Understanding Pipeline Parallelism
After tensor parallelism, the next question naturally became: What if we split the layers themselves instead of splitting tensors?
This article explored:

pipeline parallelism
model stages
pipeline bubbles
communication flow between GPU groups
and how tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism are often combined in real systems
This was also the point where the overall architecture of large-scale inference systems started becoming clearer.
Understanding Pipeline Parallelism
What Comes Next?
The next step in this journey is understanding how these systems scale to large numbers of users.
So the next article in this newsletter will focus on:

data parallelism
distributed serving
request routing
replicas
and how modern inference systems handle massive concurrency
The deeper I go into inference, the more I realize that serving LLMs is not just an AI problem. It is also a distributed systems problem, a memory management problem, and an infrastructure problem.
And honestly, that’s what makes it fascinating.
If you enjoy breaking down complex systems into practical, intuition-first explanations, this newsletter will continue exploring these ideas one step at a time.

title: Inside LLM Inference

blocks.text: Let’s build an intuition for KV caching step by step, starting from the core problem and gradually arriving at why caching is necessary—and what tradeoffs it introduces.
Why Computation Becomes Expensive Without Caching
Consider a simple input:
"The cat sat"
The model processes this and generates the next word:
"on"
Now the input becomes:
"The cat sat on"
Here is the key issue:
Without any optimization, the model recomputes everything from scratch at every step.
That means:

It reprocesses "The"
It reprocesses "cat"
It reprocesses "sat"
Then processes "on"
This happens because of how attention works.
How Attention Drives This Cost
Inside the model, each word looks at every other word to understand context.
For a sentence like:
"The cat sat"
Each word interacts with all others:

"The" looks at "cat" and "sat"
"cat" looks at "The" and "sat"
"sat" looks at "The" and "cat"
As the sentence grows longer, the amount of work increases rapidly.
If there are n words, the number of interactions is proportional to n × n.
Now combine this with generation:

Step 1: process 3 words → ~9 interactions
Step 2: process 4 words → ~16 interactions
Step 3: process 5 words → ~25 interactions
This leads to a growing amount of repeated computation.
The Core Idea Behind KV Caching
Instead of recomputing everything, we store intermediate results and reuse them.
Inside each layer of the model, for every word, two important vectors are created:

A key vector (used to determine relevance)
A value vector (used to carry information)
KV caching means:
Store these vectors so they can be reused when new words are generated.
What Exactly Is Being Stored?
Let’s define the components clearly.
A vector is simply a list of numbers, for example:
A layer is one stage of processing. Models typically have many layers, and each word is processed through all of them.
For every word and every layer, we store:

one key vector
one value vector
Building a Simple Example
Assume:

1 sentence
3 words: "The cat sat"
2 layers
For each layer:
Each word produces a key vector and a value vector
So for one layer:
3 words × 2 vectors = 6 vectors
For two layers:
2 × 6 = 12 vectors
What Happens When a New Word Is Added?
Now the sentence becomes:
"The cat sat on"
We only compute vectors for the new word.
For that new word:

Layer 1 → key + value
Layer 2 → key + value
So we add:
2 layers × 2 vectors = 4 vectors
The previously computed vectors are reused.
Why This Improves Performance
With KV caching:

Previously computed key and value vectors are reused
Only the new word is processed
This changes the cost of generation significantly.
Without caching:
Each step recomputes everything → grows rapidly
With caching:
Each step processes only the new word → grows linearly
The Memory Tradeoff
The improvement in speed comes at the cost of memory.
All stored key and value vectors must remain in memory during generation.
Where Is This Data Stored?
KV cache is stored in GPU memory (also called VRAM).
This is the same memory used for:

model weights
intermediate computations
It is stored on the GPU because:

the model runs on the GPU
accessing GPU memory is much faster than transferring data from CPU memory
Why Memory Becomes a Bottleneck
Let’s scale the earlier example.
Assume:

32 layers
1000 words
each vector contains 4096 numbers
Total vectors:
32 layers × 1000 words × 2 (key and value) = 64,000 vectors
Total numbers:
64,000 × 4096 ≈ 262 million numbers
If each number takes 2 bytes of memory:
≈ 524 MB for a single user
With multiple users, memory usage grows proportionally.
Intuition for Memory Growth
For every new word:

new key and value vectors are added
across all layers
This means memory grows linearly with:

number of words
number of layers
number of users
Putting It All Together
KV caching introduces a fundamental tradeoff:

Faster generation by avoiding repeated computation
Increased memory usage due to storing intermediate results
What Comes Next
As systems scale, memory becomes the primary constraint rather than computation.
This leads to the next set of questions:

How do we manage GPU memory efficiently?
How do we serve many users simultaneously?
How do we reduce the size of the KV cache?
These questions lead to techniques such as:

paged attention
prefix caching
quantization
memory offloading
We will explore these in the next part.
Summary

KV caching improves inference speed by storing key and value vectors for each word at every layer, avoiding recomputation. However, this shifts the bottleneck from computation to memory, making efficient memory management critical in real-world systems.

title: Understanding KV Caching in LLM Inference (A Practical, Intuitive Guide)

blocks.text: In Part 1, we understood how KV caching makes generation fast by avoiding repeated computation.
A natural next question is:
If KV caching improves speed, what problems does it introduce?
At a high level, four issues show up:

Memory explosion
Fragmentation
Duplicate computation
Low GPU utilization (we’ll cover this and large model overhead in the next part)
Let’s go step by step and build intuition the same way.
Memory Explosion
If KV caching avoids recomputation, it does so by storing everything.
For every token and every layer (and in practice, for every attention head), key and value vectors are stored. As tokens grow, memory grows.
This leads to the first real problem: memory explosion.
How do we fix memory explosion?
Three common approaches are used:

Paged attention
Quantization
Offloading
Let’s go one by one.
Paged Attention (Blocks)
To really understand why paged attention is needed, it helps to walk through a slightly more detailed example.
Without Blocks (Continuous Memory Requirement)
Assume GPU memory is arranged like this (each box is a unit of memory):

User A uses 3 units
User B uses 3 units
User C uses 3 units
Now suppose User B finishes:
We now have free memory, but it is split into two parts:

3 units in the middle
1 unit at the end
Now a new request (User D) arrives and needs 4 units.
Even though we have 4 units total, they are not continuous:
So User D cannot be allocated.
This is fragmentation.
With Blocks (Paged Attention)
Now instead of requiring one continuous chunk, we divide memory into fixed-size blocks.
Each request is allowed to use multiple blocks, even if they are not next to each other.
Let’s reuse the same scenario.
After User B finishes:
Now User D needs 4 blocks.
With paged attention, we can allocate any 4 free blocks, even if they are scattered:
Here, User D is using:

3 blocks from the middle
1 block from the end
But how does the model know the order?
This is the key idea.
Even though blocks are scattered physically, the system keeps a mapping like:
User D → Block 4, Block 5, Block 6, Block 10
This mapping is stored in something like a block table.
So when the model reads the sequence, it follows the logical order, not the physical layout.
Why this fixes the problem

We no longer require continuous memory
Any free block can be reused
Memory gaps no longer cause allocation failures
This makes memory usage much more efficient and scalable.
Quantization
Another way to reduce memory is to store numbers in lower precision.
Instead of storing:
we store:
This slightly reduces precision, but models are generally robust to this noise.
The benefit is straightforward:

less memory per value
more tokens fit in GPU memory
Offloading
If memory is still not enough, part of the KV cache can be moved out of GPU memory.
Typically:

GPU memory → fast but limited
CPU memory → slower but much larger
So active data stays on GPU, and less active data moves to CPU.
Downsides of Offloading
Offloading is useful, but it is not ideal in all cases.

Data transfer between CPU and GPU is slow
If data is needed frequently, performance drops
Real-time systems may not tolerate this latency
So offloading is best when:

data is not accessed frequently
memory is the main bottleneck
Fragmentation
Even if total memory is sufficient, allocation can still fail because memory is not arranged properly.
Example:
This is fragmentation—memory exists, but not in the shape required.
Paged attention solves this as well.
Since memory is divided into blocks, requests no longer require continuous space. Blocks can be reused and placed anywhere.
How does the GPU know where blocks are?
The system uses a mapping table (often called a block table).
This table maps:
logical token positions → physical memory blocks
So even if blocks are scattered, the model reads them as if they were continuous.
Duplicate Computation
KV caching works well within a single request, but across requests, the same work can still be repeated.
Example:
User 1: "Answer clearly: What is AI?" User 2: "Answer clearly: What is ML?"
Both share the prefix:
"Answer clearly:"
Without optimization:

the prefix is computed twice
KV cache is duplicated
Prefix Caching
Prefix caching reuses KV cache for identical prefixes across requests. Instead of recomputing the shared prefix:

compute it once
reuse it for other requests with the same prefix
This reduces computation, improves time to first token, and avoids duplicating memory.
More detailed examples
1) Simple shared prefix
User 1: "Explain transformers in simple terms" User 2: "Explain transformers with examples"
Shared prefix: "Explain transformers"

Without prefix caching: the prefix is computed twice and stored twice.
With prefix caching: compute the prefix once, reuse it, and only compute the differing suffixes.
2) System prompt (very common)
"You are a helpful assistant. Answer clearly and concisely."

Without prefix caching: recompute this for every request.
With prefix caching: compute once and reuse across users.
3) Retrieval (RAG) with large context
"Answer based on this document: "
User 1: "... What is section 1?" User 2: "... What is section 2?"

Without prefix caching: process the entire document for each request.
With prefix caching: process once and reuse KV cache for all follow-ups.
4) Repeated templates or workflows
"Summarize the following text:" or repeated agent instructions.

Without prefix caching: template is recomputed each time.
With prefix caching: template KV cache is reused.
Important nuance
Prefix caching only works when the prefix matches exactly at the token level. Small differences can prevent reuse.
Conceptually, this is similar to reusing a template instead of recreating it each time.
What Comes Next
At this point, we have handled:

memory explosion
fragmentation
duplicate computation
Two important problems remain:

low GPU utilization
large model overhead
We will cover both in the next part.

title: LLM Inference Challenges: Memory, Fragmentation, Duplicate Work

blocks.text: GPU Utilization and Model Overhead
In Part 2, we explored memory-related challenges like fragmentation and duplicate computation.
At this point, it feels like we’ve handled most of the system issues. But two things still feel off:

The GPU still doesn’t seem fully utilized
KV cache is still surprisingly large
Let’s walk through both of these the same way—as they naturally come up when trying to understand the system.
Low GPU Utilization
We know that token generation is sequential. Each token depends on the previous one.
That raises an obvious thought:
If one request is small, why not run many of them in parallel?
Why not just batch requests?
Let’s say a GPU can handle 100 units of work.
One request only uses 5 units.
So naturally, we think:
Why not run 20 requests together and fully utilize the GPU?
This is exactly what batching tries to do.
Where batching starts to break
Batching works well when all requests are similar.
But in real systems:

Requests arrive at different times
Requests have different lengths
Some finish early, others run longer
Example:
Step 1: User A, User B, User C start together
Step 2: User A finishes early User B and C are still running
Now the batch is no longer full.
The GPU starts becoming underutilized again.
Another issue with batching
Traditional batching often waits for a batch to fill before starting.
This introduces latency:

New requests have to wait
GPU sits idle during that wait
Continuous Batching
This leads to a better idea.
Instead of fixed batches, we allow requests to come and go continuously.
How it works
At any point in time:

Running requests continue
Finished requests are removed
New requests are added immediately
Example:
Step 1: User A, User B running
Step 2: User A finishes User C joins immediately
Step 3: User B finishes User D joins
Why this works better

No waiting for batch formation
No wasted GPU slots
Work is always flowing
Intuition
Batching is like waiting for a bus to fill up before leaving.
Continuous batching is like a metro system:

People get on and off continuously
The system never stops
Large Model Overhead
Even after solving scheduling and memory layout, KV cache still feels large.
This leads to a deeper question:
Where is this extra memory coming from?
Understanding attention heads and layers
We already know:
For each token and each layer, we store key and value vectors.
But there’s more structure inside a layer.
Each layer has multiple attention heads.
What does that mean?
Instead of storing one key/value pair per token, we store one per head.
Example:
If a model has 32 heads:
Head 1 → Key₁, Value₁ Head 2 → Key₂, Value₂ ... Head 32 → Key₃₂, Value₃₂
So for one token, we are storing 32 versions of key/value.
Why do we need multiple heads?
Each head captures a different type of relationship in the data.
You can think of it as:

One head focusing on syntax
Another on relationships
Another on context
They provide diversity in how the model understands the sequence.
The problem
This diversity comes at a cost.
Memory now scales with:

number of tokens
number of layers
number of heads
So larger models (with more heads) create much larger KV caches.
MQA (Multi-Query Attention)
This leads to a natural question:
Do we really need separate key/value for every head?
MQA says: not necessarily.
What MQA does

Keep multiple query heads
Share a single key and value across all heads
Before
After
Q1...Q32 K (shared) V (shared)
Why wasn’t this done originally?
Because separate key/value per head gives more flexibility.
Each head can focus on different aspects independently.
Trade-off
MQA reduces memory significantly, but:

Heads lose some independence
Model expressiveness can slightly reduce
Intuition
Originally:
Each head had its own notebook
With MQA:
All heads share one notebook
GQA (Grouped Query Attention)
MQA works well, but sometimes it is too aggressive.
So the next idea is to find a middle ground.
What GQA does
Instead of sharing across all heads, we share within groups.
Example
32 heads grouped into 4 per group:
Trade-off

Better memory efficiency than standard attention
Better quality than MQA
Intuition

Standard: everyone has their own notebook
MQA: everyone shares one notebook
GQA: small groups share notebooks
Putting It All Together
At this point, the system-level picture is clearer:

Continuous batching improves how we use compute
MQA and GQA reduce how much memory the model needs
What Comes Next
So far, we have focused on single-node inference optimization.
The next natural question is:
What happens when a single GPU is not enough?
In the next part, we’ll look at scaling inference across multiple GPUs and systems.

title: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 3)

blocks.text: In the previous parts, we explored KV caching, memory challenges like fragmentation and duplication, and GPU utilization with batching . At this point, the system feels fairly optimized. But something still doesn’t sit right. What happens when a single GPU is not enough?
Why would a single GPU not be enough?

At first glance, one powerful GPU should be sufficient. But as systems scale, something starts to break. Sometimes, the model doesn’t even fit. Other times, even if it fits, the system still struggles to handle enough users. Let’s first understand the first case.
What does it mean when we say the model doesn’t fit?
When we say a model is “too large,” what are we actually referring to?
We often hear terms like 7B or 70B models. What does that really mean?
What does it mean when we say a 7B model?
It does not mean 7 billion words or sentences. It means the model has 7 billion parameters. Each parameter is just a number like:
These numbers define how the model processes language.
What are parameters and weights?

The terms parameters and weights are often used interchangeably. In practice, they refer to the same thing. A parameter (or weight) is a number the model has learned during training. These numbers control how input text is transformed step by step inside the model. You can think of them as settings that shape the behavior of the model.
Where do these weights live?
They are stored inside weight matrices. For example, inside a layer, we might have a matrix like:
That is roughly:
≈ 16 million parameters
But that is just one matrix. A full model has many layers and many matrices per layer. All of these together add up to billions of parameters.
How does this translate to memory?
Each parameter takes memory. If we store parameters in FP16, each parameter takes 2 bytes. So:
7 billion × 2 bytes ≈ 14 GB
So a 7B model is roughly 14GB, just for the weights.
Is that all the memory we need?
Not really. We also need KV cache, which grows with tokens and users, and intermediate activations, which are temporary during computation . So actual memory usage becomes:
weights + KV cache + activations
This can easily exceed the capacity of a single GPU. So one problem becomes clear. The model is simply too large to fit into one GPU.
What if the model does fit?
Let’s assume the model fits into a single GPU. Are we done? Not necessarily.
Why can’t one GPU handle all users?

Token generation is sequential. Each request does not fully utilize the GPU. Batching helps, but has limits . Requests arrive at different times, have different lengths, and finish at different times. Even with continuous batching, utilization is not perfect.
What does this look like in practice?

Imagine one GPU can handle around 50 active requests efficiently, but the system has 500 users. Requests start waiting. Latency increases. User experience degrades. So even if the model fits, one GPU may not handle enough users.
What are the actual problems then?
At this point, we have two different problems.

The model is too large to fit. 
The system needs to handle more users.
These problems may look similar, but they are fundamentally different.
What is the key difference?
The model size problem is a memory issue. The throughput problem is a compute issue.
How do we solve this?

We introduce multiple GPUs. But using multiple GPUs is not just about adding more hardware. We need to decide how to use them. We can split the model across GPUs, replicate the model across GPUs, or combine both approaches. Each comes with its own tradeoffs.
What comes next?
Now that we understand what parameters (weights) are, how model size translates to memory, and why a single GPU is not enough, the next question becomes natural. How do we split a model across GPUs?
In the next part, we will explore this using tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism.

title: LLM Inference Challenges - Why We Need Multiple GPUs

blocks.text: In the previous part, we explored why a single GPU is often not enough. Sometimes the model itself does not fit into memory. Other times, even if it fits, one GPU cannot handle enough concurrent users.
That naturally leads to the next question. How do we actually use multiple GPUs?
One important idea here is tensor parallelism. But before understanding tensor parallelism, it helps to first understand what a tensor actually is.
What is a tensor?
The word sounds complicated, but the idea is actually simple. A tensor is just a way of organizing numbers.
Depending on how numbers are arranged, we give them different names.
A single number is called a scalar.
Example:
A list of numbers is called a vector.
Example:
A table of numbers with rows and columns is called a matrix.
Example:
A tensor is the general term that includes all of these.
So:

scalar → 0D tensor
vector → 1D tensor
matrix → 2D tensor
Anything with more dimensions is also called a tensor.
Why do tensors matter in LLMs?
LLMs operate almost entirely on tensors.
Words become numbers. Those numbers are arranged into vectors and matrices. Then the model continuously transforms these tensors during computation.
For example:

embeddings are tensors
activations are tensors
KV cache stores tensors
weights are tensors
Almost everything inside the model is represented this way.
What do weights look like?
Earlier, we discussed parameters and weights. These weights are usually stored as matrices.
For example:
That means:

4096 rows
4096 columns
millions of numbers inside one tensor
The model performs operations on these tensors repeatedly during inference.
Why do we need tensor parallelism?
Suppose we have a very large model.
Inside the model, we may have weight matrices like:
That is roughly:
≈ 16 million parameters
And this is just one matrix.
A full model contains many such matrices across many layers. Eventually, the model becomes too large for one GPU.
So the natural idea becomes:
Can we split these tensors across GPUs?
This leads to tensor parallelism.
What does splitting a tensor mean?
Suppose we have a matrix like this:

[
 [ W W W W ]
 [ W W W W ]
 [ W W W W ]
 [ W W W W ]
]
Normally, one GPU stores the entire matrix.
With tensor parallelism, we divide the matrix across GPUs.
For example:

GPU 1:
[
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
]

GPU 2:
[
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
 [ W W ]
]
Now each GPU stores only part of the weights.
What happens during computation?
Suppose an input arrives.
Example:
Input → [ x1 x2 x3 x4 ]
Normally:

one GPU multiplies the full input with the full weight matrix
and produces the output
With tensor parallelism:

the same input is sent to multiple GPUs
each GPU computes using only its portion of the weights
Example:

GPU 1 → partial computation
GPU 2 → partial computation
Each GPU produces part of the result. These partial results are then combined together.
What does this achieve?
Instead of one GPU handling the entire model, we now distribute the model across GPUs.
This helps in two ways:

the model fits into memory
computation is shared across GPUs
Large models that previously could not run on one GPU now become possible.
Is the computation completely independent?
Not really.
After each GPU computes its partial result:

outputs must be combined
GPUs must synchronize
data must move between GPUs
So tensor parallelism introduces communication between GPUs.
Why is communication important?
If GPUs constantly exchange data:

latency increases
synchronization overhead increases
bandwidth becomes important
So tensor parallelism is always a tradeoff:

better memory scaling
but more communication cost
Does tensor parallelism help with concurrent users?
Not directly.
The main goal of tensor parallelism is to make large models fit across GPUs.
In some cases, distributing weights across GPUs can free up memory for:

larger KV cache
larger batches
more active requests
So it can indirectly improve concurrency.
But scaling to many users is usually solved differently. We will come back to that later.
What does this feel like intuitively?
Imagine solving a large math problem.
Without tensor parallelism:
One person solves the entire problem
With tensor parallelism:

Multiple people solve different parts
Then combine answers
That is essentially what the GPUs are doing.
What is the key idea?
Tensor parallelism does not split users. It does not split requests. It splits the tensors themselves.
Multiple GPUs collaborate to compute a single layer of the model.
What comes next?
Tensor parallelism helps when the model itself is too large.
But there is another way to split work across GPUs.
Instead of splitting tensors inside a layer, we can split the layers themselves.
This leads to pipeline parallelism.

title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding Tensor Parallelism

blocks.text: Understanding Pipeline Parallelism

In the previous part, we explored tensor parallelism and how it helps split tensors across GPUs when a model becomes too large for a single device. That naturally leads to the next question. If tensor parallelism already helps with memory, why do we still need pipeline parallelism?
Why do we need pipeline parallelism?

Tensor parallelism helps when the individual layers are too large to fit on one GPU. But for very large models, especially models with many large layers, that alone is not always enough. Communication can become heavy, and the system can become harder to scale efficiently.
So instead of splitting the tensors inside a layer, we can split the layers themselves.
That is pipeline parallelism.
What does pipeline parallelism mean?
Pipeline parallelism means dividing the model into stages and placing those stages on different GPUs.
For example:

GPU group 1 → layers 1 to 20
GPU group 2 → layers 21 to 40
GPU group 3 → layers 41 to 60
Now each GPU group handles a different part of the model.
How does it work?
An input starts at the first stage.
The first GPU group processes its layers and produces an intermediate output. That output is then passed to the next GPU group, which continues the computation. Then the next group does the same.
So the data flows through the model stage by stage, like a pipeline.
Why is it called pipeline parallelism?
Because it behaves like an assembly line.
One stage finishes its work and passes the result to the next stage. Each GPU group works on a different part of the model, and the output keeps moving forward until the final result is produced.
What does this solve?
Pipeline parallelism reduces memory pressure by spreading the model across multiple GPUs.
Instead of one GPU holding all layers:

each GPU group holds only a portion of the layers
memory usage per GPU goes down
much larger models become possible
What is the tradeoff?
The main issue is that pipeline parallelism can create idle time.
If one GPU group finishes early and the next group is still busy, the first group has to wait. That waiting time is often called a pipeline bubble.
So pipeline parallelism saves memory, but it can reduce efficiency if the pipeline is not kept full.
How is this different from tensor parallelism?
Tensor parallelism splits the tensors inside a layer. Pipeline parallelism splits the layers themselves.
That is the key difference.
Tensor parallelism:
multiple GPUs work together on the same layer
Pipeline parallelism:
different GPU groups handle different layers
Can they be used together?
Yes, and in large systems, they often are.
For very large models:

pipeline parallelism splits the model into stages
tensor parallelism splits the work inside each stage
So one technique handles the broad model partitioning, and the other handles the computation inside each partition.
What does this look like in a real system?
Suppose we have a very large model with 80 layers.
We divide the model into stages like this:

GPU Group 1 → Layers 1–20
GPU Group 2 → Layers 21–40
GPU Group 3 → Layers 41–60
GPU Group 4 → Layers 61–80
This is pipeline parallelism.
Now assume each GPU group contains 8 GPUs.
Inside GPU Group 1:

Layers 1–20 are assigned to that group
the tensors inside those layers are split across the 8 GPUs
all 8 GPUs collaborate to compute those layers
This is tensor parallelism happening inside the pipeline stage.
Once GPU Group 1 finishes:

the intermediate output is passed to GPU Group 2
GPU Group 2 processes Layers 21–40
again using tensor parallelism internally
So the model moves stage by stage through the pipeline, while each stage itself uses tensor parallelism for computation.
What is the key intuition?
Pipeline parallelism splits the model vertically.
Tensor parallelism splits computation horizontally within each stage.
Together, they help balance:

memory usage
communication overhead
compute efficiency
What comes next?
At this point, the multi-GPU picture is becoming much clearer.
We now understand:

why a single GPU is not enough
how tensor parallelism splits tensors
how pipeline parallelism splits layers
and how both techniques work together in large systems
The next natural question is: How do these systems scale to many concurrent users?
That leads to data parallelism and distributed serving.

title: LLM Inference Challenges - Pipeline Parallelism

blocks.text: Understanding Data Parallelism

In the previous parts, we explored why a single GPU is not enough, how tensor parallelism splits tensors across GPUs, and how pipeline parallelism splits layers across stages. At this point, the multi-GPU picture starts becoming much clearer.
But one major question still remains.
Even after distributing the model across many GPUs, how do we actually serve thousands or even millions of users?
That is where data parallelism comes in.
What problem are we solving now?
Tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism help us run very large models. They solve the problem of model size and computation distribution.
But they do not fully solve concurrency.
Even if a model runs across many GPUs:

requests still queue up
decode is still sequential
KV cache keeps growing
users still compete for the same serving instance
So the next challenge becomes:
How do we scale to many concurrent users?
What does a real multi-GPU setup look like?
Let us build this step by step.
Suppose we have a very large model with 80 layers.
And suppose:

one layer itself is too large for one GPU
the full model is also too large for one GPU
and finally we also want to support many users
Now we need all three techniques together.
Step 1 — What does tensor parallelism look like?
Suppose one layer contains a huge weight matrix like:
One GPU may not have enough memory or compute power.
So we split the tensor across GPUs.
Example:

GPU 1 → first part of weights
GPU 2 → second part
GPU 3 → third part
GPU 4 → fourth part
Now all 4 GPUs cooperate on:

the same layer
the same request
the same computation
So instead of:
1 GPU handling the layer
we now have:
4 GPUs handling one layer together
This is tensor parallelism.
What problem does tensor parallelism solve?
It mainly solves:
How do we run very large layers?
It helps:

fit larger tensors
distribute compute
reduce memory pressure
But notice something important.
All 4 GPUs are still focused on:

the same request
the same model instance
So this alone does not massively increase concurrency.
Step 2 — What does pipeline parallelism look like?
Now suppose the model has:
80 transformer layers
Even with tensor parallelism, the entire model may still not fit efficiently.
So now we split the layers into stages.
Example:

Stage 1 → Layers 1–20
Stage 2 → Layers 21–40
Stage 3 → Layers 41–60
Stage 4 → Layers 61–80
Now combine this with tensor parallelism.
Suppose:

each stage uses 4 GPUs
those GPUs work together using tensor parallelism
Now the setup becomes:

Stage 1 → GPUs 1–4
Stage 2 → GPUs 5–8
Stage 3 → GPUs 9–12
Stage 4 → GPUs 13–16
Now one request flows like this:

Input
→ Stage 1 GPUs
→ Stage 2 GPUs
→ Stage 3 GPUs
→ Stage 4 GPUs
→ Output
So:

pipeline parallelism splits the layers
tensor parallelism splits the tensors inside those layers
Together:

16 GPUs cooperate
to serve ONE model instance
Does this solve concurrency now?
Not completely.
Even though 16 GPUs are involved:

they are still serving the same model instance
users still share the same serving pipeline
decode is still sequential
requests still compete for compute and KV cache
So tensor + pipeline parallelism mainly solve:
How do we run a huge model?
Not:
How do we serve huge numbers of users?
That is where data parallelism enters.
Step 3 — What does data parallelism look like?
Now we create multiple copies of that entire 16-GPU setup.
Example:

Replica 1 → GPUs 1–16
Replica 2 → GPUs 17–32
Replica 3 → GPUs 33–48
Replica 4 → GPUs 49–64
Each replica contains:

the same weights
the same architecture
the same tensor parallel setup
the same pipeline stages
Now requests can be distributed.
Example:

Batch 1 → Replica 1
Batch 2 → Replica 2
Batch 3 → Replica 3
Batch 4 → Replica 4
Or:

Users A–D → Replica 1
Users E–H → Replica 2
Users I–L → Replica 3
Users M–P → Replica 4
Now multiple batches and decode loops can run independently.
THIS is what increases concurrency.
Why does data parallelism solve concurrency?
Because replicas are independent.
Each replica has:

its own weights
its own KV cache
its own scheduler
its own batches
its own decode loop
So instead of one giant serving pipeline:
we now have multiple independent serving pipelines
This scales throughput much more effectively.
How are user sessions managed?
Once a request is assigned to a replica, it usually stays there.
Why?
Because the KV cache for that request already exists inside that replica.
If the request suddenly moves elsewhere:

the new replica would not have the KV cache
attention history would be missing
generation would break or require expensive transfer
So systems usually use:

sticky sessions
or
session affinity
Meaning:
one user stays attached to one replica during generation
What does a practical GPU cluster look like?
At a high level, a GPU cluster is simply many servers connected together.
Each server may contain:

CPUs
RAM
multiple GPUs
networking hardware
storage
Example:

Server
├── CPU
├── RAM
├── 8 GPUs
├── NVLink connections
└── Network interfaces
How are GPUs connected inside one server?
Inside the same machine:

GPUs communicate using NVLink or NVSwitch
bandwidth is extremely high
latency is very low
Example:

GPU ↔ GPU
Very high-speed communication
This is why tensor parallel GPUs are often placed inside the same server.
Because tensor parallelism requires constant GPU-to-GPU communication.
What does a larger cluster look like?
Now suppose one server is not enough.
We connect many servers together.
Example:

Rack 1
├── Server A → 8 GPUs
├── Server B → 8 GPUs
├── Server C → 8 GPUs

Rack 2
├── Server D → 8 GPUs
├── Server E → 8 GPUs
├── Server F → 8 GPUs
Now we may have:
48 GPUs total
connected into one cluster.
How do all three techniques work together in practice?
Suppose we build this setup:

4 pipeline stages
Each stage uses 8 GPUs with tensor parallelism
That becomes:
4 × 8 = 32 GPUs
This entire 32-GPU setup becomes:
ONE model replica
Now suppose we create 4 such replicas:

Replica 1 → Servers 1–4
Replica 2 → Servers 5–8
Replica 3 → Servers 9–12
Replica 4 → Servers 13–16
Now:

tensor parallelism splits tensors
pipeline parallelism splits layers
data parallelism scales concurrent users
This is very close to how large production inference systems operate.
What does request flow look like in practice?
At this point, let us connect everything together into one real inference flow.
Suppose a user sends a prompt like:
"Explain quantum computing..."
The request first reaches a router or load balancer.
The router decides:

which replica should handle the request
which replica currently has capacity
where batching and memory usage look healthy
Example:

Load Balancer
    ↓
Replica 2 selected
Now remember:

Replica 2 itself may contain multiple pipeline stages
each stage may contain multiple GPUs using tensor parallelism
Suppose Replica 2 looks like this:

Stage 1 → GPUs 17–24
Stage 2 → GPUs 25–32
Stage 3 → GPUs 33–40
Stage 4 → GPUs 41–48
Now the request flows through the model step by step.
Example:

Input Prompt
    ↓
Stage 1 GPUs
(tensor parallel computation)
    ↓
Intermediate output
    ↓
Stage 2 GPUs
    ↓
Intermediate output
    ↓
Stage 3 GPUs
    ↓
Stage 4 GPUs
    ↓
Generated token
Inside each stage:

multiple GPUs cooperate using tensor parallelism
partial computations are combined
activations are exchanged between GPUs
Then:

pipeline stages pass outputs forward
the final token is generated
KV cache is updated inside that replica
For the next token:

the request usually stays on the same replica
because the KV cache already exists there
This process repeats token by token during generation.
So at a high level:

Load Balancer
    ↓
Model Replica
    ↓
Pipeline Stages
    ↓
Tensor Parallel GPUs
    ↓
Generated Tokens
This is very close to what happens inside modern large-scale inference systems.
What is the key intuition?
Tensor Parallelism:
Split tensors
Pipeline Parallelism:
Split layers
Data Parallelism:
Replicate the entire model
Together, they make large-scale LLM inference possible.
Why is this article important?
At this point, we have built the complete foundation for understanding modern inference systems.
We now understand:

KV cache
batching
memory pressure
GPU utilization
tensor parallelism
pipeline parallelism
data parallelism
practical GPU clusters
request routing and session affinity
Honestly, this may be one of the most important parts of the series.
Before moving to the next stage, I would strongly recommend revisiting Articles 1–7 one more time.
I am personally doing the same.
As I started exploring the next phase of inference systems, I realized that if these concepts are not extremely clear, the next topics become very difficult to understand intuitively.
I have already gone through these concepts multiple times myself just to build a clearer mental model of what is actually happening inside modern inference systems.
What comes next?
Now that the multi-GPU foundation is much clearer, we can start exploring the next layer of real-world inference systems.
This includes topics like:

distributed serving
request routing
vLLM architecture
paged attention
disaggregated inference
continuous batching across replicas
multi-node communication
advanced serving optimizations
And this is where things start becoming even more interesting.

title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding Data Parallelism

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 8)
Understanding Distributed Serving & Request Routing

In the previous parts, we explored tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, and data parallelism. At this point, we understand that modern inference systems use many GPUs together to run large models and handle large numbers of users.
But something still feels incomplete.
What actually happens when a request first arrives?
And when we say a request is routed to a “replica,” what exactly does that mean?
What happens when a request first arrives?
Suppose a user sends:
"Explain quantum computing"
At first glance, it feels simple:

request goes to model
model generates response
But internally, many things happen before the first token is generated.
Step 1 — The request reaches the API layer
The request first reaches an API gateway or frontend service.
Example:

User
  ↓
API Gateway
This layer may handle:

authentication
rate limiting
logging
validation
API management
At this stage, the request has still not reached the GPUs.
Step 2 — The router/load balancer receives the request
Next, the request reaches the routing layer.
Example:

Gateway
   ↓
Router / Load Balancer
This component decides:
Which model replica should handle this request?
What is a replica?
This is where things become interesting.
At first, I was thinking about replicas similar to traditional web servers behind a load balancer. In normal applications:

each server has its own IP
the load balancer routes traffic across servers
each server independently processes requests
Example:

Load Balancer
   ↓
Web Server 1
Web Server 2
Web Server 3
But LLM inference systems are different.
A replica is usually not just:

one GPU or even
one server
A replica is actually:
one complete model-serving unit
And that unit itself may contain:

many GPUs
multiple pipeline stages
tensor parallel groups
schedulers
KV cache
communication layers
Can a replica span multiple GPUs?
Yes.
Suppose we have:

tensor parallel size = 4
pipeline parallel size = 4
Then:

4 GPUs per stage
×
4 stages
=
16 GPUs
Now these 16 GPUs together form:
ONE model replica
The request is not independently handled by one GPU.
Instead:

all GPUs cooperate together
tensor parallel GPUs compute the same layer together
pipeline stages process different parts of the model
So the replica behaves like:
one giant distributed inference engine
Does one replica always mean one server?
Not necessarily.
For smaller models:

one replica may fit inside one server
all GPUs may live in the same machine
Example:

Server A
├── GPU 1
├── GPU 2
├── GPU 3
└── GPU 4
In this case:
replica ≈ one server
But for larger models:
one replica may span many servers
Example:

Replica 1
├── Server A → GPUs 1–8
├── Server B → GPUs 9–16
├── Server C → GPUs 17–24
└── Server D → GPUs 25–32
Now:

one replica
spans multiple servers
and many GPUs
How do these servers work together?
The servers are connected using high-speed networking.
Inside one server:

GPUs often communicate using NVLink or NVSwitch
communication is extremely fast
Across servers:

systems may use InfiniBand or RDMA networking
optimized for very high throughput and low latency
This allows:

GPUs across machines
to behave like one coordinated inference system
So a useful way to think about it is:

Replica
=
a distributed cluster of GPUs
acting as one logical model instance
What does the load balancer actually balance then?
The load balancer usually routes traffic across replicas.
Example:

Load Balancer
   ↓
Replica 1 → GPUs 1–16
Replica 2 → GPUs 17–32
Replica 3 → GPUs 33–48
The load balancer is usually not routing directly to individual GPUs.
Instead:

each replica internally coordinates its GPUs
the replica itself behaves like one serving target
How does the router choose a replica?
The router may consider:

current GPU utilization
queue length
KV cache pressure
batch size
latency
memory availability
Example:

Replica 1 → overloaded
Replica 2 → healthy
Replica 3 → long queue
So the router selects:
Replica 2
Why is routing important?
Because inference systems constantly balance:

throughput
vs
latency
If too many requests go to one replica:

queues grow
latency increases
KV cache pressure increases
If requests are spread too aggressively:

GPUs become underutilized
batching efficiency drops
So routing becomes a scheduling problem.
What happens after replica selection?
Once a request reaches a replica:

Request
   ↓
Replica Scheduler
The scheduler decides:

when to execute the request
which batch it should join
whether enough memory is available
This is where continuous batching becomes important.
Why don’t requests execute immediately?
Because GPUs are more efficient with batches.
Instead of:

1 request
→ 1 GPU execution
the scheduler tries to create:
Batch = [Request A, Request B, Request C]
Now the GPUs process them together.
What happens during prefill?
The prompt tokens are first processed through the transformer layers.
Example:
"Explain quantum computing"
becomes token IDs like:
During this stage:

attention is computed
activations flow through layers
KV cache gets created
This phase is called: Prefill
What happens during decode?
Once KV cache exists:

token generation starts
one token depends on previous tokens
Example:

Token 1
→ Token 2
→ Token 3
This phase becomes sequential.
This is called the decode loop.
Why do requests usually stay on the same replica?
Because the KV cache already exists there.
Example:

User Session
   ↓
Replica 2
   ↓
KV cache stored there
If generation suddenly moves to another replica:

KV cache would need transfer
latency would increase heavily
bandwidth usage would explode
This is why systems often use:

sticky sessions
or
session affinity
What is the overall request flow?
At a high level:

User
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Router / Load Balancer
 ↓
Replica
 ↓
Scheduler
 ↓
Batch Formation
 ↓
Prefill
 ↓
Decode Loop
 ↓
Generated Tokens
This is the basic lifecycle of a request inside a modern inference system.
What still feels unclear at this point?
Honestly, while learning this myself, one thing initially confused me:

what exactly is a replica physically?
where are the GPUs located?
how do multiple servers behave like one system?
how does GPU communication actually work underneath?
At this stage, it is completely normal for these questions to appear.
Because now we are slowly transitioning from:

“running a model on GPUs” to
“understanding distributed GPU infrastructure”
And that is a very different mental model.
What comes next?
Now that we understand:

request routing
replicas
schedulers
session affinity
distributed model serving
the next natural step becomes:

How do all these GPUs and servers
actually communicate fast enough
to behave like ONE system?
In the next part, we will go deeper into:

GPU clusters
NVLink
NVSwitch
InfiniBand
inter-node communication
why networking becomes critical
and what “inside a replica” really looks like.
This is where inference systems start looking much closer to distributed supercomputing systems than traditional backend applications.

title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding Distributed Serving & Request Routing

blocks.text: In the previous part, we explored distributed serving, replicas, request routing, schedulers, and how requests flow through large inference systems.
At this point, something important starts becoming visible.
A replica is not just:

one GPU
one machine
or one server
A replica may actually contain:

many GPUs
many servers
tensor parallel groups
pipeline stages
schedulers
KV cache systems
And all of these components must constantly communicate with each other.
That naturally leads to the next question.
Why does GPU communication matter so much?
Modern inference systems are highly distributed.
During inference:

GPUs exchange activations
tensor parallel GPUs combine partial outputs
pipeline stages pass intermediate tensors
KV cache updates happen continuously
schedulers coordinate batches
So communication is happening constantly.
And this communication can become a bottleneck very quickly.
Why can communication become a bottleneck?
Suppose computation is extremely fast.
But after every computation:

GPUs must wait for data
tensors must move across devices
synchronization must happen
Then eventually:

communication time
>
compute time
At that point:

GPUs sit idle waiting for data
utilization drops
latency increases
throughput suffers
So large-scale inference is not only about GPU compute anymore.
It is also about:

moving data efficiently
between GPUs
What kinds of communication happen during inference?
Different parallelism strategies create different communication patterns.
Tensor parallelism requires very frequent GPU communication.
Why?
Because multiple GPUs cooperate on the same layer.
Example:

GPU 1 → partial computation
GPU 2 → partial computation
GPU 3 → partial computation
GPU 4 → partial computation
Now their outputs must be combined.
This may happen:

after every attention block
after matrix multiplications
after intermediate activations
So tensor parallelism is extremely communication-heavy.
What about pipeline parallelism?
Pipeline parallelism communicates differently.
Here:

one stage finishes computation
then sends activations to the next stage
Example:
Stage 1 → Stage 2 → Stage 3 → Stage 4
So communication mainly happens:

between stages
during forward progression through the model
Compared to tensor parallelism:

communication frequency is usually lower
but transferred tensors may still be large
What about data parallelism?
Data parallelism is different.
During inference:

replicas are mostly independent
requests stay within one replica
communication between replicas is smaller
So inference-time data parallelism usually creates much less communication pressure.
Why is tensor parallelism often limited to one server?
Because tensor parallelism requires extremely fast communication.
Suppose GPUs must synchronize after nearly every operation.
If those GPUs are spread across slow networks:

latency increases heavily
synchronization becomes expensive
performance collapses
So systems often try to keep tensor parallel GPUs:
inside the same machine
where communication is fastest.
How do GPUs communicate inside one server?
Inside a server, GPUs often communicate using:

NVLink
or
NVSwitch
These are specialized high-speed GPU interconnects.
What is NVLink?
NVLink is a very high-speed communication link between GPUs.
Instead of:
GPU → CPU → GPU
NVLink allows:
GPU ↔ GPU
communication directly.
This provides:

much higher bandwidth
lower latency
faster synchronization
compared to normal PCIe communication.
Why is this important?
Suppose tensor parallel GPUs constantly exchange activations.
Without fast communication:

GPUs spend time waiting
synchronization slows down
throughput decreases
NVLink helps reduce that overhead.
This is one reason modern AI servers are designed heavily around:
GPU interconnect topology
not just raw GPU count.
What is NVSwitch?
NVSwitch extends this idea further.
Instead of direct links between only certain GPUs:

NVSwitch allows many GPUs to communicate efficiently together
almost like a high-speed GPU network switch
Example:
GPU 1 ↔ NVSwitch ↔ GPU 8
This becomes important in servers with:

8 GPUs
16 GPUs
or larger GPU configurations
What happens if one server is not enough?
Eventually models become too large.
Now:

one replica may span many servers
tensor parallel groups may cross machines
pipeline stages may live on different nodes
Now communication must happen:
across servers
This is called:
inter-node communication
At this point, what exactly is a replica then?
Honestly, this was one of the points that initially confused me while learning all this.
At first, I was thinking about replicas similar to traditional backend systems:

Load Balancer
   ↓
Server 1
Server 2
Server 3
where:

one endpoint maps to one server
and each server independently handles requests
But modern inference systems work very differently.
A replica is usually not just:

one GPU
one server
or one machine
Instead, a replica is closer to:
one distributed model-serving runtime
built using:

many GPUs
multiple servers
networking
schedulers
communication libraries
and inference software
For example, systems like:

vLLM
TGI
SGLang
TensorRT-LLM
coordinate many GPUs together and expose them logically as:
ONE serving endpoint
So internally, a replica may look like:

Server A → GPUs 1–8
Server B → GPUs 9–16
Server C → GPUs 17–24
Server D → GPUs 25–32
But externally:

Load Balancer
    ↓
Replica Endpoint
still behaves like one model-serving unit.
So the important mental shift becomes:

Replica
≠
one machine

Replica
=
software + distributed hardware
working together
as one logical inference system
And honestly, this is where inference systems start feeling much closer to distributed supercomputing systems than traditional backend applications.
Why is inter-node communication harder?
Because communication across servers is slower than communication inside one server.
Inside one machine:

GPUs may use NVLink
latency is extremely low
bandwidth is extremely high
Across machines:

data travels through network hardware
switches become involved
congestion may happen
latency increases
So distributed inference systems become highly dependent on networking quality.
What networking is commonly used between servers?
Large inference clusters often use:
InfiniBand
or advanced RDMA-capable networking.
These technologies are optimized for:

very high throughput
low latency
efficient GPU communication
What is RDMA?
RDMA means:
Remote Direct Memory Access
The important idea is:

one machine can access memory on another machine
with minimal CPU involvement
This helps reduce:

latency
CPU overhead
unnecessary memory copying
which becomes very important at scale.
Why does CPU involvement matter?
Suppose every GPU communication required:
GPU → CPU → Network → CPU → GPU
Then:

CPUs become bottlenecks
memory copying increases
latency grows significantly
RDMA helps communication happen more directly.
What is NCCL?
At this point another important component appears.
NCCL
pronounced:
Nickel
NCCL is NVIDIA’s communication library for multi-GPU systems.
It helps GPUs coordinate operations like:

synchronization
tensor exchange
reductions
collective communication
What are collective operations?
Suppose multiple GPUs each compute partial outputs.
Now they must combine results.
Example:

GPU 1 → partial tensor
GPU 2 → partial tensor
GPU 3 → partial tensor
GPU 4 → partial tensor
NCCL helps efficiently perform operations like:
combine everything together
across GPUs.
What is all-reduce?
One very common communication pattern is:
all-reduce
The idea is:

every GPU contributes data
data gets combined
every GPU receives the final combined result
This is heavily used in:

distributed training
tensor parallel inference
synchronization operations
Why do communication patterns matter so much?
Because at scale:

communication architecture
=
performance architecture
Two systems with:

the same GPUs
the same model
the same software
can still perform very differently depending on:

network topology
interconnect bandwidth
communication overhead
synchronization efficiency
What does a real cluster start looking like?
At this point, inference systems start looking less like normal backend systems.
And much more like:
distributed supercomputing systems
Because now we are coordinating:

hundreds of GPUs
across many servers
with high-speed networking
while maintaining low latency
and keeping utilization high
What is the key intuition?
Tensor parallelism creates:
heavy communication
Pipeline parallelism creates:
stage-to-stage communication
Data parallelism creates:
replicated serving systems
And networking becomes the foundation that allows all of this to function efficiently.
What becomes difficult at this stage?
Honestly, this is usually the stage where the mental model becomes harder.
Because now we are no longer only thinking about:

transformers
tensors
batching
inference loops
We are also thinking about:

cluster topology
GPU placement
networking hardware
synchronization overhead
distributed communication efficiency
And this is exactly why modern inference engineering starts overlapping heavily with:
distributed systems engineering
What comes next?
At this point, we now understand:

replicas
distributed serving
request routing
GPU communication
NVLink
NCCL
multi-node inference systems
And honestly, the mental model has now shifted quite a bit.
We are no longer thinking only about:

“running a model”
or “calling an API”
We are now thinking about:

distributed GPU systems
schedulers
communication bottlenecks
and large-scale inference infrastructure
But there is still one extremely important piece missing.
Even with all this infrastructure:

why does inference still become slow?
why are GPUs sometimes underutilized?
why is batching difficult during generation?
and why do serving systems behave very differently during prompt processing vs token generation?
This leads to one of the most important runtime concepts in inference systems:
Prefill vs Decode
In the next part, we will explore:

what prefill actually does
what decode actually does
why decode becomes sequential
why GPU utilization changes dramatically
why batching becomes difficult during generation
and why modern serving systems focus so heavily on scheduler design
Honestly, this is one of the key concepts needed before understanding:

continuous batching
paged attention
and vLLM internals
Because once prefill vs decode becomes intuitive, many modern inference optimizations suddenly start making much more sense.

title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding GPU Communication & Networking

blocks.text: Understanding Prefill vs Decode
In the previous parts, we explored:

tensor parallelism
pipeline parallelism
data parallelism
distributed serving
GPU communication
replicas and routing
At this point, the infrastructure picture starts becoming much clearer.
But something important still feels confusing.
Even after building massive GPU clusters:

why does inference still become difficult?
why do GPUs sometimes remain underutilized?
why is generation much harder than prompt processing?
and why do modern systems focus so heavily on schedulers and batching?
The answer starts with understanding two runtime phases:

Prefill
and
Decode
These two phases behave very differently.
And honestly, this becomes one of the most important mental models in inference systems.
What is prefill?
Suppose a user sends:
"Explain quantum computing in simple terms"
Before the model can generate the first output token, it must first process the entire prompt.
That initial processing phase is called:
Prefill
During prefill:

prompt tokens move through all transformer layers
attention is computed
activations are generated
KV cache entries are created
So prefill is essentially:
building the initial context
before generation starts.
Why is it called prefill?
Because during this phase, the KV cache gets filled.
Example:

Prompt Tokens:
[T1, T2, T3, T4]
During prefill:

T1 → KV stored
T2 → KV stored
T3 → KV stored
T4 → KV stored
The cache becomes populated before decoding begins.
That is where the name comes from.
Why is prefill highly parallel?
This is extremely important.
During prefill:
all prompt tokens already exist
Example:
So GPUs can process many computations simultaneously.
This creates:

large matrix multiplications
high tensor core utilization
efficient batching
strong GPU utilization
This is why prefill is usually:
compute heavy
The GPUs are busy doing large amounts of parallel computation.
What happens after prefill?
Once KV cache exists:

token generation starts
the model begins generating one token at a time
This phase is called:
Decode
Example:

Token 1
→ Token 2
→ Token 3
And this phase behaves VERY differently.
Why is decode different?
Because generation is sequential.
The model cannot generate:

token 2 before
token 1 exists
So unlike prefill:
future tokens do not exist yet
This changes the entire runtime behavior.
Why does decode become difficult?
During decode:

only one new token is processed at a time
matrix multiplications become much smaller
GPU parallelism drops
synchronization overhead becomes more visible
So decode often becomes:
memory + latency heavy
instead of compute heavy.
This is one of the biggest transitions in inference systems.
How does tensor parallelism behave during prefill?
Suppose one layer is split across 4 GPUs.
Example:

GPU 1 → partial tensor
GPU 2 → partial tensor
GPU 3 → partial tensor
GPU 4 → partial tensor
During prefill:

many tokens are processed together
GPUs stay busy
large computations happen
communication overhead is relatively small compared to compute
Tensor parallelism works efficiently here.
What changes during decode?
During decode:

tensor parallel GPUs still cooperate
synchronization still happens
outputs still combine
But now:

only one token is processed
computation becomes smaller
communication overhead becomes more noticeable
So decode starts exposing:

synchronization costs
communication latency
memory bottlenecks
much more clearly.
How does pipeline parallelism behave during prefill?
Suppose we divide the model like this:

Stage 1 → Layers 1–20
Stage 2 → Layers 21–40
Stage 3 → Layers 41–60
Stage 4 → Layers 61–80
During prefill:

many prompt tokens flow through the pipeline
stages continuously receive work
GPUs remain busy
Example:

Time 1:
Stage 1 → Tokens 1–250

Time 2:
Stage 1 → Tokens 251–500
Stage 2 → Tokens 1–250

Time 3:
Stage 1 → Tokens 501–750
Stage 2 → Tokens 251–500
Stage 3 → Tokens 1–250
Eventually:

all stages stay active
the pipeline stays full
This creates good utilization.
What changes during decode?
Now decode starts.
Instead of processing:
hundreds of prompt tokens together
the system processes:
ONE token at a time
Now look at the pipeline carefully.
Decode Pipeline Example
Time 1

Stage 1 → working
Stage 2 → idle
Stage 3 → idle
Stage 4 → idle
Time 2

Stage 1 → idle
Stage 2 → working
Stage 3 → idle
Stage 4 → idle
Time 3

Stage 1 → idle
Stage 2 → idle
Stage 3 → working
Stage 4 → idle
Time 4

Stage 1 → idle
Stage 2 → idle
Stage 3 → idle
Stage 4 → working
Now something important becomes visible.
Most GPUs are waiting most of the time.
This is underutilization.
Why does this happen?
Because pipeline parallelism wants:
a continuous stream of work
Prefill provides that.
Decode naturally does not.
This creates:
pipeline bubbles
meaning:

some stages remain empty
GPUs sit idle
hardware utilization drops
Does data parallelism help here?
Yes.
Remember:

one replica contains the full distributed model
multiple replicas exist independently
Example:

Replica 1
Replica 2
Replica 3
During decode:

different users stay attached to different replicas
each replica maintains its own KV cache
decode loops continue independently
This helps increase overall throughput.
But inside each replica:
decode still remains sequential
So the challenge still exists.
Why is scheduler design so important then?
Because inference systems try extremely hard to:

keep GPUs busy
reduce idle time
continuously refill batches
overlap decode requests efficiently
This is why modern systems heavily focus on:

continuous batching
request schedulers
KV cache management
paged attention
speculative decoding
Most of these optimizations exist because:
decode naturally fights GPU efficiency
What is the key mental model?
Prefill:

Large parallel computation
High GPU utilization
Compute heavy
Decode:

Sequential token generation
Smaller workloads
Communication + memory sensitive
And this difference changes almost everything about inference system design.
What is the deeper intuition here?
At first, inference systems look like:
GPUs doing matrix multiplications
But once decode becomes clear, the mental model starts shifting toward:
distributed runtime scheduling systems
Because now the challenge is no longer only:
running the model
It becomes:

keeping GPUs utilized
coordinating requests efficiently
managing KV cache
minimizing waiting
balancing latency vs throughput
And honestly, this is where inference systems start becoming much harder than they initially appear.
What comes next?
Now that we understand:

prefill
decode
why decode becomes sequential
why GPU utilization drops
why batching becomes difficult
the next natural question becomes:

How do modern systems
keep GPUs busy during decode?
This leads directly into one of the most important concepts in modern inference systems:
Continuous Batching
Because continuous batching is essentially an attempt to solve:

decode inefficiency
idle GPUs
and pipeline bubbles
And once that clicks, systems like:

vLLM
paged attention
advanced schedulers
start making much more intuitive sense.

title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding Prefill vs Decode

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 11)
Understanding Continuous Batching
In the previous part, we explored one of the most important runtime ideas in inference systems:

Prefill
vs
Decode

Prefill is highly parallel. Decode is sequential. During prefill, the model processes many prompt tokens together. This creates large matrix operations and keeps GPUs busy. But during decode, the model generates one token at a time. That creates a very different problem. Even if we have powerful GPUs, tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, replicas, and high-speed networking, the system can still struggle because decode does not naturally give the GPU enough work. So the next question becomes:

How do modern inference systems
keep GPUs busy during decode?
This leads us to:
Continuous Batching
Continuous batching is one of the key ideas behind modern LLM serving systems.
Why do we need batching again?
Before understanding continuous batching, let us quickly revisit batching. Suppose one user sends a request:
Request A
If we run only this one request on a GPU, the GPU may not be fully utilized. So instead, the system groups multiple requests together. Example:
Batch = [Request A, Request B, Request C, Request D]
Now the GPU processes them together. This improves throughput because GPUs are much better at handling larger parallel workloads. So batching helps us turn:
many small jobs
into:
one larger GPU job
What is traditional batching?
In traditional batching, the system waits for a group of requests. Example:

Request A
Request B
Request C
Request D
Then it forms a batch:
Batch 1 = [A, B, C, D]
Then the system runs this batch. The simple mental model is:

collect requests
run batch
finish batch
start next batch
This works reasonably well when all requests are similar. But LLM inference requests are not similar.
Why are LLM requests different?
In LLM inference, every request can be different. One user may send a short prompt:
"Summarize this paragraph"
Another user may send a long prompt:
"Analyze this long document"
One user may ask for a short answer. Another user may ask for a long explanation. So requests differ in:

prompt length
output length
arrival time
stopping point
memory usage
This makes batching much harder.
What goes wrong with traditional batching?
Suppose we create a batch like this:
Batch = [A, B, C, D]

Now each request starts generating tokens. But maybe Request A only needs 5 output tokens. Request B needs 20 output tokens. Request C needs 50 output tokens. Request D needs 100 output tokens. So they finish at different times. Example:

A finishes early
B finishes later
C keeps going
D keeps going much longer
Now what should the system do? In a naive batching system, the batch may stay tied together until the slowest request finishes. That means some slots become wasted.
What does a wasted slot mean?
Imagine the batch has 4 slots:
[A, B, C, D]
After some decode steps, Request A finishes. Now the batch looks like:
[empty, B, C, D]
The system is still running decode steps. But one slot is empty. Later, Request B finishes:
[empty, empty, C, D]
Now half the batch is empty. The GPU is still doing work, but less efficiently. This is the core problem. Static batches become less useful as requests finish at different times.
Why is this especially bad during decode?
Decode already has small workloads because generation happens one token at a time. So if the batch also becomes smaller over time, the problem becomes worse. The system now has:

small decode work
+
shrinking batch
That is bad for GPU utilization. The GPU wants large parallel work. But decode gives it small sequential work. And static batching makes that work shrink even more. The batch starts full:
[A, B, C, D]
Then becomes:
[empty, B, C, D]
Then:
[empty, empty, C, D]
Then:
[empty, empty, empty, D]
At the end, we are almost back to serving one request. That is exactly what batching was supposed to avoid.
What does continuous batching change?

Continuous batching changes the batch while generation is happening. Instead of waiting for the entire batch to finish, the scheduler updates the batch continuously. When one request finishes, it leaves. When a new request is waiting, it enters. So the batch is not fixed. It is dynamic.
What does that look like?
Suppose we start with:
Batch = [A, B, C, D]
After a few decode steps, Request A finishes. Instead of leaving that slot empty, the scheduler inserts a new request.
Batch = [E, B, C, D]
Later, Request B finishes. Another request enters.
Batch = [E, F, C, D]
Then Request C finishes.
Batch = [E, F, G, D]
So the batch keeps changing. The GPU keeps receiving useful work. That is continuous batching.
What is the key idea?
Traditional batching works like this:

create batch
run until batch is done
start next batch
Continuous batching works like this:

run one decode step
remove finished requests
add waiting requests
run next decode step
repeat
The batch is updated during generation. This is why continuous batching is also often described as:
iteration-level scheduling
Because the scheduler makes decisions at the level of each generation step.
What is a decode iteration?
A decode iteration is one step of token generation. For active requests, the model generates the next token. Example:

Step 1 → generate next token
Step 2 → generate next token
Step 3 → generate next token
Each step updates the KV cache and produces the next token for each active request. With continuous batching, the scheduler can adjust the active batch between these steps.
What does the scheduler do?
The scheduler constantly decides:

Which requests should run now?
Which requests are finished?
Which new requests can enter?
Is there enough KV cache memory?
How large should the active batch be?
So the scheduler is not just forming batches once. It is managing the batch continuously. This is why modern inference systems are deeply scheduler-driven.
Why not just run every request immediately?

At first, it may seem like the best system should run every request as soon as it arrives. But this creates another problem. If the system runs very small batches immediately, throughput decreases. Why? Because every decode step has overhead. The system still needs to:

launch GPU work
read model weights
read KV cache
run attention
run matrix operations
synchronize GPUs
write updated KV cache
If the batch is very small, all of that overhead is paid for only a few tokens. Example:
Batch = [A]
The GPU is doing a full decode step, but only one request gets one token. Now compare that with:
Batch = [A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H]

The system still runs a decode step, but now many requests each receive a token. So the overhead is spread across more useful work. That is why very small batches often have poor throughput. The GPU may be active, but not efficiently used.
What does throughput mean here?
Throughput means how much useful work the system completes over time. For LLM serving, this is often measured as:
tokens per second

If the system runs one tiny batch immediately, latency for that one request may look good. But total tokens per second may be low. If the system waits a little and forms a larger batch, total tokens per second may improve. But users may wait longer before their request starts. So the system is constantly balancing:

latency
vs
throughput
Why does batching improve throughput?

Batching improves throughput because GPUs are designed for parallel computation. A GPU does not want to do a tiny amount of work. It wants large tensor operations. With a larger batch, the GPU can process more tokens together. That usually means:

better GPU utilization
more tokens per second
lower cost per token
But the system cannot wait forever to build a large batch. If it waits too long, user latency becomes bad. So the scheduler must find a balance.
What is the latency-throughput tradeoff?
If the scheduler runs requests immediately:

low waiting time
small batch
lower throughput
If the scheduler waits to collect more requests:

larger batch
higher throughput
more waiting time

Continuous batching helps because new requests do not always need to wait for a full old batch to finish. They can enter between decode steps. So continuous batching gives the system a better way to balance:

keep users moving
while also keeping GPUs busy
Does continuous batching reduce latency?

It can help, but it is not magic. Continuous batching can reduce unnecessary waiting because new requests may enter as soon as there is room. In a traditional system, a new request might wait until the entire current batch finishes. Example:

Current batch still running
New request waits
With continuous batching:

Decode step finishes
Request A leaves
Request E enters
Next decode step begins

This can reduce queueing delay. But the scheduler still needs to be careful. If it admits too many requests, active users may slow down. If it admits too few requests, GPU utilization may drop. So continuous batching improves flexibility, but scheduling is still a tradeoff.
Does every new request enter immediately?
Not always. The scheduler still considers:

available KV cache
current batch size
prompt length
decode workload
latency targets
fairness

A long prompt may require expensive prefill before it can join decode. A short request may be easier to admit. A system may also limit how many new requests enter at once to avoid hurting active users. So continuous batching is not simply:
add every request immediately
It is more like:

carefully admit requests
while keeping the system efficient
How does prefill interact with continuous batching?
A new request usually starts with prefill. The prompt must be processed first. Only after prefill does the request enter the decode loop. So there are two kinds of work:

prefill work
decode work

Prefill can be large and compute-heavy. Decode is smaller and repeated many times. A scheduler must decide how to mix them. If too much prefill is admitted at once, active decode requests may slow down. If decode is always prioritized, new requests may wait too long before their first token. So the scheduler must balance:

time to first token
vs
ongoing token generation speed
What is time to first token?
Time to first token means:

how long the user waits
before seeing the first generated token

This depends heavily on prefill. If the prompt is long, prefill takes longer. If the system queue is busy, the request waits longer. So continuous batching is not only about total throughput. It also affects perceived responsiveness.
What is token generation latency?
After the first token appears, the user cares about how quickly the remaining tokens stream. This is related to decode speed. So there are two user-facing latency experiences:
waiting for the first token
and:
waiting between generated tokens

Continuous batching affects both. If the scheduler is too aggressive, each request may wait longer between decode steps. If it is too conservative, GPU utilization may drop. This is why scheduling is such an important part of inference systems.
Why does KV cache matter here?

Every active request needs KV cache. When a request enters the batch, the system must allocate KV cache memory for it. When a request finishes, its KV cache can be freed. So continuous batching is not just about compute. It is also about memory management. The scheduler cannot simply add unlimited requests. It must check:

Do we have enough KV cache space?
Can this request fit?
How many tokens might it generate?
Will adding this request hurt latency?
This is where continuous batching starts connecting directly to paged attention.
Why does continuous batching make memory harder?
Because requests are constantly entering and leaving. That means KV cache memory is constantly changing. Example:

Request A enters → allocate KV cache
Request B enters → allocate KV cache
Request A finishes → free KV cache
