Request C enters → allocate KV cache
Request D grows → allocate more KV cache
This creates a dynamic memory problem. The system needs to manage many growing and shrinking sequences efficiently. If memory management is poor, we get:

fragmentation
wasted memory
failed allocations
lower batch size
lower throughput
So continuous batching improves GPU utilization, but it also increases the importance of KV cache management.
Why does this lead to PagedAttention?

Once batches become dynamic, KV cache memory becomes harder to manage. Requests have different lengths. They grow token by token. They finish at different times. Their memory needs change continuously. So the system needs a smarter way to store and reuse KV cache memory. This is where PagedAttention becomes important. The rough connection is:

Continuous batching
keeps the GPU busy

PagedAttention
helps manage KV cache memory efficiently
while batches change dynamically
That is why these two ideas often appear together in modern serving systems.
How does continuous batching help decode?
Decode is inefficient because each request generates only one token at a time. But if we have many active requests, we can decode one token for many requests together. Example:

A → next token
B → next token
C → next token
D → next token
This gives the GPU more useful work. Continuous batching tries to keep this active set full. So instead of decode looking like:
one request generating one token
it becomes:
many requests generating one token each
This is much better for throughput.
What does this look like inside a serving system?
At a high level:

Waiting Queue
    ↓
Scheduler
    ↓
Active Batch
    ↓
GPU Decode Step
    ↓
Finished requests leave
    ↓
New requests enter
    ↓
Repeat
The active batch is constantly changing. The scheduler keeps checking:

Who is waiting?
Who is active?
Who finished?
Who needs memory?
Who should run next?
This loop is the heart of continuous batching.
How is this different from normal backend batching?
In normal backend systems, batching often means:

collect similar requests
process them together
return results
But LLM generation is different because requests are long-running. A request does not finish after one forward pass. It may need:

10 decode steps
50 decode steps
500 decode steps
So batching must happen across time. That is the key difference. Continuous batching is designed for long-running generation.
What is the simplest intuition?
Imagine a bus. Traditional batching is like:

fill the bus
drive until every passenger reaches their destination
only then pick up new passengers
That is inefficient. Some passengers get off early, but their seats stay empty. Continuous batching is like:

passengers get off at each stop
new passengers get on
the bus keeps moving
The bus stays full more often. That is the intuition.
What is the GPU version of this?
The GPU does not want empty seats. The batch is the bus. Requests are passengers. Finished requests leave. New requests enter. The scheduler keeps the bus full. That is continuous batching.
What problem does it solve?
Continuous batching mainly helps solve:
decode underutilization
During decode, each request gives only a small amount of work. So the system needs many active requests to keep the GPU busy. Continuous batching helps maintain that active set.
What problem does it not solve?

Continuous batching does not remove the sequential nature of generation. The model still generates one token at a time. Token 2 still depends on token 1. Token 3 still depends on token 2. So continuous batching does not make one request magically parallel across future tokens. Instead, it improves system-level efficiency by batching many users together. The key distinction is:

Single request generation is still sequential.

Many requests can be scheduled together efficiently.
How does this connect to replicas?
Each replica usually has its own scheduler. Example:

Replica 1 → Scheduler 1 → Active batch
Replica 2 → Scheduler 2 → Active batch
Replica 3 → Scheduler 3 → Active batch

The router sends requests to replicas. Then each replica manages its own continuous batching loop. This means batching happens inside each serving replica. The router balances traffic across replicas. The scheduler balances work inside a replica.
Why can’t we freely move requests between replicas?

Because each request has KV cache stored inside its assigned replica. If a request moves to another replica, its KV cache would also need to move. That is expensive. So once a request starts generating, it usually stays on the same replica. This is why earlier we talked about:

sticky sessions
or
session affinity
Continuous batching works within that constraint.
What does continuous batching optimize for?
It tries to improve:

GPU utilization
throughput
queue waiting time
decode efficiency
batch occupancy
But it must also protect:

latency
fairness
memory safety
user experience
So the scheduler is constantly making tradeoffs.
Why is this harder than it sounds?

Because every request is different. Some requests have long prompts. Some have short prompts. Some generate short outputs. Some generate very long outputs. Some arrive during quiet periods. Some arrive during traffic spikes. Some need streaming responses. Some may stop early. Some may hit max token limits. So the scheduler is managing a moving target. There is no single fixed batch. There is only a constantly changing set of active sequences.
What is the key mental model?
Traditional batching:

Batch is fixed.
Requests enter together.
Requests leave together.
Continuous batching:

Batch is dynamic.
Requests enter when there is room.
Requests leave when they finish.
That is the core idea.
Why is continuous batching so important?

Because decode is where inference systems often struggle. Prefill gives the GPU large parallel work. Decode gives the GPU small repeated work. Continuous batching helps convert many small decode steps into one larger repeated workload. So instead of thinking:
one user generating tokens
we should think:
many users advancing one token at a time together
That is much closer to how modern serving systems keep GPUs busy.
What does this teach us about inference systems?
At this point, inference starts looking less like a simple model call. It looks more like a runtime scheduling problem. The system is constantly asking:

Which requests should run now?
How much memory do they need?
How do we keep the GPU busy?
How do we avoid making users wait too long?
How do we handle requests finishing at different times?
This is why scheduler design is such a central part of modern LLM serving.
What comes next?

Now we understand why continuous batching matters. It keeps the active batch full during decode by allowing requests to enter and leave dynamically. But this creates another major problem. If requests are constantly entering, growing, and leaving, then KV cache memory becomes difficult to manage efficiently. The system needs a way to store KV cache without wasting huge amounts of GPU memory. That leads directly to one of the most important ideas in vLLM:
PagedAttention
In the next part, we will explore:

why KV cache memory becomes fragmented
why fixed allocation wastes memory
how paging helps
why PagedAttention is similar to virtual memory
how it works together with continuous batching
Because continuous batching keeps the compute side busy. PagedAttention helps make the memory side efficient.

title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding Continuous Batching

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges: The Best Model Router May Not Be the Best Conversation Router
I have been writing about routing at different layers of LLM inference: routing requests to the right replica, routing based on KV cache locality, and now routing across models or providers.
They sound similar, but they solve different problems.

An inference router may decide where a request should run so that it gets the best latency, capacity, or cache reuse. A model router may decide which model should answer based on quality, cost, capability, or availability.
Both decisions influence the final user experience.

But there is an important complication when the application is conversational: the next user message is not always a completely new request. It may be continuing computation that the system has already paid for.
That is where model routing becomes much more than choosing the cheapest or most capable model for a prompt.
The simple routing mental model
At first, model routing feels straightforward:
A request arrives, the router selects the best model, and the model generates a response.
This works well for independent requests.

For example, a router could send a coding task to one model, a short summary to a smaller model, and a complex reasoning task to another. If every request starts fresh, the router has considerable freedom to optimize each decision.
But a multi-turn conversation changes the unit of work.

Imagine that a user has already shared a long document, several code snippets, and detailed instructions with an assistant. The first turn is handled by a larger model. On the next turn, the user asks:
Can you make the introduction shorter?
A stateless model router may decide that a smaller, less expensive model is enough for this specific task.
That sounds efficient. But the smaller model has not processed the earlier conversation. It does not have the work already completed by the first model.
It has to start again.
KV cache is where the earlier work lives
During prefill, the model processes the input prompt and creates attention keys and values for the tokens it has already seen. This is the KV cache.

When the model continues generating, it can reuse that cached state instead of recalculating attention over the entire prior context. This is one reason a warm continuation can respond much faster than a cold request with the same conversation history.
The important detail is that KV cache is not a universal conversation cache.
In most serving environments, it is tied to:

The exact model and model version
The model architecture and configuration
The token sequence and positional state
Often, the specific replica or GPU that processed the request
A cache created by one model cannot normally be reused by a different model. Even if the next request goes to the same model, the cache may not be available if it lands on a different replica.

Some inference systems can transfer or externalize KV cache, which is useful. But that introduces its own trade-offs: network movement, memory management, cache lookup, scheduling, and failure handling.
So a model-routing decision can turn a warm continuation into a cold prefill.
Request routing versus conversation routing
This distinction helped me think about model routing more clearly.
Request routing asks:
Which model is best for this input?
Conversation routing asks:
Where should this turn go, considering the state and computation already created by earlier turns?
The first question is important for independent workloads. The second becomes important when a user is working through a longer interaction.
This does not mean model routing is a bad idea for chat applications. It means the router needs more context than only the current prompt.
If it optimizes each turn independently, it may accidentally create:

Repeated prefill work
Higher time to first token
Higher token cost
More variable latency across a conversation
Different response style or behavior between turns
Session affinity helps, but it creates another trade-off
One answer is session affinity.
Instead of treating every request as independent, the system tries to send follow-up turns from the same conversation back to the model or replica that handled the earlier turn.
There are two useful ways to think about this:

Model affinity keeps the conversation on the same model.
Replica affinity keeps the conversation on the same model instance or replica, where its KV cache is more likely to be local.
Replica affinity can reduce repeated prefill work and improve time to first token. But it also makes load balancing harder.

A very active conversation may continue to send work to one replica while other replicas have capacity. And if that replica fails, its local cache may disappear, forcing the conversation to move and start cold anyway.
So affinity is not simply something to enable everywhere. It is a routing policy with real benefits and costs.
Cache-aware routing adds another signal
A cache-aware router does not only ask which model has the right capability. It also considers where useful context may already exist.
Its decision can include:

Model quality for the task
Queue time and available capacity
Cost per request or token
Cache residency or prefix-cache hit probability
Session ownership
Latency targets
Whether the request is new work or a continuation
These signals will not always agree.
The best model for a task may be overloaded. The least busy replica may not have the cache. The cheapest model may require a full prefill of a very long conversation.
That means the best model-selection decision is not always the best end-to-end routing decision.
Different workload shapes need different policies

A one-shot RAG question can often benefit from flexible per-request routing. The retrieved context may be different for every question, and the router can optimize for task complexity, latency, or cost.

But a multi-turn RAG assistant is different. If the user keeps asking follow-up questions about the same documents, preserving the active context may matter more than selecting a new model for every turn.
The same is true for agentic systems.

A planning conversation may benefit from affinity because it builds on earlier reasoning and context. An isolated classification, extraction, or tool-use step may be safe to route independently to a smaller specialized model.
So the important question is not whether something is “RAG,” “chat,” or “an agent.”
The real question is:
Does this request depend on state that the system has already paid to compute?
A hybrid approach is probably the practical answer
A fully stateless router has maximum flexibility, but it can lose useful cache locality. Permanent stickiness preserves context, but it can reduce load-balancing flexibility.
A hybrid policy feels more realistic.
For example, a system could:

Select the best model for the first turn.
Prefer the same model or replica for follow-up turns.
Use cache locality as a strong routing signal, not an absolute rule.
Reroute when there is a failure, overload, context reset, task change, or a meaningful quality requirement.
This preserves the value of model routing without assuming that every request begins from zero.

It also makes conversation boundaries important. A user moving to a completely different task may be a good point to reconsider the model. A user asking another question about the same document or codebase may be a reason to preserve affinity.
What should we measure?
If a router is making cache-aware decisions, raw throughput is not enough.
I would want to measure:

Time to first token for warm versus cold turns
Prefill tokens recomputed per conversation
Cache-hit and cache-transfer rates
P95 latency as conversations become longer
Session migration rate
Load imbalance across replicas
Goodput: how many requests actually meet the intended latency target
A routing policy can look efficient in tokens per second but still produce a poor user experience if it repeatedly turns warm conversations into cold requests.

That is where goodput becomes more useful than raw throughput. The system is not successful only because it generated many tokens. It is successful when it delivers useful responses within the experience users expect.
The routing decision influences everything after it
This topic changed how I think about model routing.
A router is not simply choosing a model. It is influencing the rest of the inference path:

Whether prefill work is reused or repeated
Where KV cache needs to live
How evenly replicas can be loaded
How much tail latency a conversation experiences
Whether the system optimizes one request or the full interaction
The first question for a router should not always be:
Which model should answer this request?
Sometimes it should be:
Is this request continuing work that the system has already done?
The best model router may not be the best conversation router.
And the best inference system may be the one that knows when not to forget the computation it has already paid for.

title: The Best Model Router May Not Be the Best Conversation Router

blocks.text: Over the last few weeks, I’ve been exploring how modern LLM inference systems actually work internally.
What started with a simple question around KV cache slowly expanded into:

batching
GPU memory
multi-GPU inference
distributed serving
replicas
GPU communication
and finally runtime behavior during generation
While writing these articles, I noticed something interesting myself.
Many concepts keep reappearing:

KV cache
batching
parallelism
replicas
scheduling
GPU communication
At first I thought I was repeating things too much.
But over time I realized something: these concepts keep reappearing because modern inference systems themselves are deeply interconnected.
So before moving into:

vLLM internals
paged attention
continuous batching
advanced schedulers
I wanted to take one step back and review the foundation we have built so far.
Part 1 — Understanding KV Cache
We started with one of the most important concepts in inference systems: KV cache.
This article explored:

why transformers repeatedly recompute attention
how KV cache avoids redundant computation
why generation becomes faster after caching
and how memory usage grows during inference
This became the starting point for understanding why inference systems are fundamentally memory-sensitive systems.
Understanding KV Cache
Part 2 — Memory Challenges During Inference
After understanding KV cache, the next question became: what happens when memory usage keeps growing?
This article explored:

memory fragmentation
duplication
dynamic allocation problems
why serving systems struggle with memory efficiency
and why inference becomes difficult at scale
This was also where the connection between user concurrency and memory pressure started becoming visible.
Memory Challenges During Inference
Part 3 — GPU Utilization & Batching
This article focused on one core idea: GPUs are efficient only when we keep them busy.
We explored:

why single requests underutilize GPUs
how batching improves throughput
why requests are grouped together
and how serving systems try to maximize utilization
This became the foundation for understanding scheduling later.
GPU Utilization & Batching
Part 4 — Why We Need Multiple GPUs
At this stage, one question became unavoidable: why is one GPU not enough anymore?
This article explored:

model size vs GPU memory
what parameters and weights actually are
why large models cannot fit into one GPU
and why throughput requirements also force distributed systems
This was the transition point into multi-GPU inference.
Why We Need Multiple GPUs
Part 5 — Understanding Tensor Parallelism
Once we understood why one GPU is insufficient, the next step was understanding how models are split across GPUs.
This article explored:

what tensors actually are
how weights are represented as tensors
how tensor parallelism splits tensors across GPUs
and how multiple GPUs cooperate on the same layer computation
This introduced the idea that one layer itself may require many GPUs working together.
Understanding Tensor Parallelism
Part 6 — Understanding Pipeline Parallelism
After tensor parallelism, the next question became: what if even splitting tensors is not enough?
This article explored:

splitting transformer layers into stages
how activations move through pipeline stages
why pipeline bubbles happen
and how tensor + pipeline parallelism work together in real systems
This was where the inference system started feeling much more like distributed infrastructure.
Understanding Pipeline Parallelism
Part 7 — Understanding Data Parallelism
At this point, the infrastructure picture became much larger.
This article explored:

how entire model replicas are duplicated
why data parallelism scales concurrent users
how replicas maintain independent KV cache
and how tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism combine together
This article also connected all three forms of parallelism into one complete mental model.
Understanding Data Parallelism
Part 8 — Distributed Serving & Request Routing
Once replicas were clear, the next question became: how are requests actually managed?
This article explored:

load balancers
routers
request scheduling
session affinity
distributed serving systems
and what a “replica” physically means
This was the point where the mental model started shifting from: “running a model”
to:
“operating a distributed GPU system.”
Distributed Serving & Request Routing
Part 9 — GPU Communication & Networking
As systems scaled across many GPUs and servers, communication itself became a major topic.
This article explored:

NVLink
NVSwitch
InfiniBand
NCCL
inter-node communication
all-reduce operations
and why networking becomes critical in large inference systems
This was also where replicas started feeling less like servers and more like distributed supercomputing systems.
GPU Communication & Networking
Part 10 — Understanding Prefill vs Decode
This article became one of the most important runtime concepts so far.
We explored:

why prompt processing is highly parallel
why generation becomes sequential
why decode underutilizes GPUs
why pipeline bubbles appear
and why scheduler design becomes so important
This article connected almost everything learned earlier:

batching
KV cache
replicas
tensor parallelism
pipeline parallelism
and distributed serving
into one runtime mental model.
Understanding Prefill vs Decode
What Comes Next?
At this point, the foundation feels much stronger.
We now understand:

how requests flow
how GPUs cooperate
how replicas scale
how communication happens
and why inference systems become difficult during decode
The next stage will focus much more on:

vLLM architecture
continuous batching
paged attention
scheduler design
and modern inference optimizations
And honestly, this is where inference systems start becoming even more interesting.

title: LLM Inference Challenges — Building the Mental Model for Modern Inference Systems

blocks.text: In the previous part, we explored continuous batching.
The main idea was:

Traditional batching:
Batch is fixed.

Continuous batching:
Batch keeps changing.
Requests enter. Requests leave. Some finish early. Some continue generating. New requests join between decode steps.
This helps keep GPUs busy during decode.But it also creates another problem.If the active batch is constantly changing, then the KV cache memory is also constantly changing.
That leads us to one of the most important ideas in modern LLM serving systems:
PagedAttention
PagedAttention is one of the core ideas behind vLLM. It helps manage KV cache memory more efficiently by using an idea similar to paging in operating systems.
The simple connection is:

Continuous batching
keeps the compute side busy.

PagedAttention
keeps the memory side efficient.
Why does KV cache memory become difficult?
During generation, every token creates key and value tensors. These are stored in the KV cache so the model does not need to recompute previous attention information again.
For one request, the KV cache grows like this:

Prompt processed → KV cache created
Token 1 generated → KV cache grows
Token 2 generated → KV cache grows
Token 3 generated → KV cache grows
Now imagine many requests running together:

Request A → 100 tokens
Request B → 500 tokens
Request C → 50 tokens
Request D → 2000 tokens
Each request has its own KV cache.
Each request grows at a different speed.
Each request finishes at a different time.
This is already difficult. Continuous batching makes it even more dynamic.
Why continuous batching makes memory harder
With continuous batching, the active batch changes during generation.
Example:

Step 1:
Batch = [A, B, C, D]

Step 2:
A finishes
E enters

Batch = [E, B, C, D]

Step 3:
C finishes
F enters

Batch = [E, B, F, D]
This is great for GPU utilization.
But memory management now becomes more complicated.
The system constantly needs to:

allocate KV cache
extend KV cache
free KV cache
reuse KV cache
So the system is not only scheduling compute.
It is also continuously managing GPU memory.
Why not reserve memory upfront?
A simple strategy would be:
Give each request one large memory region.
For example:

Request A → space for 2048 tokens
Request B → space for 2048 tokens
Request C → space for 2048 tokens
This sounds simple, but it wastes a lot of memory.Suppose Request A only generates 100 tokens.Then we reserved space for 2048 tokens, but used only 100.

Reserved:
2048 token slots

Used:
100 token slots

Wasted:
1948 token slots
That is expensive because GPU memory is limited.
And during inference, memory is not only used for model weights. It is also used for KV cache, activations, and active requests.
If KV cache memory is wasted, fewer requests can fit in the active batch.
That directly hurts throughput.
Why not allocate exactly what each request needs?
Because we usually do not know the final length in advance.
One user may ask for a short answer.
Another user may ask for a long explanation.
Some requests stop early.
Some reach the max token limit.
Some continue generating for a long time.
So when a request starts, the system does not always know how much KV cache memory it will eventually need.
What if memory grows dynamically?
That sounds better.
Start small, then allocate more memory as the request grows.
Example:

Request A starts → allocate memory
Request A generates more tokens → allocate more memory
Request A keeps going → allocate more memory
But this can create another problem:
fragmentation
GPU memory may start looking like this:
[A][A][B][free][C][A][free][D][C]
There is free memory.
But it is scattered.
So the system may have enough total free memory, but not enough usable continuous memory.
That is fragmentation.
Why fragmentation is bad for inference
KV cache memory controls how many active requests can fit on the GPU.
If memory becomes fragmented, the scheduler may not be able to admit new requests.
Example:

Waiting Queue:
[E, F, G, H]

GPU memory:
fragmented
The GPU may still have compute capacity.
But the system cannot add more requests because KV cache memory is not available in a useful form.
So throughput drops.
This is the core problem PagedAttention is trying to solve.
What is the key idea behind PagedAttention?
PagedAttention borrows an idea from operating systems.
In an operating system, a program may think it has one continuous memory space.
But physically, memory can be split into small pages.
The operating system maps:
virtual pages → physical pages
PagedAttention applies a similar idea to KV cache.
Instead of storing one request’s KV cache in one large continuous memory region, it splits the KV cache into smaller fixed-size blocks.
So the mapping becomes:
logical KV blocks → physical KV blocks
The request can still behave as if its KV cache is continuous.
But physically, those blocks can live in different places in GPU memory.
What does this look like?
Without paging, Request A may need one continuous region:

Request A:
[A A A A A A A A]
With PagedAttention, Request A can be split into blocks:

Request A logical view:
[A1][A2][A3][A4]
But physically, those blocks may be stored like this:

GPU memory:
[A1][B1][free][A3][C1][A2][A4]
The blocks are not next to each other.
That is okay.
The system keeps a mapping table that tells it where each logical block is stored physically.
This mapping is called a block table.
What is a block table?
A block table maps the logical order of a sequence to physical GPU memory blocks.
Example:

Request A logical blocks:

A0 → physical block 7
A1 → physical block 2
A2 → physical block 9
A3 → physical block 4
So the request sees:
But GPU memory may store them as:

Block 2 → A1
Block 4 → A3
Block 7 → A0
Block 9 → A2
The block table connects the logical sequence order with the actual physical memory locations.
This is the main trick.
PagedAttention separates:
logical KV cache order
from:
physical GPU memory layout
Why does this help?
Because now the system does not need one large continuous memory region for each request.
It can allocate small blocks as needed.
Example:

Request A starts:
allocate block A0

Request A grows:
allocate block A1

Request A grows more:
allocate block A2
The blocks can come from anywhere in the free block pool.
When the request finishes, its blocks are returned:

Request A finishes:

A0 → free
A1 → free
A2 → free
Now other requests can reuse those blocks.
This makes memory allocation and reuse much more flexible.
Why fixed-size blocks help
Fixed-size blocks simplify memory management.
Instead of handling many differently sized memory chunks:

small request memory
medium request memory
large request memory
very large request memory
the system mostly handles one unit:
KV cache block
This makes allocation easier.
It also makes freeing memory easier.
And because blocks do not need to be physically contiguous, fragmentation becomes much less harmful.
Is memory waste completely removed?
Not completely.
There can still be unused space in the last block.
Example:

Block size = 16 tokens
Request uses 35 tokens
Then:

Block 1 → 16 tokens used
Block 2 → 16 tokens used
Block 3 → 3 tokens used
The last block still has unused space.
But this is much better than reserving memory for thousands of tokens upfront.
So instead of wasting huge continuous memory regions, the waste is mostly limited to the final partially used block.
How does this work with continuous batching?
Continuous batching keeps changing the active batch.
PagedAttention makes that manageable.
Example:

A finishes → free A's blocks
E enters → allocate blocks to E
B grows → allocate one more block to B
C finishes → free C's blocks
F enters → allocate blocks to F
This is why continuous batching and PagedAttention fit together so naturally.
Continuous batching creates a dynamic scheduling problem.
PagedAttention provides a memory system that can handle that dynamism.
Does PagedAttention make attention computation cheaper?
Not exactly.
PagedAttention does not remove attention.
It does not remove autoregressive generation.
It does not make one request generate all future tokens in parallel.
The model still needs the KV cache.
The model still generates tokens one by one.
The main improvement is memory management.
So the key idea is not:
do less attention
The key idea is:
store and access KV cache more efficiently
Why does better memory usage improve throughput?
Throughput is not only limited by compute.
It is also limited by how many active requests can fit in memory.
If KV cache memory is wasted, the system may only fit a small active batch:
Active batch = [A, B, C]
If memory is managed efficiently, the system may fit more active requests:
Active batch = [A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H]
Now each decode step generates tokens for more users.
That usually means:

better GPU utilization
higher tokens per second
lower cost per token
So PagedAttention improves throughput indirectly by allowing the system to use GPU memory more efficiently.
What is the simplest analogy?
Imagine a notebook.
Without paging, every request needs a long continuous set of pages.
If the notebook has scattered empty pages, they may be hard to use.
With paging, each request can use any available page.
The index tells us the correct order.
Example:

Request A:
page 12 → page 3 → page 18 → page 7
The pages are scattered.
But the index makes them readable in order.
PagedAttention does something similar for KV cache.
The KV blocks are scattered.
The block table provides the order.
Why is this important for vLLM?
vLLM is strongly associated with PagedAttention because this memory-management idea is one of the reasons vLLM can serve LLMs efficiently.
Modern serving systems need to handle many active sequences at the same time.
Those sequences:

start at different times
grow token by token
finish at different times
need different amounts of memory
PagedAttention makes this easier by treating KV cache memory more like a paged memory system.
Instead of forcing each request into one large continuous region, it allows the system to allocate and reuse smaller blocks dynamically.
That is a powerful idea.
What is the key mental model?
Without PagedAttention:

KV cache needs large continuous memory.
Requests have unpredictable lengths.
Memory gets wasted or fragmented.
Batch size becomes limited.
Throughput suffers.
With PagedAttention:

KV cache is split into blocks.
Blocks can live anywhere in GPU memory.
Block tables preserve logical order.
Blocks are allocated on demand.
Finished requests return blocks to the pool.
That is the core idea.
What does PagedAttention not solve?
PagedAttention does not solve every inference problem.

It does not remove sequential decoding.
It does not eliminate the KV cache.
It does not replace scheduling.
It does not remove the need for batching.
It mainly improves how KV cache memory is:

allocated
stored
accessed
reused
shared
So the limitation is important:

PagedAttention improves memory efficiency.

It does not remove the fundamental
autoregressive generation loop.
Final intuition
Continuous batching answers:
How do we keep the active batch full during decode?
PagedAttention answers:

How do we store KV cache efficiently
while that active batch keeps changing?
Together:

Continuous batching:
dynamic compute scheduling

PagedAttention:
dynamic KV cache memory management
This is why these two ideas appear together so often in modern LLM serving systems.
At this point, inference starts looking less like a simple model call and more like a runtime system.
The system is constantly asking:

Which requests should run now?
How much KV cache memory do they need?
Can we admit more requests?
Which blocks are free?
Which requests have finished?
How do we keep GPUs busy without wasting memory?
That is why PagedAttention matters.It is not just a small implementation detail.
It is one of the ideas that makes high-throughput LLM serving practical.
What comes next?
Now that continuous batching and PagedAttention are clearer, the next natural step is to zoom out and understand how these ideas fit inside a real serving engine.
That leads directly to:
vLLM architecture
Because vLLM brings together:

scheduler
continuous batching
PagedAttention
KV cache block manager
prefill and decode execution
request lifecycle
So next, we can move from individual concepts to the bigger picture:
How does a real inference engine combine all of this?

title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding PagedAttention

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 13)
Understanding vLLM Architecture
In the previous parts, we explored two very important ideas:

Continuous Batching
and
PagedAttention
Continuous batching helped us understand how modern inference systems keep GPUs busy during decode.
PagedAttention helped us understand how KV cache memory can be managed efficiently while requests are constantly entering, growing, and leaving.
At this point, we understand the individual pieces better.
But one question still remains:

How does a real inference engine
combine all of this together?
That leads us to vLLM.
Why talk about vLLM now?
Until now, we have been mostly learning concepts one by one.
We explored:

KV cache
batching
prefill vs decode
continuous batching
PagedAttention
multi-GPU inference
request routing
GPU communication

These are all important. But in real systems, these ideas do not exist separately. They come together inside an inference engine. vLLM is one of the most important open-source examples of this. So this article is not about every detail inside vLLM. Instead, the goal is simpler:
Build a mental model of how vLLM works as a serving engine.
I want to understand where the major pieces fit before jumping into code.
What is vLLM?
At a high level, vLLM is an LLM inference and serving engine.
That means it helps run language models efficiently for real user requests.
A user sends a prompt.

vLLM receives it.
vLLM schedules it.
vLLM runs the model.
vLLM manages KV cache.
vLLM streams tokens back.
So instead of thinking of vLLM as only:
a library to run an LLM
I think it is better to view it as:
a runtime system for serving LLM requests efficiently
That word “runtime” is important. Because vLLM is not just executing one model call. It is continuously managing many requests at the same time.
What problem is vLLM trying to solve?
LLM inference is difficult because requests are dynamic.
One user may send a short prompt.
Another user may send a long prompt.
One request may generate 10 tokens.
Another may generate 1000 tokens.
Some requests finish early.
Some keep running.
Some are waiting.
Some are in prefill.
Some are in decode.
At the same time, the system must manage:

GPU memory
KV cache blocks
batching
scheduling
latency
throughput
token streaming
So vLLM is not only asking:
How do I run the model?
It is also asking:

Which requests should run now?
How much memory do they need?
Can more requests enter?
Which requests have finished?
How do we keep GPUs busy?
How do we avoid wasting KV cache memory?
This is why vLLM architecture matters.
What are the major pieces inside vLLM?
At a high level, we can think of vLLM as having a few major parts:

API Server
Request Queue
Engine Core
Scheduler
KV Cache Manager
Model Executor
GPU Workers
PagedAttention
Output Processor
This may sound like a lot.
But the flow is actually understandable if we follow one request.
What happens when a request arrives?
Suppose a user sends:
"Explain quantum computing in simple terms"
The request first reaches the serving layer. In vLLM, this is usually the API server. The API server is responsible for things like:

receiving the request
parsing the input
tokenizing the prompt
sending work to the engine
streaming generated tokens back
So the API server is the entry point. But the API server itself is not the main brain of inference scheduling. The request must move into the engine. A simple view looks like this:

User
 ↓
API Server
 ↓
Engine Core
 ↓
Scheduler
 ↓
GPU Workers
 ↓
Generated Tokens
What is the engine core?
The engine core is where the main inference loop lives.
This is where vLLM keeps track of active requests, waiting requests, scheduled work, KV cache usage, and model execution.
A useful mental model is:

API Server = receives and returns requests

Engine Core = decides how inference work runs
The engine core is not just passively forwarding requests. It is continuously making scheduling decisions.
It asks:

Which requests are waiting?
Which requests are already running?
Which requests need prefill?
Which requests are decoding?
Which requests finished?
How many tokens can we process now?
Is there enough KV cache memory?
This is where inference starts feeling like a runtime scheduling system.
What does the scheduler do?
The scheduler is one of the most important parts of vLLM. It decides which requests get executed in each step. Earlier, when we discussed continuous batching, we learned that batches are not fixed.

Requests enter.
Requests leave.
The active set keeps changing. The scheduler manages that process. A simple scheduler loop looks like this:

Check waiting requests
Check active requests
Check available KV cache
Choose what runs next
Send work to GPU workers
Receive outputs
Update request states
Repeat
This is why continuous batching belongs naturally inside vLLM.
The scheduler is the component that makes continuous batching practical.
How does this connect to prefill and decode?
Every request usually goes through two broad phases:

Prefill
Decode
During prefill, the prompt is processed. The system creates the initial KV cache for the prompt tokens.
Example:

Prompt tokens:
[T1, T2, T3, T4]

Prefill creates:
KV cache for T1, T2, T3, T4
After prefill, decode begins. During decode, the model generates one token at a time.
Example:

Decode step 1 → generate next token
Decode step 2 → generate next token
Decode step 3 → generate next token
The scheduler must manage both types of work. That is not trivial. Prefill can be large and compute-heavy. Decode is smaller, repeated, and latency-sensitive. So the scheduler must balance:
new requests waiting for first token
with:
active requests waiting for next token
This is where metrics like time to first token and inter-token latency start to make more sense.
Where does KV cache management happen?
Every active request needs KV cache. During prefill, vLLM creates KV cache entries for the prompt. During decode, vLLM appends new KV entries token by token. So memory must be managed continuously.
Example:

Request A enters → allocate KV cache
Request A prefills → store prompt KV
Request A decodes → append new KV
Request A finishes → free KV cache
But vLLM does not want to allocate one huge continuous memory region for every request. That would waste memory. This is where the KV cache manager and PagedAttention become important.
Where does PagedAttention fit?
PagedAttention is the memory idea behind efficient KV cache storage. Instead of storing each request’s KV cache as one large continuous block, the KV cache is divided into smaller blocks.
A request sees a logical sequence:

Token 1
Token 2
Token 3
Token 4
But physically, its KV cache blocks may live in different places in GPU memory.
Example:

Logical KV blocks:
[A0][A1][A2]

Physical memory:
[A1][B0][free][A0][C0][A2]

The system keeps track of where the blocks are. So the request can still use its KV cache correctly, even if the physical memory is not continuous. This is the bridge between Part 12 and vLLM architecture.
PagedAttention is not floating separately.
It supports the scheduler by making KV cache allocation more flexible.
Why does the scheduler need the KV cache manager?
The scheduler cannot simply admit every request. Before adding more work, it must know whether there is enough KV cache space.
For example:

Waiting requests:
E, F, G

Active requests:
A, B, C, D

Free KV blocks:
limited
The scheduler must ask:

Can E fit?
Can F fit?
Should G wait?
Do active requests need more blocks?
Did any request finish and free blocks?
So scheduling and memory management are tightly connected. This is a key idea.
In LLM inference, scheduling is not only about compute. It is also about memory.
What are GPU workers?
Eventually, the work must run on GPUs. That is where GPU workers come in.
A simple mental model is:

Engine Core
 ↓
GPU Workers
 ↓
Model Execution

The engine core decides what should run. The GPU workers execute model computation. They load model weights, run forward passes, and manage GPU-side execution. If there are multiple GPUs, vLLM may use distributed execution strategies such as tensor parallelism.
But for this article, the important idea is simple:

Scheduler decides the work.
GPU workers execute the work.
What happens during one inference step?
Let us simplify one engine step. Suppose the system currently has active requests:
A, B, C
And waiting requests:
D, E
The scheduler checks:

A needs next decode token
B needs next decode token
C needs next decode token
D needs prefill
E is waiting
It also checks memory:

Are KV cache blocks available?
Can D be admitted?
Can active requests continue?
Then it creates a plan for the next step.
Example:

Run decode for A, B, C
Run prefill chunk for D
Keep E waiting
Then the work is sent to GPU workers.

The model runs.
Outputs come back.
The scheduler updates states.
Example:

A generated one token
B generated one token
C finished
D completed part of prefill
C's KV blocks can be freed
E may enter next step
Then the loop continues. This is the heart of an inference engine.
How does continuous batching appear inside this loop?
Continuous batching means the active batch can change between generation steps.
In vLLM, this is naturally handled by the scheduler.
Example:

Step 1:
Active = [A, B, C, D]

Step 2:
C finishes
E enters

Active = [A, B, D, E]

Step 3:
A finishes
F enters

Active = [F, B, D, E]
The key idea is:

The batch is not frozen.
The scheduler keeps updating it.
This is why vLLM can keep GPUs more fully utilized.
It does not wait for an entire static batch to finish before admitting new work.
How does PagedAttention support this loop?
Continuous batching makes memory dynamic. PagedAttention makes dynamic memory easier to manage. Without PagedAttention, the system may struggle with:

fragmentation
over-allocation
wasted KV cache memory
limited active batch size
With PagedAttention, vLLM can allocate KV cache in smaller blocks. When a request grows, it gets more blocks. When a request finishes, its blocks return to the free pool. Example:

A finishes → free A's blocks
E enters → allocate blocks to E
B grows → allocate one more block to B
So the scheduler and memory manager work together. Continuous batching asks:
Can we add more useful work?
PagedAttention helps answer:
Do we have memory blocks available for that work?
What is the model executor?
The model executor is the part responsible for actually running the model computation.
The scheduler does not itself multiply matrices.
The KV cache manager does not itself generate tokens.
Those components decide what should happen and how memory should be organized.
The model executor runs the forward pass.
A simplified view:

Scheduler
 ↓
Model Executor
 ↓
GPU Workers
 ↓
Forward Pass
 ↓
Logits
 ↓
Sampling
 ↓
Next Token
After the model produces logits, vLLM still needs to choose the next token.
That may involve sampling settings like:

temperature
top-p
top-k
max tokens
stop conditions
Then the generated token is returned to the request state. If streaming is enabled, it can be sent back to the user.
What does the full request lifecycle look like?
Now we can connect the full flow.

User sends prompt
 ↓
API Server receives request
 ↓
Prompt is tokenized
 ↓
Request enters engine
 ↓
Scheduler decides when it runs
 ↓
KV cache blocks are allocated
 ↓
Prefill processes prompt
 ↓
Initial KV cache is created
 ↓
Request enters decode loop
 ↓
Continuous batching keeps active set full
 ↓
PagedAttention manages KV cache blocks
 ↓
GPU workers execute model forward passes
 ↓
Sampler selects next tokens
 ↓
Tokens stream back to user
 ↓
Request finishes
 ↓
KV cache blocks are freed
This is the mental model I wanted. vLLM is not one single trick. It is a system where many pieces work together.
Why is this architecture powerful?
The power comes from combining multiple optimizations into one runtime.

Continuous batching improves GPU utilization.
PagedAttention improves KV cache memory efficiency.
The scheduler coordinates active and waiting requests.
The KV cache manager tracks memory availability.
GPU workers execute the model efficiently.
The API server handles client-facing request and response flow.
Together, these pieces turn LLM inference into a managed runtime system.
That is very different from simply calling:
model.generate()
Why is this different from a simple inference script?
In a simple script, we may do:

load model
send prompt
generate output
return response
That is fine for learning. But production serving is different. A real serving system may have:

many users
many active requests
different prompt lengths
different output lengths
streaming responses
GPU memory limits
parallel GPUs
latency targets
throughput targets
So the problem becomes much larger than running one forward pass. The system must operate continuously. This is why vLLM feels more like an operating system for inference workloads.
It manages compute, memory, scheduling, and execution.
What should we not overcomplicate yet?
At this point, I do not want to dive too deeply into every internal class or source file. That will come later.
For now, the important mental model is:

API Server receives requests.
Engine Core manages inference.
Scheduler decides what runs.
KV Cache Manager manages memory.
PagedAttention stores KV cache efficiently.
GPU Workers execute model computation.
Tokens are streamed back.
This is enough to start reading the vLLM codebase more comfortably later. Without this map, the source code can feel overwhelming. With this map, each component has a place.
How do the previous articles connect now?
Part 10 explained:
Prefill vs Decode
Part 11 explained:
Continuous Batching
Part 12 explained:
PagedAttention
Now Part 13 connects them:

vLLM uses these ideas together
inside a real inference engine.
The picture becomes:

Prefill creates KV cache.
Decode generates one token at a time.
Continuous batching keeps decode efficient.
PagedAttention keeps KV cache memory efficient.
The scheduler coordinates everything.
GPU workers execute the model.
This is the architecture-level understanding.
What is the key mental model?
I would summarize vLLM like this:

vLLM is a scheduling + memory management + model execution system
for high-throughput LLM serving.
Or even simpler:

vLLM keeps GPUs busy
and keeps KV cache memory efficient
while serving many dynamic requests.
That is the core idea.
Why does this article matter?

This article feels like a transition point. Before this, I was mostly learning separate concepts. Now those concepts are starting to form a system. vLLM gives us a concrete place to connect them. It shows why inference is not only about model architecture. It is also about runtime architecture. The model is important. But the serving engine decides how efficiently that model can serve real users.
What comes next?
Now that the high-level vLLM architecture is clearer, the next step is to go one level deeper.
The most natural next topic is:
Inside the vLLM Scheduler
Because the scheduler is where many important decisions happen:

Which requests enter?
Which requests wait?
How are prefill and decode balanced?
How is the token budget used?
How does the system protect latency?
How does it keep throughput high?
How does it work with KV cache limits?
After that, we can go deeper into:

KV cache block manager
request lifecycle
chunked prefill
prefix caching
running vLLM locally
reading vLLM source code
And this is also where I think the series can start becoming more hands-on.
The conceptual foundation is finally strong enough.
Now the next step is to connect this mental model with actual implementation, experiments, and code.

title: LLM Inference Challenges: Understanding vLLM Architecture

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 14)
Understanding CUDA, vLLM, CPU Inference, Model Routing, and Agentic AI
In the previous parts, we explored:

KV cache
batching
multi-GPU inference
distributed serving
GPU communication
prefill vs decode
continuous batching
PagedAttention
vLLM architecture
At this point, the inference system picture started becoming clearer. But then I started getting confused by another set of questions.

Where does CUDA fit? 
Where does PyTorch fit? 
Where does vLLM fit? 
Why are people suddenly talking about CPU inference? 
Does small model inference mean GPUs become less important? 
How does model routing work? 
Where do load balancers fit? 
And finally, where does Agentic AI fit in all of this?
This article is my attempt to connect all of these ideas into one mental model.
What is the first confusion?
The first confusion is usually this:

Is CUDA similar to vLLM?
Is PyTorch similar to CUDA?
Is vLLM doing the computation?
Is the GPU doing the computation?
These things are connected, but they are not the same layer.
What actually performs the computation?
The GPU performs the actual computation. The GPU is the hardware. It contains:

GPU cores
tensor cores
HBM memory
caches
When an LLM runs, the GPU performs operations like:

matrix multiplication
attention computation
tensor operations
So the GPU is the actual worker.
Then what is CUDA?

CUDA is NVIDIA’s software platform for programming NVIDIA GPUs. The GPU performs the computation. CUDA provides the software layer that allows programs to tell the GPU what to do. A simple mental model:

GPU = hardware that performs computation

CUDA = software layer used to control NVIDIA GPUs
CUDA helps with:

launching GPU kernels
moving data to GPU memory
running optimized GPU libraries
coordinating GPU execution
So CUDA is not replacing the GPU. CUDA is how software talks to the GPU.
What is PyTorch then?
PyTorch sits above CUDA. When we write:
torch.matmul(A, B)

we are not manually writing CUDA code. PyTorch handles the tensor operation at a higher level. Under the hood, PyTorch may call CUDA libraries, and CUDA then launches work on the GPU. So the stack looks like:

PyTorch
  ↓
CUDA
  ↓
GPU
PyTorch manages tensors and model execution. CUDA manages GPU execution. The GPU performs the actual math.
Where does vLLM fit?
vLLM sits even higher. vLLM is not mainly about writing matrix multiplication kernels. vLLM is an inference serving engine. It focuses on:

request scheduling
continuous batching
KV cache management
PagedAttention
prefill and decode execution
token streaming
serving many users efficiently
So vLLM is not competing with CUDA. vLLM uses lower-level systems underneath it. A simplified stack looks like:

Application
  ↓
vLLM
  ↓
PyTorch / CUDA kernels
  ↓
GPU
What is the simplest mental model?
I think about it like this:

GPU = does the math

CUDA = tells NVIDIA GPU how to do the math

PyTorch = expresses model computation using tensors

vLLM = manages inference serving for many requests
So when a user sends a prompt, vLLM is not personally multiplying every matrix. vLLM decides what should run and when. Then the model execution happens through lower-level compute layers.
What does vLLM actually manage?
Suppose many users send requests:

Request A
Request B
Request C
Request D
vLLM decides:

Which requests enter the batch?
Which requests wait?
Which requests are in prefill?
Which requests are in decode?
How much KV cache memory is available?
Which requests finished?
Which requests can be admitted next?
That is why I now think of vLLM as:
a runtime system for LLM inference
It is not just:
run model.generate()
It is more like:
manage many dynamic generation workloads efficiently
What is a useful analogy?

Imagine a restaurant. The GPU is the kitchen. CUDA is the kitchen equipment and controls. PyTorch is the chef who knows how to use the equipment. vLLM is the restaurant manager. The restaurant manager does not cook every dish directly. Instead, the manager decides:

which orders enter
which orders wait
which orders can be grouped
which tables need service
how to keep the kitchen busy
That is very similar to what vLLM does for inference.
Why did this matter before talking about CPU inference?
Because once the stack is clear, CPU inference becomes easier to understand. The question is not:
Can CUDA run on CPU?
CUDA is NVIDIA GPU-specific. The better question is:
Can LLM inference run on hardware other than GPUs?
And the answer is yes. Inference can run on:

GPU
CPU
NPU
integrated GPU
edge devices
But the engine and optimization strategy may change.
Why are people suddenly talking about inference on CPUs?
Because the industry is realizing something important:

Training is usually GPU-heavy.

Inference depends on the workload.
Training large models requires enormous compute. GPUs are extremely important there. But inference is different. Inference happens repeatedly, for every user request. So the question becomes:

Can this request be served cheaper?
Can it be served locally?
Can it be served with lower power?
Can it be served without sending data to the cloud?
That is where CPU inference and edge inference become interesting.
Does this mean CPUs are replacing GPUs?
No. That is not the right mental model. The shift is not:
GPU → CPU
The shift is:
Use the right hardware for the right inference workload.
Large models, large context windows, and high-throughput serving still heavily benefit from GPUs. But smaller models and simpler tasks may run well enough on CPUs or edge accelerators.
What changed to make CPU inference more practical?
A few things changed at the same time. First, smaller models became much better. Models like:

1B
3B
7B
8B
can now solve many practical tasks. Second, quantization became much better. Third, CPUs, NPUs, and local AI hardware became more capable. So now the question is not always:
Do we need the biggest model?
The question becomes:
What is the smallest model that can solve this task well enough?
What is quantization again?
A model is mostly weights. Weights are numbers. For example:
If we store each number in FP16, each weight takes:
16 bits = 2 bytes
So a 7B model in FP16 needs roughly:
7 billion × 2 bytes ≈ 14 GB
just for weights.
What does quantization do?
Quantization stores approximate versions of those weights using fewer bits. Instead of:
FP16
we may use:

INT8
INT4
So memory can shrink like:

FP16 → 16 bits per weight
INT8 → 8 bits per weight
INT4 → 4 bits per weight
A rough mental model:

14 GB in FP16
≈ 7 GB in INT8
≈ 3.5 GB in INT4
This is one reason smaller models can run on laptops, desktops, and CPU servers.
Why does quality not completely collapse?
Because neural networks are often tolerant to small approximation errors. If a weight changes from:
to:

the model may still behave similarly. Of course, there is a tradeoff. More aggressive quantization can reduce quality. But for many workloads, the quality loss is acceptable compared to the gain in cost, memory, and deployment flexibility.
Does a small LLM work as well as a large LLM?
Not always. This is important. A small model is not universally as good as a large model. But for many tasks, a small model may be good enough. Examples:

simple summarization
classification
basic Q&A
routing decisions
template-based assistance
local assistant tasks
For harder reasoning, long context, coding, research, or complex analysis, a larger model may still be needed. So the question becomes:
Which model is good enough for this request?
This leads directly to model routing.
What is model routing?
Model routing means the system decides which model should handle a request. Instead of:
All requests → Large LLM
we get:

Request
  ↓
Router
  ↓
Best model for this request
For example:

Simple question
  ↓
Small model on CPU

Complex reasoning
  ↓
Large model on GPU

Research task
  ↓
Specialized research model

Document understanding
  ↓
Document AI service
The goal is:

Use the cheapest model and hardware
that can still produce a good answer.
Is this similar to what we learned about replicas?
Yes, but at a different level. Earlier we learned:

Load Balancer
  ↓
Replica 1
Replica 2
Replica 3
That was mostly about distributing requests across replicas of the same service. Model routing is higher level. It asks:
Which service or model should handle this request?
Then load balancing happens inside that chosen service.
Does vLLM do this routing?
Usually, no. vLLM has an internal scheduler. That scheduler decides:

which requests run now
which requests wait
how batching works
how KV cache is allocated
But vLLM is usually not the outer system deciding:

Should this request go to a CPU model?
Should it go to a GPU model?
Should it go to a research model?
Should it go to a document model?
That outer decision is usually handled by a router or AI gateway above the inference engine.
So does the router replace the load balancer?
No. This was an important clarification for me. The router and the load balancer solve different problems. The router decides:
WHAT should handle the request?
The load balancer decides:
WHERE exactly should the request go?
So the router chooses the service. The load balancer chooses the replica.
What does this architecture look like?
A useful production mental model is:

User
  ↓
API Gateway
  ↓
AI Router
  ├── Small Model Service
  │       ↓
  │   Load Balancer
  │       ↓
  │   CPU Replicas
  │
  ├── Large LLM Service
  │       ↓
  │   Load Balancer
  │       ↓
  │   GPU Replicas
  │
  ├── Research Model Service
  │       ↓
  │   Load Balancer
  │       ↓
  │   GPU Replicas
  │
  └── Document Understanding Service
          ↓
      Load Balancer
          ↓
      Replicas

This matches the mental model I was trying to build. The router is not simply replacing the load balancer. The router sits above multiple model services. Each service may still have its own load balancer and replicas.
What does the router use to make decisions?
The router may use:

rules
metadata
prompt length
user tier
cost limits
privacy requirements
latency targets
model availability
It may also use a small model or classifier. For example:

Request
  ↓
Small router model
  ↓
Classify request complexity
  ↓
Choose destination
What is a model cascade?
A cascade means we try a cheaper model first. If it is confident, return the answer. If it is not confident, escalate. Example:

Request
  ↓
Small model

Confident?
  ↓
Return answer

Not confident?
  ↓
Send to larger model
This can reduce cost because not every request needs the largest model.
What routers do people use in practice?
Many companies build custom routers. Common approaches include:

rule-based routing
classifier-based routing
semantic routing
confidence-based cascades
AI gateways
There are also products and projects in this space, such as:

LiteLLM
Portkey
Semantic Router style systems
custom internal gateways
But the important idea is not the specific tool. The important idea is the layer:

a routing layer sits above model endpoints
and decides where each request should go
How does this connect to CPU inference?
CPU inference becomes useful when the router has cheaper destinations available. For example:

Simple request
  ↓
Small quantized model
  ↓
CPU inference service
A more complex request may go to:

Large model
  ↓
GPU inference service
So CPU inference is not necessarily replacing GPU inference. It becomes one more option in the routing system.
What does a CPU inference service look like?
A CPU inference service may still have:

API endpoint
request queue
scheduler
batching
KV cache
replicas
load balancer
So many inference concepts still apply. But the hardware constraints are different.
What is different about CPU inference?
A GPU usually has:

very high parallel compute
very high memory bandwidth
limited HBM capacity
A CPU server may have:

less parallel compute
larger system RAM
lower cost
simpler deployment
So CPU inference is often attractive for:

small models
quantized models
low-throughput workloads
local inference
edge inference
privacy-sensitive tasks
Does everything we learned apply only to GPU clusters?
No. Some ideas are universal. For example:

request routing
load balancing
batching
scheduling
KV cache
replicas
latency vs throughput
These apply to CPU and GPU inference. But some ideas are much more GPU-specific:

CUDA
tensor parallelism
pipeline parallelism across GPUs
NCCL
NVLink
GPU communication
TensorRT-LLM
So the higher-level inference system concepts apply broadly. The low-level optimization details depend on the hardware.
Can vLLM run on CPU?
vLLM is mostly known for high-throughput GPU serving. But vLLM also has CPU backend support. However, the reason vLLM became popular is strongly connected to:

continuous batching
PagedAttention
GPU memory efficiency
high-throughput serving
So while vLLM can be used with CPUs in some cases, most people associate vLLM with GPU inference systems.
Can TensorRT-LLM run on CPU?

TensorRT-LLM is different. TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA’s optimized LLM inference stack for NVIDIA GPUs. So this is much more GPU-specific. If the system is CPU-only, TensorRT-LLM is usually not the right tool.
What do people use for CPU inference then?
This is where llama.cpp becomes important. llama.cpp is widely used for running LLMs locally and efficiently, especially quantized models. It is common in:

local inference
CPU inference
edge inference
laptop inference
small model experimentation
Tools like Ollama made this local inference experience much easier for many users. A simple mental model:

vLLM → production GPU serving

TensorRT-LLM → optimized NVIDIA GPU inference

llama.cpp → local / CPU-friendly / quantized inference

Ollama → easy local model running experience
Why is llama.cpp important?
Because it helped make local LLM inference practical. Instead of needing a large GPU cluster, users can run smaller quantized models on:

laptops
desktops
CPU servers
edge devices
This connects directly to the broader CPU inference discussion. If a model can fit in local memory and run fast enough, then not every request has to go to the cloud.
What is edge inference?
Edge inference means running inference close to the user or device. Instead of:

User
  ↓
Cloud GPU
  ↓
Response
we may have:

User
  ↓
Local device
  ↓
CPU / NPU / integrated GPU
  ↓
Response
This can help with:

latency
privacy
offline usage
cost
What role do NPUs play?
An NPU is a neural processing unit. A simple mental model:

CPU = general purpose compute

GPU = massively parallel compute

NPU = low-power AI acceleration
Many modern devices now include CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs together. So future inference may not be only cloud GPU inference. It may be a mix of:

local CPU
local NPU
local GPU
cloud GPU
How would routing work at the edge?
This is where the architecture becomes very interesting. Imagine a laptop or phone with a local router. A request arrives:
Summarize this email
The router may decide:

Small local model is enough
  ↓
Run locally
Another request arrives:

Analyze this long legal contract
and identify business risks
The router may decide:

Too complex for local model
  ↓
Send to cloud GPU model
So edge inference may use the same routing idea:

local if possible
cloud if needed
Why are people talking about CPUs, ARM, Intel, Dell, and AI PCs?
Because inference is no longer only about giant GPU clusters. There is a growing need to run AI across many types of hardware:

cloud GPUs
CPU servers
AI PCs
phones
edge devices
enterprise servers

Chip companies, server companies, and device companies all become relevant because inference workloads may spread across the entire compute stack. This does not mean GPUs become unimportant. It means inference becomes more distributed and more workload-specific.
Where does Agentic AI fit in all of this?
This was another major clarification for me. Agents are usually not LLMs themselves. Agents are orchestration systems. They sit above model calls. A simple stack looks like:

User
  ↓
Agent Runtime
  ↓
Router
  ↓
LLM Endpoint
  ↓
Inference Engine
  ↓
Hardware
The agent decides what needs to be done. The router decides which model or service should handle it. The inference engine generates tokens. The hardware runs the computation.
What does an agent actually do?
Suppose the user asks:

Find last month’s invoices
and summarize unusual expenses.
An agent may:

call accounting system
retrieve invoice data
call search tool
call LLM for analysis
call database
generate final answer

The agent is coordinating a workflow. It may call an LLM multiple times. It may call tools. It may store intermediate state. It may decide the next step based on previous results. But the agent itself is usually just software running on CPU.
Does an agent need a GPU?
Usually, no. The agent orchestration layer is often:

Python service
Java service
Node service
workflow runtime
This can run on CPUs. The GPU is needed when the system performs actual model inference on a GPU-backed model. So:

Agent orchestration = usually CPU

LLM inference = CPU, GPU, NPU, or cloud endpoint
How do agents and routing work together?
An agent may decide:
I need to call a model now.
Then the routing layer decides:
Which model should be called?
For example:

Agent needs simple classification
  ↓
Small CPU model

Agent needs deep reasoning
  ↓
Large GPU model

Agent needs document extraction
  ↓
Document model service

Agent needs local private answer
  ↓
Local model
So agents and routers solve different problems. The agent decides the workflow. The router chooses the model endpoint.
What does the full modern AI stack look like?
A more complete picture now looks like:

User
  ↓
API Gateway
  ↓
Agent Layer
  ↓
Model Router
  ├── Small CPU Model Service
  ├── Local Edge Model
  ├── Large GPU Model Service
  ├── Research Model Service
  └── Document Understanding Service
        ↓
     Load Balancer
        ↓
     Replicas
        ↓
     Inference Engine
        ↓
     Hardware
This is much bigger than just:
User → LLM
What is the difference between agent, router, load balancer, and inference engine?
This is the cleanest separation I now have:

Agent
= decides what steps need to happen

Router
= decides which model/service should handle a model call

Load Balancer
= decides which replica inside that service gets the request

Inference Engine
= runs the model efficiently

Hardware
= performs the computation
So:

Agent decides the workflow.

Router decides the destination.

Load balancer decides the replica.

Inference engine manages execution.

Hardware does the math.
How does this connect back to vLLM?
vLLM sits inside the inference service. For example:

Large LLM Service
  ↓
Load Balancer
  ↓
vLLM Replica
  ↓
GPU Workers
The outer router may choose the Large LLM Service. The load balancer may choose a specific vLLM replica. Then vLLM manages:

scheduling
continuous batching
PagedAttention
KV cache
prefill
decode
token generation
So vLLM is not the whole AI platform. It is a critical part of the inference layer.
What is the biggest mental shift?
Earlier, I was mostly thinking about:

one model
many requests
Now the picture is more like:

many models
many hardware types
many services
many workflows
This changes the architecture. The system is no longer only asking:
How do we run this model efficiently?
It is also asking:

Should this request run locally?
Should it use a small model?
Should it use a large model?
Should it use CPU?
Should it use GPU?
Should it call a tool first?
Should an agent break it into steps?
What is the key intuition?
The modern inference stack is becoming layered. At the bottom:
CPU / GPU / NPU
Above that:
CUDA / CPU kernels / hardware runtime
Above that:
PyTorch / llama.cpp / TensorRT-LLM / other execution layers
Above that:
vLLM / inference engine / serving runtime
Above that:
load balancer
Above that:
model router
Above that:
agent workflow
So the full system is not just about generating tokens. It is about deciding:

what to do
which model to use
where to run it
how to serve it efficiently
how to keep cost and latency under control
What does this teach us about CPU inference?
CPU inference is not a separate universe. It is one part of a larger inference platform. For some requests:
CPU + small quantized model
may be enough. For others:
GPU + large model
is needed. For local tasks:
edge model
may be best. For complex workflows:
agent + tools + multiple model calls
may be required. So the future is not:
CPU vs GPU
It is:
CPU + GPU + NPU + routing + agents
working together.
What comes next?
This article helped me connect several pieces:

CUDA
PyTorch
vLLM
CPU inference
GPU inference
quantization
llama.cpp
model routing
load balancers
edge inference
Agentic AI
The next natural step is to go deeper into CPU and local inference. That probably means exploring:

llama.cpp
GGUF models
quantized inference
Ollama
local model serving
CPU vs GPU performance tradeoffs
Because now the high-level architecture is clearer. The next question becomes:
How does local CPU inference actually work in practice?

title: LLM Inference Challenges -Understanding the Modern AI Inference Stack

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 15)
Understanding Inference Metrics
In the previous parts, we built a mental model for modern LLM inference systems.
We covered:

KV cache → Part 1 
Memory challenges → Part 2 
GPU utilization and batching → Part 3 
Multi-GPU inference → Parts 4, Part 5, Part 6, Part 7
Distributed serving and routing → Part 8 
GPU communication and networking → Part 9 
Prefill vs Decode → Part 10 
Continuous batching → Part 11 
PagedAttention → Part 12 
vLLM architecture → Part 13 
CUDA, PyTorch, vLLM, CPU inference, routing, and agents → Part 14
At this point, the system picture is much clearer.
But once we understand how inference works, the next question becomes:
How do we know if the inference system is working well?
That leads us to inference metrics.
Why do inference metrics matter?
Until now, we were mostly building intuition.
But real systems need measurement.
Metrics help answer questions like:

Are users waiting too long?
Is the GPU actually being used well?
Is batching working?
Is prefill slow?
Is decode slow?
Is KV cache memory becoming the bottleneck?
Are queues building up?
Can the system handle more users?
Did our latest change improve performance or hurt it?
Without metrics, we are mostly guessing.
With metrics, we can start observing the system.
What does the user experience look like?
From the user’s point of view, inference feels simple:

send prompt
wait for response to start
watch tokens stream
receive final answer
So the user mostly experiences two things:

how long it takes before the first token appears
how fast the remaining tokens continue appearing
These map to two important metrics:

Time To First Token
Inter-token latency
What is Time To First Token?
Time To First Token is usually written as:
TTFT
It means:
how long the user waits before the first generated token appears
Example:

user sends request at 10:00:00.000
first token appears at 10:00:01.200
TTFT = 1.2 seconds
TTFT is important because it controls the first impression.
If TTFT is high, the system feels slow even if the rest of the answer streams quickly.
What happens before the first token?
Before the first token appears, several things happen:

request arrives
request may wait in a queue
scheduler admits the request
prompt is tokenized
prefill runs
KV cache is created
first decode step runs
first token is produced
A simple mental model:
TTFT = queue time + prefill time + first decode step + system overhead
This connects directly to Prefill vs Decode, which we covered in Part 10.
Why can TTFT become high?
TTFT can increase because of:

long prompts
high queue time
overloaded replicas
slow prefill
limited KV cache memory
scheduler delays
too many active requests
traffic spikes
So when TTFT is high, the better question is not:
Why is the model slow?
The better question is:
Where is the time being spent?
What is inter-token latency?
After the first token appears, generation continues token by token.
Inter-token latency means:
how much time passes between generated tokens
Example:

token 1 appears
100 ms later, token 2 appears
100 ms later, token 3 appears
Inter-token latency is roughly:
100 ms per token
This metric tells us how smooth the streaming experience feels.
Why is inter-token latency connected to decode?
After prefill, the system enters decode.
Decode generates one token at a time:

token 1
token 2
token 3
token 4
Each token depends on the previous token.
So inter-token latency is mostly connected to decode speed.
Can TTFT be good while inter-token latency is bad?
Yes.
A system can start quickly but stream slowly.
Example:

TTFT = good
inter-token latency = bad
This usually means:

request admission was fast
prefill was acceptable
but decode is slow
Possible causes:

small active batch
memory bandwidth pressure
KV cache access overhead
communication overhead
inefficient scheduling during decode
This connects to continuous batching, which we covered in Part 11.
Can TTFT be bad while inter-token latency is good?
Yes.
A request can wait a long time before starting, but stream quickly once it begins.
Example:

TTFT = 5 seconds
inter-token latency = 50 ms
This may indicate:

queueing problem
long prefill
scheduler pressure
KV cache memory pressure
overloaded serving replica
So TTFT and inter-token latency tell different stories.
We need both.
What is total request latency?
Total request latency means:
time from request arrival to final token
It includes:

queue time
prefill
decode
streaming
final completion
A simple mental model:
Total latency = TTFT + time to generate remaining tokens
But total latency can be misleading.
Why?
Because output length matters.
A request generating 20 tokens and a request generating 1000 tokens should not be compared directly without context.
So total latency should be interpreted together with:

input tokens
output tokens
TTFT
inter-token latency
concurrency level
What is throughput?
Throughput means:
how much useful work the system completes over time
For LLM inference, this is usually measured as:
tokens per second
Example:

system generates 10,000 output tokens in 10 seconds
throughput = 1000 tokens/sec
Throughput matters because inference systems usually serve many users.
Higher throughput usually means:

more users served
better GPU efficiency
lower cost per token
better batching efficiency
What kinds of throughput should we track?
There are a few useful throughput metrics:

Output tokens/sec
Input tokens/sec
Total tokens/sec
Requests/sec
Tokens/sec is usually more meaningful than requests/sec because LLM requests vary a lot.
One request may generate 10 tokens.
Another may generate 1000 tokens.
So request count alone does not describe system load very well.
Why separate input and output tokens?
Because prefill and decode behave differently.
Prefill processes input tokens.
Decode generates output tokens.
Example workloads:

long prompt + short answer
short prompt + long answer
long prompt + long answer
many short chat requests
Each workload stresses the system differently.
So we should ask:

Are we measuring prefill throughput?
Are we measuring decode throughput?
Are we measuring total throughput?
This again connects to Part 10 — Prefill vs Decode.
What is queue time?
Queue time means:
how long a request waits before the inference engine starts processing it
Queue time affects TTFT directly.
Queue time can grow when:

too many requests arrive
active batch is full
KV cache memory is limited
GPU workers are busy
prefill workload is large
scheduler cannot admit new requests quickly
Queue time is often one of the clearest signs that demand is exceeding capacity.
What is batch size?
Batch size means:
how many requests or tokens are processed together
In LLM inference, batching can mean different things:

number of active requests
number of active sequences
number of tokens processed in a step
number of prefill tokens
number of decode tokens
The simple intuition:

larger batches usually improve GPU utilization
but larger batches can increase waiting time
This is the latency-throughput tradeoff we covered in Part 11 — Continuous Batching.
What is batch occupancy?
Batch occupancy means:
how full the active batch is compared to what the system can handle
Example:

system can efficiently handle 32 active decode requests
currently running only 8 active decode requests
batch occupancy is low
Low batch occupancy can mean:

GPU is not receiving enough work
throughput may be low
batching is not effective
This matters especially during decode because each request only contributes one token of work at a time.
Why does batch occupancy matter during decode?
During decode:

each active request generates one token
each decode step is relatively small
GPU efficiency depends on having enough active requests
Example:
Batch = [A]
The system runs a decode step for one request.
Now compare:
Batch = [A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H]
