The system still runs a decode step, but many users receive tokens.
That is why continuous batching tries to keep the active batch full.
What is GPU utilization?
GPU utilization tells us how busy the GPU is.
Simple mental model:

high GPU utilization = GPU is actively doing work
low GPU utilization = GPU is waiting or underused
This matters because GPUs are expensive.
If utilization is low, we may be paying for hardware that is not doing enough useful work.
Is high GPU utilization always good?
Not always.
High GPU utilization can mean the system is efficient.
But it can also mean the system is overloaded.
Example:

GPU utilization = 99%
queue time = high
TTFT = bad
p99 latency = bad
That means the GPU is busy, but users are waiting too long.
So GPU utilization must be read together with:

TTFT
queue time
throughput
p95/p99 latency
error rate
Is low GPU utilization always bad?
Not always.
Low utilization may be fine during low traffic.
But low utilization during high traffic can indicate a problem.
Possible causes:

batches are too small
scheduler is not filling batches
requests are spread across too many replicas
CPU bottleneck
tokenization bottleneck
network bottleneck
memory bottleneck
communication overhead
So utilization only makes sense with workload context.
What is GPU memory utilization?
GPU memory is used for:

model weights
KV cache
activations
temporary buffers
runtime overhead
Model weights are mostly fixed after loading.
KV cache grows with:

active requests
prompt length
generated tokens
context window size
So GPU memory utilization tells us how much memory capacity is still available.
What is KV cache utilization?
KV cache utilization tells us:
how much KV cache memory is currently occupied
This is important because KV cache often limits concurrency.
If KV cache utilization is high:

fewer new requests can enter
active batch size may be limited
queue time may increase
TTFT may increase
throughput may stop improving
This connects directly to:

Part 1 — KV Cache 
Part 2 — Memory Challenges 
Part 12 — PagedAttention
Why can KV cache limit concurrency?
Every active request needs KV cache.
Longer sequences need more cache.
Example:

Request A → 500 tokens
Request B → 4000 tokens
Request C → 8000 tokens
As active sequences grow, KV cache memory fills up.
Eventually, the system may have compute capacity but not enough memory to admit more requests.
This is one of the most important inference lessons:

LLM inference is not only compute-limited.
It can also be memory-limited.
Why does this connect to PagedAttention?
PagedAttention helps manage KV cache memory more efficiently.
The key idea from Part 12 :

KV cache is split into fixed-size blocks
blocks do not need to be physically contiguous
requests can grow dynamically
finished requests return blocks to the pool
memory fragmentation becomes less harmful
So when KV cache utilization is high, we start seeing why memory management matters so much.
What are p50, p95, and p99?
Average latency is not enough.
We also need percentiles.
Common latency percentiles:
These help us understand tail latency.
Why does tail latency matter?
Tail latency shows the slow cases.
Example:

p50 TTFT = 500 ms
p99 TTFT = 12 seconds
This means most users are fine, but some users wait a very long time.
For production systems, p95 and p99 matter because users often remember the bad cases.
Tail latency can increase because of:

long prompts
large outputs
traffic spikes
queue buildup
memory pressure
scheduler delays
replica imbalance
network issues
What is error rate?
Error rate tells us how often requests fail.
Failures may include:

timeouts
out-of-memory errors
server errors
cancelled requests
rate limit errors
model worker crashes
unhealthy replicas
A fast system is not useful if it fails often.
So error rate is an important operational metric.
What is timeout rate?
Timeout rate tells us how often requests take too long and get cancelled or rejected.
Timeouts may happen because:

queues are too long
responses are too long
replica is overloaded
model worker is stuck
network call is slow
system capacity is too low
Timeouts usually mean latency has become bad enough to break the user experience.
What is cost per token?
Cost per token means:
how much it costs to process or generate each token
Simple mental model:
GPU cost / tokens generated = cost per token
This is where inference metrics become business metrics.
If throughput improves while hardware cost stays the same:

cost per token goes down
GPU usage becomes more efficient
serving economics improve
This is why batching, scheduling, and memory efficiency matter.
They are not just technical optimizations.
They directly affect cost.
How do these metrics connect to earlier concepts?
A useful mapping:
This table helped me connect the conceptual articles to real system operations.
What does an overloaded system look like?
An overloaded inference system may show:

queue time increasing
TTFT increasing
p95/p99 latency getting worse
KV cache utilization near limit
GPU utilization very high
timeout rate increasing
error rate increasing
Possible fixes:

add more replicas
improve routing
reduce max context length
reduce max output tokens
use a smaller model
improve batching
improve KV cache efficiency
autoscale earlier
What does an underutilized system look like?
An underutilized system may show:

low GPU utilization
low batch occupancy
low throughput
good latency
This may be fine during low traffic.
But if traffic is high, possible causes include:

requests spread across too many replicas
batch sizes too small
scheduler not filling batches
routing is inefficient
workload is too fragmented
This is the other side of the latency-throughput tradeoff.
What does a memory-limited system look like?
A memory-limited system may show:

high GPU memory usage
high KV cache utilization
limited ability to admit new requests
queue time increasing
batch size capped
GPU compute not fully used
This is where the system may have compute available but still cannot serve more users because memory is the bottleneck.
What does a decode bottleneck look like?
A decode bottleneck may show:

TTFT is acceptable
tokens stream slowly
inter-token latency is high
decode throughput is low
active requests keep running for a long time
GPU utilization may be uneven
Possible causes:

small active batches
KV cache access overhead
memory bandwidth pressure
communication overhead
too many long-running requests
This is why continuous batching matters.
What does a prefill bottleneck look like?
A prefill bottleneck may show:

TTFT is high
long prompts are especially slow
input tokens/sec is low
queue time may increase
decode may be fine after generation starts
This often happens with:

long documents
long RAG contexts
large prompts
many new requests arriving together
Why is workload shape important?
Metrics only make sense if we understand the workload.
Important workload dimensions:

prompt length
output length
concurrency
model size
context window
streaming vs non-streaming
sampling parameters
hardware type
number of replicas
quantization level
Example:

short prompts + short outputs
short prompts + long outputs
long prompts + short outputs
long prompts + long outputs
Each workload stresses the system differently.
So benchmark numbers without workload details are not very useful.
What should a good benchmark mention?
A useful benchmark should include:

model name
model size
hardware
serving engine
number of GPUs
quantization
prompt length
output length
concurrency level
streaming or non-streaming
measured metrics
p50/p95/p99 values
any important config settings
Without these details, performance numbers are hard to compare.
What is the simplest metric set to start with?
For the first hands-on experiment, I would start with:

TTFT
inter-token latency
total request latency
output tokens/sec
requests/sec
GPU utilization
GPU memory usage
Then later add:

queue time
KV cache utilization
batch occupancy
p50/p95/p99 latency
error rate
cost per token
The goal is not to measure everything on day one.
The goal is to start connecting concepts to real observations.
How does this connect to LLMOps?
This is where inference becomes operational.
LLMOps is not only:
deploy the model
It is also:

monitor the model service
understand latency
watch GPU usage
detect queue buildup
track failures
understand cost
scale replicas
debug bottlenecks
compare serving configurations
So inference metrics are the bridge between:
understanding inference systems
and
operating inference systems
What is the key mental model?
I would summarize inference metrics like this:

TTFT
Inter-token latency
Throughput
Queue time
GPU utilization
GPU memory utilization
KV cache utilization
Batch occupancy
p95/p99 latency
Error rate
Cost per token
Together, these metrics tell us whether the inference system is healthy.
Why this article matters
Until now, I was mostly asking:
How does inference work?
Now the question becomes:
How do we observe inference working?
That is a big shift.
Because real inference engineering is not only about knowing the concepts.
It is also about:

measuring behavior
finding bottlenecks
understanding tradeoffs
improving latency
improving throughput
reducing cost
keeping the system reliable
This is where the learning starts moving from mental models into hands-on systems work.
What comes next?
Now that the key inference metrics are clearer, the next step is to measure them in a real serving system.
So the next part will be: Running vLLM Locally and Measuring Inference Metrics
This is also a good point to start a small GitHub repo.
The goal is not to build a perfect benchmarking system immediately.
The goal is to start building intuition from real measurements.
Because once we can measure the system, we can finally start experimenting with it.

title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding Inference Metrics

blocks.text: Lab 1 — Running a Local LLM Server
In the previous articles of this series, I talked about core LLM inference concepts: latency, throughput, TTFT, ITL, batching, concurrency, prompt processing, decode cost, and system utilization.
Now it is time to make those ideas measurable.
This is the first hands-on lab in the series, and I intentionally started local.

For this lab, I used a Mac setup with llama.cpp. The lab is designed for Apple Silicon, but the same learning pattern can run on CPU-only setups as well. It may be slower, and your numbers will be different, but the concepts remain the same.
The goal of this first lab is not to build the fastest inference server. The goal is to understand what actually happens when we run a local model, send real requests, and measure the behavior.
You can follow the full lab here:
GitHub Lab: https://github.com/aruanurag/llm-inference-lab/tree/main/labs/01-local-llm-serving-apple-silicon
Why start local?
Before moving to vLLM, cloud GPUs, managed inference endpoints, Kubernetes, autoscaling, and cost optimization, I wanted a simple baseline where the moving parts are visible.
This first lab uses:

A local machine.
A small quantized GGUF model.
llama.cpp as the runtime.
An OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint.
A benchmark script to measure inference metrics.
Simple system tools to observe CPU, memory, and GPU activity.

This gives us a controlled starting point. Later in the series, I will move to vLLM and cloud environments where GPU access is easier and more cost-efficient. I may also start with simple CPU-based cloud runs before moving to GPU, just to keep the comparisons clean.
Runtime choice: llama.cpp
For Lab 1, I used llama.cpp.
Why?

It works well on Apple Silicon.
It supports Metal acceleration.
It runs quantized GGUF models.
It exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API.
It is simple enough for a first reproducible lab.
Once the server is running, requests go to:
http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions

That is useful because the client-side benchmarking flow can stay familiar even when the backend changes later. Today it is llama.cpp; in future labs, it can be vLLM or a cloud-hosted inference endpoint.
Model choice: start small
For the first run, I used:
Qwen2.5 1.5B Instruct, Q4_K_M
This is not about using the smartest model. It is about using a model that starts reliably, fits comfortably, and lets us focus on inference behavior.
Good first model choices for this lab include:

Qwen2.5 1.5B Instruct GGUF, Q4 or Q5.
Llama 3.2 1B or 3B Instruct GGUF, Q4 or Q5.
Phi-3 Mini GGUF, Q4, if memory allows.
The first rule of inference labs: make the first experiment reproducible before making it impressive.
What this lab measures
This lab focuses on the same metrics we discussed in the earlier inference articles.
Core latency metrics:

TTFT: time to first token.
Approximate ITL: time between streamed output chunks.
End-to-end latency: total time from request start to completed response.
Throughput metrics:

Output tokens per second.
Requests per second.
Approximate total tokens per second.
System behavior:

Startup time.
CPU usage.
Memory usage.
GPU / Metal activity.
Concurrency level.
Batch size.
Micro-batch size.
p50, p95, and p99 latency.
These metrics will continue to matter as the labs move from local serving to GPU-backed serving.
Lab flow
The lab follows a simple sequence:

Set up llama.cpp.
Download a small GGUF model.
Start a local llama-server.
Verify the server health endpoint.
Send one OpenAI-compatible chat request.
Run benchmark experiments.
Observe CPU, memory, and GPU behavior.
Change batching settings.
Collect and compare results.
Visualize the benchmark outputs.
This is the basic habit I want to build in the series: change one thing, measure again, and compare.
Experiment 1: Single request, short prompt, short output
The first experiment sends one short prompt and asks for a short response.
Example:
Explain KV cache in two sentences.
This establishes the baseline.
The main question is:
How long does the server take to produce the first token?
This is where TTFT becomes real. It is no longer just a definition. You can actually see the delay before the first streamed chunk arrives.
This matters because users often judge responsiveness by the time it takes for the first token to appear, not only by the total completion time.
Experiment 2: Long prompt, short output
The second experiment keeps the output short but increases the prompt length.
This helps isolate prefill cost.
In transformer inference, the model has to process the input prompt before it can generate the next token. So longer prompts usually increase the amount of work before generation starts.
The question here is:
Does TTFT increase when the prompt gets longer?
This is especially important for real-world applications like:

RAG systems with retrieved documents.
Chat applications with long conversation history.
Agents with tool outputs.
Code assistants with large context.
Enterprise assistants with policy, ticket, or document context.
Even if the final answer is short, the prompt can be long. That means the user may still experience high TTFT.
Experiment 3: Short prompt, long output
The third experiment does the opposite.
The prompt is short, but the output length is increased.
Example:
Write a compact tutorial on continuous batching.
Now the goal is to observe decode cost.
The question becomes:
Does end-to-end latency increase mostly because more output tokens are generated?
This is why max token settings matter so much in production. They are not just safety limits. They directly affect latency, capacity, and cost.
Two requests can have similar TTFT but very different end-to-end latency if one generates 50 tokens and the other generates 500.
Experiment 4: Multiple concurrent requests
After single-request testing, the lab adds concurrency.
Example:

concurrency = 4
requests = 12
Now we are no longer testing only one request. We are testing serving behavior under load.
The important questions are:

Does throughput improve?
What happens to p50 latency?
What happens to p95 latency?
Does approximate ITL get worse?
Does the server remain stable?

This is where inference tradeoffs become visible. A system may produce better throughput with concurrency, but tail latency can get worse because requests are competing for the same compute resources.
That tradeoff will become even more important in later labs with vLLM, continuous batching, and GPU-backed serving.
Experiment 5: Batch size and micro-batch size
The final experiment changes server-side batching knobs in llama.cpp.
The two knobs are:

BATCH_SIZE: logical batch size. This affects how much prompt work the server tries to process together.
UBATCH_SIZE: physical micro-batch size. This controls how that work is split into smaller chunks.
The lab compares a conservative setting:

BATCH_SIZE=256
UBATCH_SIZE=64
with a larger setting:

BATCH_SIZE=1024
UBATCH_SIZE=256
The benchmark stays the same. Only the server configuration changes.
The questions are:

Did TTFT improve or get worse?
Did p95 latency improve or get worse?
Did throughput improve?
Did memory usage change?
Did the server become unstable?
This is the important lesson: there is no universal best batch size. The right value depends on model size, context size, memory, hardware, runtime, and concurrency.
Guessing is not enough. You have to measure.
CPU, GPU, and Metal observation
Another part of the lab is watching the machine while inference is running.
On macOS, I used tools like:

top
ps
Activity Monitor
powermetrics
The goal is not perfect profiling yet. The goal is to connect inference metrics with system behavior.
Things to observe:

Is CPU usage high?
How much memory is the server using?
Does Activity Monitor show GPU activity?
Do startup logs mention Metal?
What happens with CPU-only mode?
What changes when Metal offload is enabled?
In this lab, GPU_LAYERS controls offload behavior:

GPU_LAYERS=0      -> CPU-only
GPU_LAYERS=auto   -> let llama.cpp decide Metal offload
GPU_LAYERS=all    -> try to offload all possible layers

This habit will matter even more later in cloud GPU labs. Having a GPU does not automatically mean the system is efficient. We still need to understand utilization, memory pressure, batching behavior, and latency.
Failure is also a valid result
The lab includes a place to record failures.
If something fails, record:

Exact command.
Exact error.
Machine type.
Model file.
What you tried next.
This is useful because inference work often starts with constraints:

This model does not fit.
This quantization is not stable.
This runtime setting does not work on this machine.
This batch size causes memory pressure.
This offload mode does not behave as expected.
A good inference experiment does not only collect successful benchmark numbers. It also collects limits.
Why this lab matters
This first lab is small by design.
But it creates the foundation for everything that comes next.
From here, we can change one layer at a time:

Move from llama.cpp to vLLM.
Move from local CPU or Metal acceleration to cloud GPU.
Compare prompt-heavy workloads with decode-heavy workloads.
Study continuous batching more directly.
Observe KV cache behavior.
Explore concurrency limits.
Compare cost per request.
Compare latency under different serving configurations.
The infrastructure will become more advanced, but the measurement mindset will stay the same:

Start with a question.
Run a controlled experiment.
Measure TTFT, ITL, latency, throughput, and utilization.
Change one thing.
Measure again.
That is how inference stops being a black box.
Final thought
It is tempting to start LLM inference learning with the biggest model and the fastest GPU available.
But for learning, that is not always the best first step.
A small local lab can teach the fundamentals clearly:

You see the server start.
You see the model load.
You send the request.
You watch the first token.
You increase the prompt.
You increase the output.
You add concurrency.
You change batching.
You observe CPU, memory, and GPU behavior.
And suddenly, the metrics from earlier articles are no longer theoretical. They are measurements from a real system.
That is the goal of Lab 1:
Start local. Measure carefully. Build intuition. Then scale.

title: LLM Inference Learning Series: Running a Local LLM Server Before Moving to GPUs

blocks.text: A Local Workbench for Running LLM Inference Experiments on OCI
https://github.com/aruanurag/llm-inference-lab/tree/main/apps/oci-inference-cloud

Over the last few articles, I have been learning and writing about LLM inference systems. I started with concepts like KV cache, batching, GPU utilization, multi-GPU inference, request routing, prefill vs decode, continuous batching, PagedAttention, vLLM architecture, CPU inference, and model routing.
Most of those articles were conceptual. But while writing them and doing hands-on experiments, I noticed something very practical: I was repeating the same setup steps again and again.
Each experiment usually involved:

creating infrastructure
setting up a machine
installing the inference runtime
deploying llama.cpp
downloading a model
starting the server
exposing an endpoint
running benchmarks
comparing results
cleaning up infrastructure
That repetition made me think:

Can I build a small tool
that helps me set up inference experiments faster?
That is where this project started.

The app is an early MVP of a local inference cloud workbench. The goal is simple: provision infrastructure, deploy an inference runtime, expose a local endpoint, run benchmarks, try small apps, compare results, and repeat quickly.
It is not a finished product. It is more like a learning tool that I can keep improving as I move deeper into inference systems.
Why did I build this?
When learning infrastructure-heavy topics, reading alone is not enough. At some point, I want to actually run things.
I want to:

measure latency
compare throughput
test CPU inference
try different model sizes
compare shapes and OCPU counts
eventually move to GPUs
later explore Kubernetes and cluster deployments
But every experiment has setup cost. If setup takes too long, I run fewer experiments. If I run fewer experiments, I learn slower.
So the goal of this tool is to reduce friction. I wanted something that lets me quickly:

create an experiment
pick infrastructure
deploy a model
run inference
benchmark results
try an app
clean everything up
The faster this loop becomes, the more experiments I can run.
What is this app?
The app is called:
OCI Inference Cloud
It is a local hackathon-style workbench for inference experiments. Right now, it focuses on OCI and uses your existing OCI CLI profiles.
The current MVP can:

provision an OCI CPU/HPC instance for an experiment
deploy llama.cpp
expose a private OpenAI-compatible endpoint through a local backend proxy
run benchmark presets
provide sample applications for direct chat and routing experiments
terminate app-created infrastructure from the selected experiment
Instead of manually setting up everything each time, the app gives me a repeatable workflow for running inference experiments.
Why local-first?
This part was important to me. The app is intentionally local-first.
It:

uses existing OCI CLI profiles
does not store OCI API keys
generates SSH keys under ~/.llm-inference-cloud/
keeps benchmark results outside the Git repo
uses SSH tunnels instead of exposing llama-server publicly
can terminate the infrastructure it created for an experiment
That design keeps the system easier to understand, easier to debug, and easier to clean up.
What does it do today?
The current flow looks like this:

Create or select an experiment.
Load OCI context.
Select existing networking.
Provision a CPU/HPC instance.
Deploy llama.cpp.
Select a GGUF model.
Run benchmark presets.
Start the local endpoint proxy.
Try sample apps.
Delete infrastructure when done.
That is already enough to make hands-on inference experimentation much more enjoyable.
The current model catalog includes:

Qwen2.5 1.5B Instruct Q4_K_M
Qwen2.5 7B Instruct Q4_K_M
Qwen2.5 7B Instruct Q8_0
Qwen2.5 14B Instruct Q4_K_M
custom directly downloadable GGUF URL
The custom GGUF option is useful because I do not want the tool to be limited to only a few hardcoded models.
Why llama.cpp first?
For the first version, I started with llama.cpp because I wanted to explore CPU inference seriously.
A lot of inference discussions quickly move to GPUs, and GPUs are obviously important. But CPU inference is also interesting for:

smaller models
quantized models
local inference
edge inference
cost-sensitive workloads
experimentation without large GPU infrastructure
It is also just fun. Running your own model, exposing your own endpoint, and talking to it through a small app feels very different from only calling a hosted API.
Why OCI?
Right now, this MVP is based on OCI because that is where I was testing infrastructure and CPU/HPC shapes.
I was also surprised by the performance I was seeing for CPU-based inference. That made the experiment more interesting.
The broader question I wanted to explore was:

How far can we push useful inference
without immediately jumping to GPUs?
This does not mean CPU replaces GPU. That is not the point.
The better mental model is:

Use the right hardware
for the right inference workload.
A small quantized model may work well on CPU. A larger model, long-context workload, or high-throughput serving system may need GPUs. A future inference platform may use both.
The bigger vision
The longer-term idea in my mind is something like a small personal inference cloud.

I was thinking about platforms like Nebius and other AI cloud systems where you can provision inference infrastructure and then connect applications to model endpoints. I wanted a much smaller, learning-focused version of that idea.
A future version could look like this:

Choose cloud.
Choose hardware.
Choose model.
Choose inference engine.
Deploy endpoint.
Run benchmark.
Connect app.
Compare cost and performance.
Today, the app starts with OCI and llama.cpp. Later, I can imagine adding:

GPU inference
vLLM
Kubernetes
multi-node deployments
model routing
benchmark dashboards
observability
cost comparison
experiment history
The current version is only the first step, but it gives me a foundation to keep building on.
What are the sample apps?
Right now, the project includes two simple sample apps.
The first one is a direct CPU chat app. It talks directly to the local endpoint exposed by the OCI inference workbench.
The second one is a router chat app. It can use the CPU endpoint and also connect to an OpenAI model.
This makes it useful for exploring basic routing ideas:

Simple request → local CPU model

More complex request → larger hosted model

This connects nicely to the model routing ideas I have been exploring. Eventually, I want this to become a playground for testing routing strategies, comparing outputs, and understanding when smaller local models are good enough.
What does the architecture look like?
At a high level, the app has two main parts:

Backend
Frontend
The structure looks like this:

apps/oci-inference-cloud/
├── backend/
│   ├── app/
│   ├── tests/
│   └── requirements.txt
└── frontend/
    ├── src/
    └── package.json
The backend and frontend run locally. The OCI instance runs the remote llama-server, but the remote server stays bound to:
on the OCI instance. The local backend reaches it through an SSH tunnel.
The local app exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint like this:
POST http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/experiments/{experiment_id}/endpoint/v1/chat/completions
The simple mental model is:

Browser
  ↓
Local frontend
  ↓
Local backend
  ↓
SSH tunnel
  ↓
Remote llama-server on OCI
So the model server is not publicly exposed. The app talks to it through a local proxy.
Before trying it
You should have:

OCI CLI configured
an OCI profile available
access to create compute instances
existing OCI networking
Python 3
Node.js and npm
Git
The app uses your existing OCI CLI context, so you do not need to paste OCI API keys into the app.
Run the backend
From the repository:

cd apps/oci-inference-cloud/backend
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8090
The backend runs on:
Run the frontend
In another terminal:

cd apps/oci-inference-cloud/frontend
npm install
npm run dev
Open:
Now the local UI should be available.
Create your first experiment
Inside the UI, create or select an experiment.
I like this structure because each test becomes easier to track. For example:

Experiment 1 → Qwen2.5 1.5B on a smaller CPU shape
Experiment 2 → Qwen2.5 7B on a larger CPU shape
Experiment 3 → same model with native build enabled
Experiment 4 → different OCPU count
This makes comparison easier than running disconnected scripts.
Experiment flow
A typical experiment looks like this:

Create or select an experiment.
Load OCI context.
Select existing networking.
Provision a CPU/HPC instance.
Deploy llama.cpp.
Pick a model from the catalog or provide a custom GGUF URL.
Run benchmark presets.
Start the local endpoint proxy.
Use the endpoint from a sample app.
Delete infrastructure when done.
For the first run, I would start with a smaller quantized model. A smaller model gives a faster feedback loop. Once that works, move to larger models and compare behavior.
Native build mode
The app also supports advanced deploy settings.
By default, the portable llama.cpp build is safer because it works across different shapes. But if you want better performance for a specific machine, you can enable native build mode:
-DGGML_NATIVE=ON
This lets llama.cpp compile for the selected shape’s available CPU features.
If native mode fails with:
unsupported instruction 'vpdpbusd'
keep native mode enabled but also enable:
Disable VNNI instructions
in Advanced settings.
This is exactly the kind of hands-on detail that makes experimentation useful. You do not just learn the theory. You learn what actually breaks.
Run benchmarks
After deployment, run benchmark presets.
The app includes a Throughput comparison preset. The recommended flow is:

Create experiment 1.
Deploy llama.cpp.
Run the Throughput comparison preset as the Primary run.
Create experiment 2.
Change one variable.
Run the same preset as the Comparison run.
Review the comparison table.
The important part is:
Change one variable.
For example:

Experiment 1:
Qwen2.5 7B Q4_K_M
Portable build
Shape A

Experiment 2:
Qwen2.5 7B Q4_K_M
Native build
Same shape
Now the comparison is meaningful.
The benchmark comparison focuses on:

approximate output tokens/sec
output characters/sec
requests/sec
p95 latency
p95 TTFT
relative throughput versus the best Primary run
These metrics connect directly to the inference concepts I have been learning: TTFT, latency, throughput, and tokens/sec.
Start the endpoint proxy
After the model is deployed, open the Hackathon view and start the local endpoint proxy.
The generated endpoint looks like this:
CPU_ENDPOINT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/experiments/1/endpoint/v1
This is the endpoint the sample apps can use.
Run the direct CPU chat app
The first sample app talks directly to the CPU endpoint:

cd examples/direct-cpu-chat
npm install
CPU_ENDPOINT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/experiments/1/endpoint/v1 PORT=3001 npm run dev
Now you can talk to your own model running on the OCI instance.
This is the fun part. After spending so much time reading about inference systems, there is something satisfying about sending a message to your own endpoint and seeing the response come back.
Run the router chat app
The second sample app can use the CPU endpoint and an OpenAI model:

cd examples/router-chat
npm install
CPU_ENDPOINT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/experiments/1/endpoint/v1 \
OPENAI_API_KEY=replace-with-your-key \
OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini \
PORT=3002 \
npm run dev
This starts connecting to a bigger idea:
Not every request needs the same model.
A local CPU model may be enough for some requests. A larger hosted model may be better for others.
Eventually, this can evolve into a routing playground:

Simple chat → CPU model
Complex reasoning → hosted model
Private local task → local model
Long analysis → stronger endpoint
That is the type of experiment I want to run more often.
Where is app data stored?
The app stores generated state outside the repo:

~/.llm-inference-cloud/
├── state.db
├── keys/
├── prompts/
├── benchmarks/
└── logs/
This keeps generated keys, logs, prompts, and benchmark results separate from the Git repo.
Cleanup
When the experiment is done, use:
Delete infra
from the selected experiment.
This terminates the app-created OCI infrastructure.
For any tool that provisions cloud resources, cleanup should be part of the normal workflow:

Create experiment
Run benchmark
Save results
Delete infra
Not:

Create experiment
Forget instance
Find surprise bill later
Why this matters for my learning series
This project feels like a transition point in my learning.
The earlier articles helped build the mental model. Now I want to move more toward implementation.
I still want to write conceptual articles, but I also want more hands-on work:

run models
measure latency
compare throughput
test CPU shapes
move to GPUs
deploy with Kubernetes
try routing
visualize benchmark results
This app gives me a small lab environment for future articles.
What comes later?
This MVP starts with OCI, CPU inference, llama.cpp, benchmarks, and two sample apps.
Future improvements could include:

GPU support
vLLM deployments
Kubernetes support
multi-node experiments
better benchmark dashboards
cost comparison
more model catalogs
model routing policies
observability
experiment export
team or hackathon workflows
As I continue the learning series, I want the tool to grow with the topics I am learning.

When I study GPU inference, the app should support GPU experiments. When I study Kubernetes, the app should support Kubernetes deployments. When I study routing, the router app should become more capable. When I study observability, benchmark visualization should improve.
Main idea
The main idea is simple:
Make inference experiments easier to repeat.
Once experiments become easier to repeat, learning becomes faster.
I can test more models, compare more shapes, see real numbers, understand latency and throughput through actual runs, and connect theory with practice.
Final thoughts
This is still an MVP. There will be rough edges, missing features, and many things to improve.
But I am happy with this first version because it solves a real problem in my own learning workflow.
It helps me move from:
reading about inference systems
to:
running inference systems
If you are also learning LLM inference, CPU inference, model serving, or LLMOps, feel free to try it out.
Fork the repo. Run an experiment. Try the sample apps. Open an issue if something breaks. Raise a PR if you want to improve it.
I will keep working on this as I move deeper into GPUs, Kubernetes, routing, and distributed inference.
This is just the first iteration, but it already makes the learning process much more fun.

title: Building My Own Small Inference Cloud

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 15)
In the previous part, I tried to connect a few confusing pieces together:

CUDA
PyTorch
vLLM
CPU inference
GPU inference
model routing
load balancers
edge inference
Agentic AI

That article helped me build a better layered mental model. At the bottom, there is hardware. Above that, there are compute runtimes. Above that, there are model execution frameworks. Above that, there are inference engines. Above that, there are routers, gateways, and agent systems. But after writing that, one question became more interesting to me:
How does local or CPU-friendly inference actually work?
That leads naturally to:

llama.cpp
GGUF
quantized models
local inference
CPU inference
This article is my attempt to understand that layer better.
Why talk about llama.cpp now?
So far, a lot of the inference series focused on large-scale serving concepts:

KV cache
batching
multi-GPU inference
distributed serving
request routing
GPU communication
prefill vs decode
continuous batching
PagedAttention
vLLM architecture
Those concepts are very important for production GPU inference. But inference is not only about massive GPU clusters. There is another important side:

Can we run useful models locally?
Can we run smaller models on CPUs?
Can we use quantized models efficiently?
Can we build simple private endpoints?
Can we experiment without always needing GPUs?
This is where llama.cpp becomes very interesting.
What is llama.cpp?
At a simple level:

llama.cpp
=
a lightweight inference runtime
for running LLMs efficiently
in C/C++
It became popular because it made local LLM inference much more practical. Instead of needing a large cloud GPU setup just to experiment, we can run smaller and quantized models on:

laptops
desktops
CPU servers
edge devices
small cloud instances
That does not mean it is only for CPUs. It can also use GPU acceleration depending on the hardware and backend. But the important point is:
llama.cpp made local and resource-conscious inference much more accessible.
How is llama.cpp different from vLLM?
This was one of the first things I wanted to clarify for myself. Both can run LLM inference. But they are optimized for different situations. A simple mental model:

vLLM
=
high-throughput serving engine
for many concurrent requests,
especially GPU-backed serving

llama.cpp
=
lightweight local / CPU-friendly / quantized inference runtime
for running models efficiently on commodity hardware
That is not a perfect definition, but it is useful. vLLM shines when we care about:

serving many users
continuous batching
PagedAttention
GPU utilization
distributed inference
production serving
llama.cpp shines when we care about:

local inference
small models
quantized models
simple deployment
CPU-friendly experiments
edge-style workloads
Are they competing tools?
Not exactly. I think it is better to see them as tools for different parts of the inference landscape. For example:

Large model
many concurrent users
GPU cluster
production endpoint
This sounds like a vLLM-style problem. But:

small model
local machine
quantized model
private experiment
CPU server
This sounds like a llama.cpp-style problem. So the question is not:
Which one is better?
The better question is:
Which runtime matches the workload?
Why is llama.cpp important for learning?
For me, llama.cpp is useful because it makes inference feel tangible. When learning only through diagrams, concepts can remain abstract. But when I can actually:

download a model
run a local server
send a prompt
measure latency
compare quantization formats
change CPU threads
observe tokens/sec
the concepts become more real. This is especially useful after writing so many conceptual articles. At some point, I want to move from:
understanding inference systems
to:
running inference systems
llama.cpp is a very good bridge for that.
What problem does llama.cpp solve?
The basic problem is:

How can we run LLMs efficiently
without always needing a huge GPU setup?

Large models are expensive to serve. They need memory. They need compute. They need optimized runtimes. But not every task needs the largest model. For many practical tasks, a smaller model may be good enough. Examples:

basic summarization
classification
simple chat
routing decisions
local assistant tasks
structured extraction
draft generation
If a small quantized model can solve the task, then running it locally or on CPU can be very attractive.
What makes CPU inference difficult?

CPUs are general-purpose processors. They are flexible, but they do not have the same massive parallel compute profile as GPUs. A GPU is built for large parallel tensor operations. A CPU is built for broader general-purpose workloads. So for LLM inference, CPUs usually face challenges like:

lower parallel compute
lower memory bandwidth compared to GPU HBM
slower token generation for larger models
limited throughput for high concurrency
So CPU inference is not magic. It is a tradeoff.
Then why use CPUs at all?
Because CPUs are everywhere. They are available in:

laptops
desktops
cloud VMs
enterprise servers
edge devices
developer machines

They are also simpler to access than GPUs in many cases. For learning and experimentation, that matters a lot. If I can run a small model quickly on CPU, I can test ideas without waiting for GPU capacity. For some workloads, CPU inference may also be cheaper or easier to operate. So the value is not:
CPU beats GPU
The value is:
CPU is useful for the right workload.
What changed to make CPU inference more practical?
A few things came together. First, smaller models became much better. Today, models in the range of:

1B
3B
7B
8B
can be useful for many tasks. Second, quantization became more practical. Third, tools like llama.cpp made it easier to run quantized models efficiently. So the question shifted from:
Can I run the biggest model?
to:

What is the smallest model
that can solve this task well enough?
That question is very important for real inference systems.
What is GGUF?
GGUF is a model file format commonly used with llama.cpp. A simple mental model:

GGUF
=
a packaged model file format
that llama.cpp can load and run
When downloading models for llama.cpp, we often see files like:

model.Q4_K_M.gguf
model.Q8_0.gguf
model.F16.gguf
These filenames usually tell us something about the quantization format. For example:
represent different ways the model weights are stored.
Why does the model file format matter?
Because running an LLM is not only about the model architecture. The runtime needs to load:

weights
metadata
tokenizer information
quantization details
architecture details

The file format helps package these things in a way the runtime understands. So when I use llama.cpp, I am usually not downloading a raw PyTorch checkpoint directly. I am downloading a GGUF version that has already been converted and often quantized for this runtime.
What is quantization again?
A model is mostly weights. Weights are numbers. For example:
If we store these numbers in high precision, the model needs more memory. For example, FP16 uses:
16 bits per weight
So a rough estimate for a 7B model is:

7 billion weights × 2 bytes
≈ 14 GB
That is just for weights. It does not include KV cache, activations, runtime overhead, or other memory usage. Quantization stores weights with fewer bits. For example:

FP16 → 16 bits
INT8 → 8 bits
INT4 → 4 bits
The rough memory idea becomes:

FP16 model → larger
Q8 model → smaller
Q4 model → much smaller
Why does quantization help local inference?
Because local machines and CPU servers may not have enough memory or bandwidth for large full-precision models. Quantization helps by:

reducing model size
reducing memory usage
improving cache efficiency
making models easier to load
making inference possible on smaller machines
For example, a model that is too large in FP16 may become practical in Q4. This is one of the main reasons local inference became more accessible.
Does quantization make the model worse?
Sometimes. Quantization is a tradeoff. We are storing approximate versions of the original weights. That can reduce quality. But the quality drop may be acceptable depending on:

model size
quantization level
task difficulty
prompt style
expected answer quality
For many tasks, a quantized model can still be useful. For harder reasoning, coding, long-context analysis, or high-accuracy tasks, the difference may become more visible. So again, the question is:
Is this model good enough for this task?
Not:
Is this model universally best?
How should I think about Q4, Q5, Q8, and F16?
A simple mental model:

F16
=
larger memory usage,
better precision

Q8
=
smaller than F16,
often still strong quality

Q4 / Q5
=
much smaller,
more practical for local inference,
possible quality tradeoff

This is not a universal rule for every model and every task. But it helps as a starting point. If I want maximum quality and have enough memory, I may try higher precision. If I want local speed and lower memory usage, I may try Q4 or Q5. If I want a middle ground, Q8 may be useful.
Why do GGUF filenames look confusing?
Because the filename often includes both the model name and quantization type. Example:
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf
This tells us:

Model family: Qwen2.5
Model size: 7B
Instruction-tuned: Instruct
Quantization: Q4_K_M
Format: GGUF
At first, these names look noisy. But once the pattern becomes clear, they are useful. They tell us what we are about to run.
What happens when llama.cpp runs a model?
At a high level:

Load GGUF model
Initialize runtime
Tokenize prompt
Run prefill
Create KV cache
Run decode loop
Generate tokens
Stream or return output
This should look familiar now. Even though we are using llama.cpp instead of vLLM, many inference concepts still apply:

tokens
prefill
decode
KV cache
batching
latency
tokens/sec
memory usage
That is important. The runtime is different, but the core inference behavior is still related.
Does llama.cpp also use KV cache?

Yes. Autoregressive generation still needs previous context. During prefill, the model processes the prompt and builds KV cache. During decode, new tokens are generated one at a time, and the KV cache grows. So even in local inference, the same mental model applies:

Prompt tokens fill the KV cache.
Generated tokens extend the KV cache.
Longer context uses more memory.
This is why context length matters even for CPU inference.
Why does context length matter?
Because the longer the context, the more KV cache memory is needed. A short prompt may be easy. A long document may be much harder. For example:
500 tokens
is very different from:
32,000 tokens

Even if the model weights fit, the KV cache can become a major memory consumer. This connects directly to the earlier inference articles. Model size is not the only memory problem. Runtime state matters too.
What is prefill like in llama.cpp?
Prefill is when the prompt is processed. If the prompt is long, prefill takes longer. That affects:
time to first token
So when I benchmark local inference, I should not only look at final generation speed. I should also measure:
How long until the first token appears?
A model may generate tokens quickly after it starts, but still have slow prefill for long prompts.
What is decode like in llama.cpp?
Decode is the token-by-token generation loop. This affects:

tokens per second
inter-token latency
streaming speed
If the decode speed is low, the response feels slow even after the first token appears. So for local inference, I want to measure both:

TTFT
and
tokens/sec
because they show different parts of the user experience.
Why does tokens/sec matter?
Tokens/sec tells us how quickly the model generates output. For example:
5 tokens/sec
feels very different from:
40 tokens/sec
For interactive chat, tokens/sec matters a lot. For batch processing, throughput may matter more than streaming feel. So again, the right metric depends on the workload.
Why does TTFT matter?
TTFT means:
Time To First Token
This is how long the user waits before seeing the first generated token. TTFT is affected by:

queueing
prompt length
prefill speed
runtime overhead
hardware speed
model size
For a chat application, TTFT strongly affects perceived responsiveness. Even if total generation is fast, a long pause before the first token can feel bad.
What should I benchmark first?
For my own learning, I would start simple:

same model
same prompt
different quantization
Example:

Qwen2.5 7B Q4_K_M
vs
Qwen2.5 7B Q8_0
Then compare:

memory usage
TTFT
tokens/sec
latency
answer quality
After that, change one more variable:

same model
same quantization
different CPU shape
Then compare again. The important rule is:
Change one variable at a time.
Otherwise, the benchmark becomes hard to understand.
What variables matter in CPU inference?
A few important ones are:

model size
quantization format
number of CPU cores
CPU generation
memory bandwidth
thread count
context length
prompt length
output length
batch size
runtime build options
This is why CPU inference experiments can be surprisingly interesting. There are many small knobs that affect performance.
Why does thread count matter?
llama.cpp can use CPU threads to parallelize work. But more threads are not always automatically better. At some point:

thread overhead
memory bandwidth limits
CPU topology
can affect scaling. So it is useful to benchmark different thread counts instead of assuming the highest number is always best. This is a very practical learning point.
Why does native build matter?

A portable build is safer because it can run across more machines. A native build can compile for the specific CPU features available on the machine. That may improve performance. But it may also introduce compatibility issues if certain instructions are not supported. This is exactly the kind of thing I want to learn from hands-on experiments. Conceptually, we can say:

portable build
=
more compatible

native build
=
potentially faster,
but more hardware-specific
How does this connect to my OCI inference workbench?
Wokbench: https://github.com/aruanurag/llm-inference-lab/tree/main/apps/oci-inference-cloud
This is where the topic becomes hands-on for me. I recently started building a small inference cloud workbench for my own learning. The idea is simple:

provision infrastructure
deploy llama.cpp
download a GGUF model
start an endpoint
run benchmarks
compare results
clean up infrastructure

This gives me a repeatable loop. Instead of manually setting up everything every time, I can create experiments and compare them. That matters because inference learning needs repetition. One benchmark is not enough. I want to compare:

different models
different quantization formats
different shapes
different CPU counts
different prompts
different workloads
Why start with CPU on OCI?
Because it is simpler and still useful. Before jumping into GPUs, I want to understand:

How far can CPU inference go?
What does performance look like?
Which small models are usable?
How does quantization affect latency?
How does model size affect memory?
What does routing to a CPU model feel like?
Starting with CPU also keeps the feedback loop smaller. It lets me focus on fundamentals:

model loading
endpoint serving
benchmarking
TTFT
tokens/sec
latency
cleanup
These concepts will still matter later when I move to GPU inference.
Does CPU inference replace GPU inference?

No. This is important. CPU inference is not replacing GPU inference. For large models, high concurrency, long context, and low-latency production serving, GPUs are still extremely important. The better mental model is:

CPU inference
=
useful for smaller models,
local workloads,
experiments,
edge use cases,
and cost-sensitive tasks

GPU inference
=
important for larger models,
higher throughput,
lower latency,
and production-scale serving
So the future is not:
CPU vs GPU
It is more like:
CPU + GPU + NPU + routing
where the system chooses the right destination for each workload.
How does this connect to model routing?
Once we have a CPU inference endpoint, we can start routing requests. For example:

Simple request
  ↓
small quantized model on CPU

Complex request
  ↓
larger model on GPU or hosted endpoint

This is a very practical architecture. Not every request needs the most expensive model. If a smaller CPU model can answer well enough, that may reduce cost and improve privacy. If the request is too hard, the router can escalate to a stronger model. So CPU inference becomes one destination in a broader model routing system.
What does the architecture look like?
A simple local experiment may look like:

User
  ↓
Local app
  ↓
Router
  ├── CPU model endpoint
  └── Hosted LLM endpoint
The CPU model endpoint may be backed by:

llama.cpp
+
GGUF model
+
quantized weights
This is a small version of a bigger production idea:

route each request to the cheapest model
that can still solve it well enough
Where does Ollama fit?
Ollama is often used as an easy local model running experience. It makes it simple to download and run models locally. A useful mental model:

llama.cpp
=
low-level local inference runtime

Ollama
=
developer-friendly local model experience

This is not a deep technical comparison. But for learning, it helps. If I want more direct control over flags, builds, models, and benchmarks, llama.cpp is very useful. If I want a smoother local user experience, Ollama is very convenient.
Where does GGUF fit in that ecosystem?

GGUF is the model format that makes these local inference workflows easier. A model in GGUF format can be distributed with quantization already applied. Then tools like llama.cpp can load it and run inference. So the flow often looks like:

Choose model
Choose GGUF quantization
Download file
Run with llama.cpp
Benchmark
Compare output
This is why GGUF appears so frequently in local inference discussions.
What is the biggest mental shift for me?
Earlier, I mostly thought about inference in terms of:
large GPU serving systems
Now I am starting to see a broader picture:

large GPU serving
+
local CPU inference
+
quantized models
+
routing
+
edge use cases
This makes inference feel more like a platform problem. The platform may include:

small local models
CPU endpoints
GPU endpoints
hosted APIs
routers
benchmarking
observability
cost controls
The model is only one part. The system around the model decides how useful and efficient it becomes.
What should we not overclaim?
It is easy to get excited about local inference and say:
Everything will run locally.

I do not think that is the right view. Local inference is powerful, but it has limits. Small models are improving, but large models still matter. CPU inference is useful, but GPUs still matter. Quantization helps, but it can affect quality. So the practical view is:

Use local inference where it fits.
Use larger GPU models where they are needed.
Use routing to decide between them.
What is the key mental model?
I would summarize this article like this:

llama.cpp
helps run LLMs efficiently
on local and CPU-friendly environments.

GGUF
packages models in a format
that works well with llama.cpp.

Quantization
reduces model size
so models can run on smaller hardware.

CPU inference
does not replace GPU inference,
but it expands where inference can run.
How does this connect back to the full inference stack?
The stack now looks something like:

Application
  ↓
Router
  ↓
Inference endpoint
  ↓
Runtime
  ↓
Hardware
For a llama.cpp CPU endpoint:

Application
  ↓
Router
  ↓
llama.cpp server
  ↓
GGUF model
  ↓
CPU
For a vLLM GPU endpoint:

Application
  ↓
Router
  ↓
vLLM replica
  ↓
GPU workers
  ↓
GPU
The outer architecture can be similar. But the runtime and hardware are different.
Why does this matter for LLMOps?
Because LLMOps is not only about deploying the biggest model. It is about:

choosing the right model
choosing the right hardware
measuring performance
controlling cost
monitoring latency
maintaining reliability
improving user experience
CPU inference gives one more option in that toolbox. And once model routing becomes part of the system, this becomes even more important.
What comes next?
Now that llama.cpp, GGUF, quantization, and CPU inference are clearer, the next natural step is hands-on. The next article should probably be:
Running CPU Inference Experiments on OCI
That would connect this concept article with actual experiments:

provisioning an instance
deploying llama.cpp
choosing a GGUF model
starting an endpoint
running benchmarks
measuring TTFT
measuring tokens/sec
comparing quantization formats
cleaning up infrastructure
That is the direction I am personally excited about now. The conceptual foundation has been useful. But the next phase should be much more practical. I want to see:

real latency numbers
real throughput numbers
real model behavior
real tradeoffs
Because at the end of the day, inference systems are learned best by running them.

title: Understanding llama.cpp, GGUF, and Local CPU Inference

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 16)
In the previous part, I explored:

llama.cpp
GGUF
quantized models
local CPU inference
That article helped me understand how smaller models can run on CPUs, local machines, and cloud CPU instances.
But once I started thinking more practically, another question became very important:

How much memory do we actually need
to run LLM inference?
At first, I used to think about this mainly as:
Can the model fit?
But that is only one part of the story.
For inference, memory is not only used by the model weights.
Memory is also used by:

KV cache
temporary compute buffers
activations
runtime overhead
framework overhead
OS memory
safety margin
So the real question is not just:
Can I load the model?
The better question is:

Can I load the model
and still have enough memory
for the actual inference workload?
That is what this article is about.
Why does memory planning matter?
When running LLM inference, memory decides many practical things.
It decides:

which model can load
how long the context can be
how many users can run at once
how many tokens can be generated
how large the batch can be
whether the system crashes or stays stable
This is why memory planning is one of the most important parts of inference.
A model may run fine for one request.
But when we increase:

context length
concurrent users
batch size
output tokens
the same model may suddenly fail.
That is because the memory requirement is not fixed.
It grows with the workload.
What memory are we talking about?
The word memory can mean different things depending on where inference is running.
For CPU inference:
memory = system RAM
For GPU inference:
memory = GPU VRAM / HBM
For Apple Silicon or unified memory systems, CPU and GPU may share memory.
But the high-level idea is the same.
The model and runtime need enough memory to hold everything required for inference.
What are the main memory components?
A simple formula is:

Total inference memory
=
model weights
+
KV cache
+
temporary compute memory
+
runtime overhead
+
safety margin
The two biggest pieces are usually:

model weights
+
KV cache
Weights decide whether the model can load.
KV cache decides how much context and concurrency the system can handle.
That distinction is very important.
What are model weights?
Model weights are the learned parameters of the model.
When we say:
7B model
we mean the model has roughly:
7 billion parameters
Each parameter is a number.
For example:
These numbers are stored in memory.
So the first memory calculation is simple:

model weight memory
=
number of parameters
×
bytes per parameter
How many bytes does each parameter need?
That depends on precision.
A rough guide:

FP32  = 4 bytes per parameter
FP16  = 2 bytes per parameter
BF16  = 2 bytes per parameter
INT8  ≈ 1 byte per parameter
INT4  ≈ 0.5 byte per parameter
So for a 7B model in FP16:

7 billion × 2 bytes
≈ 14 GB
That means the weights alone need roughly 14 GB.
But that does not mean a 16 GB machine is enough.
Because we still need memory for KV cache and runtime overhead.
What happens with quantized models?
Quantization stores model weights using fewer bits.
For example:

FP16 → 16 bits
INT8 → 8 bits
INT4 → 4 bits
So the rough memory estimate becomes:

7B FP16
≈ 14 GB

7B INT8
≈ 7 GB

7B INT4
≈ 3.5 GB
In practice, there is some extra metadata and format overhead.
So the exact number may not be perfectly equal to the simple formula.
For GGUF models, the easiest practical estimate is often:

model weight memory
≈
GGUF file size
That is not perfect, but it is a very useful starting point.
Why is this useful for CPU inference?
When using llama.cpp, I usually download a GGUF model.
Example:
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf
The file size gives a practical sense of how much memory the model weights need.
If the GGUF file is around 4.5 GB, then the system needs at least that much memory just for loading the model.
But again, that is only the starting point.
The full memory requirement is larger.
What is KV cache?
KV cache stores key and value tensors from previous tokens.
During generation, the model needs to attend to previous tokens.
Without KV cache, it would need to recompute a lot of previous attention information again and again.
KV cache avoids that.
The simple mental model is:

Prompt tokens create KV cache.

Generated tokens extend KV cache.

Longer sequence means larger KV cache.
So KV cache grows with the number of tokens being processed.
Why does KV cache matter so much?
Because KV cache grows with:

context length
number of active requests
number of layers
number of KV heads
head dimension
KV cache precision
This means memory usage increases when we increase:

longer prompts
longer generated outputs
more concurrent users
larger batch sizes
larger context windows
This is why KV cache is central to inference memory planning.
What is the KV cache formula?
A useful formula is:

KV cache memory
=
active sequences
×
tokens per sequence
×
number of layers
×
2
×
number of KV heads
×
head dimension
×
bytes per KV element
The 2 is because we store:

K cache
+
V cache
A more accurate version is:

KV cache memory
=
total active tokens
×
number of layers
×
2
×
number of KV heads
×
head dimension
×
bytes per KV element
This is the formula I want to remember.
What are active tokens?
Active tokens means all tokens currently stored in KV cache across active requests.
For one request:

active tokens
=
prompt tokens
+
generated tokens so far
For multiple requests:

total active tokens
=
request A tokens
+
request B tokens
+
request C tokens
+
...
So if we have:

Request A → 1000 tokens
Request B → 2000 tokens
Request C → 500 tokens
then:

total active tokens
=
3500 tokens
That total drives KV cache memory.
What is a simple KV cache example?
Suppose a model has:

number of layers = 32
number of KV heads = 8
head dimension = 128
KV cache dtype = FP16
FP16 means:
2 bytes per element
Now KV cache per token is:
That equals:
131,072 bytes
or roughly:
128 KB per token
That means every token for every active request needs around 128 KB of KV cache memory.
What does that mean for one request?
If one request uses a 4096-token context:
So one request may need around:
512 MB of KV cache
That is only KV cache.
It does not include model weights.
What about multiple active requests?
If we have 16 active requests, each using 4096 tokens:
Now KV cache alone is around:
8 GB
This is where inference memory becomes interesting.
A model may fit.
But the workload may not.
What does total memory look like?
Suppose:

model weights = 14 GB
KV cache = 8 GB
runtime overhead = 3 GB
Then total memory becomes:

14 GB
+
8 GB
+
3 GB
=
25 GB
So even though the model weights are only 14 GB, a 16 GB system would not be enough for this serving workload.
This is the key lesson.
What is the most important intuition?
The simplest intuition is:

Model weights decide if the model can load.

KV cache decides how much inference workload can run.
Or:

Weights are mostly fixed.

KV cache grows with users and tokens.
This is why memory planning for inference is not only about model size.
It is also about workload shape.
What is workload shape?
Workload shape means the kind of requests the system is serving.
For example:

short prompts
short outputs
few users
is very different from:

long prompts
long outputs
many users
Even if both use the same model, the memory requirements can be very different.
A chatbot with short messages may be manageable.
A document analysis system with long context may need much more memory.
Why does context length matter?
Context length directly affects KV cache.
If we increase context from:
4096 tokens
to:
8192 tokens
then KV cache roughly doubles.
If we increase it again to:
32768 tokens
then KV cache becomes much larger.
That means long-context inference can become memory-heavy very quickly.
This is why setting a large context window is not free.
Why does concurrency matter?
Concurrency means how many requests are active at the same time.
If one request needs 512 MB of KV cache, then:

1 request  → 512 MB
4 requests → 2 GB
8 requests → 4 GB
16 requests → 8 GB
So concurrency multiplies KV cache memory.
This is why serving many users requires much more memory than running one local prompt.
How does this connect to batching?
Batching improves throughput by processing multiple requests together.
But batching also means more active sequences.
More active sequences means more KV cache memory.
So batching creates a tradeoff:

larger batch
=
better GPU/CPU utilization
+
more KV cache memory
This connects directly to continuous batching.
Continuous batching tries to keep the active batch full.
But every active request needs KV cache.
So the scheduler must constantly balance:

compute utilization
vs
memory capacity
How does this connect to PagedAttention?
PagedAttention exists because KV cache memory is difficult to manage efficiently.
Requests have different lengths.
They start at different times.
They finish at different times.
They grow token by token.
So the memory system needs to handle dynamic KV cache allocation.
The core idea is:

Continuous batching
keeps compute busy.

PagedAttention
helps manage KV cache memory efficiently.
This is why memory planning connects directly to vLLM internals.
What about temporary compute memory?
Besides weights and KV cache, inference needs temporary memory.
This includes:

activations
attention workspace
logits
sampling buffers
runtime buffers
communication buffers
framework overhead
During inference, activations are much smaller than training because we do not store everything for backpropagation.
But they still matter.
They can become more noticeable during:

large prefill
large batch size
long prompts
multi-GPU communication
So we should not plan memory with zero overhead.
What is a practical safety margin?
A practical estimate is:

total memory
≈
weights
+
KV cache
+
10% to 30% overhead
For small local experiments, the overhead may be smaller or manageable.
For production systems, I would be more conservative.
I do not want to run memory at 99%.
Because once the system is near the limit, small changes can cause failures.
Examples:

slightly longer prompt
more concurrent requests
larger batch
different model format
larger tokenizer buffers
runtime allocation spike
can push the system over the edge.
How should I calculate memory for CPU inference?
For CPU inference with llama.cpp, a practical formula is:

Required RAM
≈
GGUF model size
+
KV cache memory
+
compute buffers
+
OS memory
+
safety margin
The easiest first estimate:

Required RAM
≈
GGUF file size
+
KV cache estimate
+
20% overhead
This is not perfect, but it is useful.
Then the real measurement should come from running the server and reading the logs.
What should I check in llama.cpp logs?
When starting llama-server, I should look for memory-related logs such as:

model buffer size
KV buffer size
compute buffer size
graph memory
backend buffer size
These logs are very useful because they show what the runtime actually allocated.
So the practical workflow becomes:

estimate memory first
start the server
read actual memory logs
compare estimate vs reality
adjust settings
benchmark again
This is how the concept becomes practical.
Which llama.cpp settings affect memory?
Important settings include:

model file
context size
parallel slots
batch size
ubatch size
KV cache type
GPU offload layers
thread count
For CPU inference, context size is especially important.
A larger context means more KV cache memory.
More parallel slots means more simultaneous sequences.
So even with the same model, changing these settings can change memory usage significantly.
What does context size mean practically?
If I set a very large context size, I am asking the runtime to support more tokens.
That requires more KV cache memory.
For example:
context size = 4096
uses less KV cache than:
context size = 32768
So I should not set context length much larger than what my workload actually needs.
Large context is useful, but it has a memory cost.
How does this connect to the LLM Inference Workbench?
This is exactly the kind of thing I want the workbench to help me understand.
For each experiment, I want to track:

model
quantization
GGUF size
CPU shape
RAM
context size
parallel slots
batch size
TTFT
tokens/sec
p95 latency
memory usage
Then I can compare experiments.
For example:

Experiment 1:
Qwen2.5 7B Q4_K_M
context 4096
parallel 1

Experiment 2:
same model
context 8192
parallel 1

Experiment 3:
same model
context 4096
parallel 4
Now I can observe how memory changes.
This is much better than guessing.
What should I compare first?
I would start with one model and change one variable.
Example:

same model
same CPU shape
different context sizes
Then compare:

memory usage
TTFT
tokens/sec
latency
stability
After that, I can compare quantization formats:

Q4_K_M
vs
Q8_0
Then compare model sizes:

1.5B
vs
7B
vs
14B
The important rule is:
change one variable at a time
Otherwise, the results become hard to understand.
How should I calculate memory for GPU inference?
For GPU inference, the formula is similar:

Required GPU memory
≈
model weights in VRAM
+
KV cache in VRAM
+
activation / workspace memory
+
runtime overhead
+
safety margin
But there is one extra consideration.
If the model is split across multiple GPUs, the weight memory may be divided.
For tensor parallelism:
each GPU stores part of the model weights
For pipeline parallelism:
each GPU group stores some layers
For data parallelism:
each replica stores its own copy
So multi-GPU memory planning depends on the parallelism strategy.
What happens with tensor parallelism?
Suppose a model needs 80 GB of weights.
If we use tensor parallelism across 4 GPUs, then roughly:

80 GB / 4
=
20 GB per GPU
for weights.
This is simplified, but it gives the intuition.
By sharding weights, each GPU has more remaining memory for KV cache. That can help support larger context or more active requests. But tensor parallelism also adds communication cost.
So memory improves, but communication becomes important.
What happens with data parallelism?
Data parallelism is different. If we create 4 replicas, each replica has its own model copy. So memory is not divided across replicas.
Instead:

Replica 1 → full model copy
Replica 2 → full model copy
Replica 3 → full model copy
Replica 4 → full model copy
Data parallelism helps concurrency because requests can be spread across replicas.
But each replica needs enough memory to run the model and KV cache for its assigned users.
What is the difference between fitting and serving?
This is a very important distinction.
Fitting means:
Can I load the model?
Serving means:

Can I load the model
and handle the expected workload?
A model may fit for one request.
But it may not serve many users.
That is because serving adds:

concurrency
longer KV cache
batching
runtime overhead
latency constraints
So when planning inference memory, I should not stop at:
model loaded successfully
That only proves the first step.
What is the simplest capacity planning process?
I can use this process:

1. Estimate model weight memory.

2. Estimate KV cache per token.

3. Estimate total active tokens.

4. Multiply KV per token by active tokens.

5. Add temporary and runtime overhead.

6. Add safety margin.

7. Run the actual system.

8. Compare estimate with real measurements.
This gives both a mental model and a practical workflow.
What is a simple example?
Suppose:

model weights = 8 GB
KV cache per token = 128 KB
max tokens per request = 4096
active requests = 8
overhead = 3 GB
First calculate KV per request:
Then calculate KV for 8 requests:
Now total memory:

8 GB weights
+
4 GB KV cache
+
3 GB overhead
=
15 GB
Then add safety margin.
If we add 20%:
So I would not choose a 16 GB system for this workload.
I would want something closer to:
24 GB or more
That gives space for overhead and variance.
Why can estimates be wrong?
Memory estimates can be wrong because real systems have details like:

alignment
metadata
quantization overhead
framework buffers
fragmentation
memory preallocation
backend-specific buffers
different KV cache dtypes
different attention implementations
So the formula is not meant to be perfect.
It is meant to help us reason before running.
The real answer still comes from measurement.
What metrics should I track?
For memory experiments, I want to track:

model file size
loaded model memory
KV cache memory
total process memory
available system memory
context size
parallel slots
batch size
TTFT
tokens/sec
p95 latency
failure point
The failure point is useful.
For example:

works at context 4096
works at context 8192
starts swapping at context 16384
fails at context 32768
That teaches more than a single successful run.
What does this teach about inference systems?
It teaches that inference is not just compute.
Inference is also memory management.
The system is constantly balancing:

model size
context length
concurrency
latency
throughput
memory capacity
This is why modern serving engines spend so much effort on:

KV cache management
continuous batching
PagedAttention
prefix caching
chunked prefill
routing
scheduling
The hard part is not only generating tokens.
The hard part is generating tokens efficiently for many different requests under limited memory.
How does this connect to CPU inference?
For CPU inference, memory planning helps answer:

Can this model run on this machine?
How large can the context be?
How many parallel requests can I support?
When does the system start swapping?
Which quantization is practical?
This is very relevant for my LLM Inference Workbench.
If I can automate experiments around these questions, I can learn much faster.
Instead of saying:
this model feels slow
I can say:

this model uses this much memory,
with this context size,
and produces this tokens/sec,
on this CPU shape.
That is a much better learning loop.
How does this connect to GPU inference?
For GPU inference, memory planning helps answer:

Can this model fit in VRAM?
How much KV cache can we support?
How many active requests can run?
Do we need tensor parallelism?
Do we need more replicas?
Do we need a smaller context limit?
Do we need quantization?
This is where memory planning becomes architecture planning.
If one GPU is not enough, we need multi-GPU inference.
If one replica is not enough, we need more replicas.
If routing needs to consider cache locality, we need smarter distributed serving.
And that leads toward systems like llm-d.
What is the key mental model?
The key mental model is:

Total memory
=
weights
+
KV cache
+
overhead
But the deeper intuition is:

Weights are the cost of loading the model.

KV cache is the cost of serving the workload.
So when someone asks:
How much memory do I need for this model?
the answer should be:

For what context length?
For how many active requests?
With what precision?
On CPU or GPU?
Using which runtime?
Because the model alone is not enough information.
What comes next?
Now that memory planning is clearer, the next topic becomes very natural.
Once we understand that inference memory depends on:

KV cache
context length
active requests
routing
replicas
scheduling
the next question is:

How do large systems manage this
across a Kubernetes cluster?
That leads to:
llm-d
Because llm-d is about distributed LLM inference.
It connects many ideas we have already discussed:

vLLM
Kubernetes
replicas
routing
KV-cache-aware scheduling
disaggregated serving
distributed inference
So the next article can move from:
How much memory does one inference system need?
to:

How do we distribute inference
across many systems intelligently?
That feels like the right next step.

title: Understanding Memory Requirements for LLM Inference

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 17)
In the previous part, we explored how to estimate memory for an LLM inference workload.
The basic equation was:

Total memory
=
model weights
+
KV cache
+
runtime overhead
But the deeper lesson was:

Weights determine whether the model can load.

KV cache determines how much workload
the system can serve.
We also saw that memory requirements grow with:

context length
concurrent requests
batch size
generated tokens
That naturally leads to the next question:

What happens when one inference server
is no longer enough?
We can create more replicas.
We can add more GPUs.
We can deploy the model across a Kubernetes cluster.
But once we do that, another set of problems appears:

Which replica should receive each request?

Where is the request's KV cache?

Which replica has enough memory?

Which replica has the shortest queue?

Should prefill and decode run together?

How should the system scale?
This is where llm-d becomes interesting.
This article continues directly from the memory-planning questions in Part 16.
What is llm-d?
At a high level:

llm-d
=
a distributed inference serving stack
It helps coordinate LLM inference across multiple model servers, accelerators, nodes, and replicas.
A model server such as vLLM or SGLang runs the actual model.
llm-d sits around those model servers and helps coordinate them as one distributed serving system.
A simple mental model is:

vLLM / SGLang
=
runs the model efficiently

llm-d
=
coordinates many model servers efficiently

The project’s primary architecture is Kubernetes-native. Its official documentation describes llm-d as a composable stack that coordinates model-server pods using LLM-aware routing, distributed KV-cache management, disaggregated serving, multi-node execution, and autoscaling. It supports multiple inference engines and accelerator platforms. (llm-d)
Is llm-d an inference engine like vLLM?
No.
This distinction is very important.
vLLM is an inference engine.
It handles things like:

model execution
continuous batching
PagedAttention
KV cache allocation
prefill
decode
token sampling
llm-d operates at a higher level.
It handles things like:

routing between model servers
cluster-level request scheduling
KV-cache locality across replicas
prefill/decode disaggregation
flow control
autoscaling
multi-node deployment patterns
So the architecture may look like:

User
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
vLLM Model Server
  ↓
GPU Workers
  ↓
Model Computation
llm-d does not replace vLLM.
It coordinates a fleet of engines such as vLLM or SGLang.
What problem does llm-d solve?
Suppose we deploy three replicas of the same model:

Replica 1
Replica 2
Replica 3
Each replica may have:

its own scheduler
its own KV cache
its own request queue
its own GPU memory
its own active batches
Now requests start arriving.
A traditional load balancer may distribute them without understanding the internal state of each inference replica.
For example:

Request A → Replica 1
Request B → Replica 2
Request C → Replica 3
Request D → Replica 1
That may work for normal web applications.
But LLM requests are not normal web requests.
The best destination may depend on:

which replica already has the prompt prefix cached
which replica has free KV-cache capacity
which replica has the shortest queue
which replica can meet the latency target
which replica is a prefill worker
which replica is a decode worker
A generic load balancer usually does not understand these details.
llm-d introduces an inference-aware routing and scheduling layer.
Why is normal load balancing not enough?
Imagine two model replicas:

Replica 1 → 40% GPU utilization
Replica 2 → 40% GPU utilization
At first glance, both look equally healthy.
But internally:

Replica 1:
- has the request's prefix cached
- has enough free KV blocks
- has a short decode queue

Replica 2:
- does not have the prefix cached
- has high KV-cache pressure
- has several long prompts waiting
A normal load balancer might see:

Replica 1 = healthy
