Replica 2 = healthy
An inference-aware router sees:
Replica 1 is probably a much better destination.
That difference can affect:

time to first token
queueing time
prefill work
KV-cache hit rate
GPU utilization
total throughputIs llm-d only a smarter load balancer?
No.
Intelligent routing is one of its central capabilities, but llm-d covers a larger distributed inference problem.
A useful mental model is:

Load balancer
=
send traffic across endpoints

llm-d
=
understand inference state
and coordinate traffic, memory,
workers, phases, and scaling
Its major capabilities include:

LLM-aware routing
KV-cache-aware scheduling
distributed KV-cache indexing
KV-cache offloading
prefill/decode disaggregation
flow control
autoscaling
multi-node serving patterns
benchmarking and deployment recipes
The stack is composable, so operators can adopt only the pieces they need rather than deploying every capability at once. (GitHub)
What are the main parts of llm-d?
The current architecture is organized around three core concepts:

Router
InferencePool
Model Server
The official architecture describes them as follows:

Router
=
the intelligent entry point

InferencePool
=
the group of eligible model servers

Model Server
=
the engine that executes the model
(GitHub)
What is the llm-d Router?
The Router receives inference traffic and decides where it should go.
It has two major functional parts:

Proxy
+
Endpoint Picker
The proxy handles the actual network request.
The Endpoint Picker, usually called the EPP, provides the routing intelligence.
The flow looks like:

Request
  ↓
Proxy
  ↓
Endpoint Picker
  ↓
Selected Model Server
The proxy may be an L7 proxy such as Envoy.
The Endpoint Picker examines the eligible model servers and scores them.
It then tells the proxy which endpoint should receive the request.
What does the Endpoint Picker consider?
The Endpoint Picker can consider signals such as:

prefix-cache locality
KV-cache utilization
queue depth
session affinity
model metadata
configured routing policies
So it is not simply asking:
Which replica is next?
It is asking:

Which replica is currently
the best destination for this request?
The official llm-d documentation identifies prefix-cache locality, available KV-cache capacity, and queue depth as core scoring signals. (GitHub)
What is an InferencePool?
An InferencePool groups model-server endpoints that can serve the same base model.
Imagine:

InferencePool: Qwen-Model

├── Model Server A
├── Model Server B
├── Model Server C
└── Model Server D
The Router does not need to manually track every server.
It discovers the eligible servers through the InferencePool.
A useful mental model is:

Kubernetes Service
=
generic group of application endpoints

InferencePool
=
LLM-aware group of model-server endpoints
The InferencePool becomes the Router’s discovery target.
What is an InferencePool variant?
Not every server inside an InferencePool must have the same role.
Some servers may be optimized for:
prefill
Others may be optimized for:
decode
Some may use:

different hardware
different cost profiles
different latency profiles
different throughput profiles
llm-d represents these logical subgroups using labels called variants.
For example:

InferencePool: Model-X

Prefill Variant:
├── Prefill Server 1
└── Prefill Server 2

Decode Variant:
├── Decode Server 1
├── Decode Server 2
└── Decode Server 3
The Router can then choose endpoints based on the role needed for that request.
What is a Model Server?
The Model Server is the component that actually executes the model.
Examples include:

vLLM
SGLang
The Model Server handles the local inference work:

tokenization
prefill
decode
KV-cache operations
continuous batching
model execution
token generation
The Model Server may use:

one GPU
multiple GPUs
tensor parallelism
pipeline parallelism
multi-node workers
From llm-d’s perspective, it is an endpoint capable of performing a particular inference role.
What does a basic llm-d architecture look like?
At a high level:

Client
  ↓
Gateway / Proxy
  ↓
Endpoint Picker
  ↓
InferencePool
  ├── Model Server A
  ├── Model Server B
  ├── Model Server C
  └── Model Server D
Or more simply:

User
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
Best Model Server
  ↓
Inference Engine
  ↓
Accelerators
What happens when a request arrives?
Suppose the user sends:
"Explain distributed inference"
The flow may look like this:

1. Request reaches the gateway.

2. Proxy asks the Endpoint Picker
   where the request should go.

3. Endpoint Picker examines
   the available model servers.

4. It considers:
   - queue depth
   - cache locality
   - KV-cache pressure
   - server role
   - routing policy

5. It selects a model server.

6. Proxy forwards the request.

7. The model server performs
   prefill and decode.

8. Generated tokens stream
   back to the user.
The important point is:

The routing decision is aware
of LLM inference state.
How is the llm-d Router different from the vLLM scheduler?
This is another important distinction.
The llm-d Router decides:
Which model server should receive the request?
The vLLM scheduler decides:

Which requests inside this model server
should run during the next engine step?
So:

llm-d Router
=
cluster-level scheduling

vLLM Scheduler
=
engine-level scheduling
The full flow is:

Incoming Request
  ↓
llm-d chooses a model server
  ↓
vLLM admits the request
  ↓
vLLM places it into prefill/decode batches
  ↓
GPU executes the work
Both schedulers matter.
They simply operate at different levels.
How is this different from model routing?
Earlier in the series, we discussed model routing.
A model router may decide:

Simple request → small CPU model

Complex request → large GPU model

Document request → document model
That answers:
Which model or service should handle this request?
llm-d usually answers a different question:

Which serving endpoint for the selected model
should handle this request?
So:

Model Router
=
choose the model or service

llm-d Router
=
choose the best inference endpoint
inside the distributed serving system
A complete platform may use both:

User
  ↓
Model Router
  ↓
Large Model Service selected
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
Best model-server endpoint
  ↓
vLLM
  ↓
GPU
Why is KV-cache-aware routing important?
Suppose every request begins with the same large system prompt:

"You are an enterprise support assistant.
Follow these policies...
Use these product documents..."
That shared prefix may contain thousands of tokens.
Replica 1 has already processed that prefix.
Its KV cache contains the corresponding blocks.
Now another request arrives with the same prefix.
The Router has two choices.
Choice 1
Send the request to Replica 2:

Replica 2 has no cached prefix.

It must recompute the full prefill.
Choice 2
Send it to Replica 1:

Replica 1 already has the prefix cached.

It can reuse the cached computation.
Choice 2 may avoid a large amount of repeated prefill work.
That can improve:

TTFT
throughput
GPU efficiency
cost per request
What does normal round-robin routing do here?
A simple routing policy may produce:

Request 1 → Replica A
Request 2 → Replica B
Request 3 → Replica C
Request 4 → Replica A
Even when all four requests share the same prefix.
The cache becomes scattered.
Each replica may repeatedly process the same tokens.
The cluster has more hardware, but it is still wasting computation.
KV-cache-aware routing tries to preserve locality:

Requests with reusable prefixes
→ replicas containing those prefixes
llm-d supports prefix-cache-aware routing and can maintain an index of which token blocks are present on which model servers. (GitHub)
Is prefix-cache-aware routing the same as a sticky session?
Not exactly.
A sticky session usually means:

Same user
→ same replica
Prefix-cache-aware routing means:

Request
→ replica containing the most useful prefix
Sometimes these result in the same choice.
But not always.
For example, many different users may share:

the same system prompt
the same document prefix
the same agent instructions
the same cached conversation history
Prefix-aware routing can potentially reuse that shared state even when the users are different.
So the routing decision is based on:
cache similarity
not only:
user identity
What does distributed KV cache mean?
It does not necessarily mean there is one giant shared GPU memory space.
Instead, it usually means:

KV-cache blocks are distributed
across multiple model servers.
For example:

Replica A:
Prefix X blocks

Replica B:
Prefix Y blocks

Replica C:
Prefix Z blocks
The distributed serving system needs to know:

which blocks exist
where they exist
whether they can be reused
whether they should be transferred
whether they should be offloaded
So a better mental model is:

Distributed KV cache
=
many local caches
+
cluster-level knowledge
+
routing and transfer mechanisms
What is KV-cache indexing?
KV-cache indexing means maintaining information about where cached token blocks live.
Imagine a logical index:

Prefix A → Replica 1
Prefix B → Replica 3
Prefix C → Replica 1 and Replica 2
When a request arrives, the Router can consult this information.
It may discover:

Replica 1 has 80% of the prefix cached.

Replica 2 has 20% cached.

Replica 3 has none.
But cache locality is not the only factor.
Perhaps Replica 1 is overloaded.
Then the Router must balance:

reuse cached computation
vs
avoid an overloaded replica
That is what makes inference routing a real scheduling problem.
Does the Router always choose the replica with the largest cache hit?
Not necessarily.
Suppose:

Replica 1:
90% prefix match
very long queue

Replica 2:
70% prefix match
almost idle
The best choice may depend on:

estimated prefill cost
queue waiting time
KV-cache capacity
latency target
request priority
So an intelligent policy may calculate something like:

Expected completion time
=
queue delay
+
missing prefill work
+
decode time
The best destination is not always the emptiest replica.
It is also not always the replica with the highest cache match.
The router must consider both.
How does this connect to memory planning?
In Part 16, we used:

Total memory
=
weights
+
KV cache
+
overhead
That formula still applies to every model server.
llm-d does not make the memory requirement disappear.
Instead, it helps coordinate memory across the fleet.
For example:

Replica A is low on KV space.

Replica B has more free blocks.

Replica C contains a valuable cached prefix.
The Router can consider that information when selecting a destination.
So the memory question becomes:

Not only:
Does the cluster have enough memory?

But also:
Where is that memory available?
Where is useful state already cached?
Does llm-d make model weights smaller?
No.
llm-d does not quantize the model.
It does not reduce the parameter count.
It does not replace tensor parallelism.
If a model needs 80 GB of weight memory, the model still needs approximately that memory somewhere in the serving topology.
llm-d helps coordinate:

where model servers run
how requests reach them
how KV cache is reused
how workers are scaled
how runtime phases are distributed
It improves orchestration.
It does not change the mathematical size of the model.
What is KV-cache offloading?
GPU memory is fast, but limited.
Once GPU HBM becomes full, the system may need another place to store less-active KV-cache blocks.
A memory hierarchy may look like:

GPU HBM
  ↓
CPU memory
  ↓
local or shared storage
The fastest and most active blocks remain close to the accelerator.
Other blocks may be moved to a slower, larger tier.
When those blocks are needed again, they can be restored.
A useful analogy is:

GPU KV cache
=
hot working set

CPU memory
=
warm cache tier

Storage
=
larger cold cache tier
llm-d supports KV-cache management patterns that include cache indexing and tiered offloading beyond accelerator memory. (GitHub)
Does offloading make memory unlimited?
No.
Offloading expands effective capacity, but slower tiers have costs.
Moving data between:

GPU
CPU
storage
takes time and bandwidth.
So the tradeoff becomes:

recompute the prefix
vs
reload cached KV blocks
If loading the cache is faster than recomputing it, reuse may help.
If the cache is stored too far away or the network is slow, recomputation may be cheaper.
Again, the correct decision depends on the workload and infrastructure.
What is prefill/decode disaggregation?
Earlier, we learned that inference has two different runtime phases:

Prefill
and
Decode
Prefill processes the prompt.
Decode generates tokens one at a time.
These phases have different performance characteristics.
A simple model server handles both:

Model Server
├── Prefill
└── Decode
This is called a monolithic deployment.
Prefill/decode disaggregation separates them:

Prefill Workers
+
Decode Workers
Now one set of workers processes prompts.
Another set generates output tokens.
How is this different from tensor or pipeline parallelism?
The distinction is:

Tensor Parallelism
=
split tensors inside a layer

Pipeline Parallelism
=
split model layers

Data Parallelism
=
replicate the model-serving unit

Prefill/Decode Disaggregation
=
split runtime phases
With prefill/decode disaggregation:

Prefill cluster
=
optimized for prompt processing

Decode cluster
=
optimized for token generation
Each cluster may still use:

tensor parallelism
pipeline parallelism
data parallelism
So disaggregation does not replace the earlier parallelism strategies.
It exists at another layer.
What does a disaggregated request flow look like?
Suppose a user sends a long prompt.
The flow may be:

User
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
Prefill Worker
  ↓
Prompt is processed
  ↓
KV cache is created
  ↓
KV cache is transferred
  ↓
Decode Worker
  ↓
Tokens are generated
  ↓
Response streams to user
The Router must therefore choose two destinations:

Which prefill worker?

Which decode worker?
It must also coordinate the handoff between them.
Why separate prefill and decode?
Because they stress hardware differently.
Prefill usually involves:

many input tokens
large matrix operations
high compute utilization
Decode usually involves:

one token per sequence per step
repeated weight and KV-cache reads
latency-sensitive execution
memory-bandwidth pressure
When both phases share the same workers, large prefill requests can interfere with active decode requests.
For example:

Long prompt arrives
  ↓
Large prefill starts
  ↓
Existing decode requests slow down
  ↓
Inter-token latency increases
By separating the phases, operators can scale and tune them independently.
What does independent scaling mean?
Suppose the workload has very long prompts but short outputs.
The system may need:

more prefill capacity
fewer decode workers
Another workload may have short prompts but very long responses.
It may need:

fewer prefill workers
more decode capacity
With a monolithic deployment, each replica contains both capabilities.
With disaggregation, the ratio can be adjusted:

2 Prefill Workers
+
6 Decode Workers
or:

6 Prefill Workers
+
2 Decode Workers
That can better match the workload shape.
What is the major cost of disaggregation?
The KV cache must move from the prefill worker to the decode worker.
That transfer can be large.
The request cannot begin decode until the required KV-cache state is available.
So networking becomes part of the critical path.
The flow is now:

Prefill compute
+
KV-cache transfer
+
Decode compute
A slow transfer directly increases time to first token.

Current llm-d disaggregated serving uses transfer mechanisms such as NIXL with high-speed network transports. The project’s networking guidance emphasizes that KV-cache transfer time becomes a first-order contributor to TTFT. (GitHub)
Does prefill/decode disaggregation always improve performance?
No.
It depends on:

prompt length
output length
request concurrency
GPU topology
network bandwidth
transfer latency
prefill/decode worker ratio
For a small model with short prompts, the transfer overhead may not be worthwhile.
For long-context workloads where prefill heavily interferes with decode, separation may be useful.
So disaggregation should not be treated as:
always faster
It should be treated as:

a topology that may improve performance
for the right workload

Official llm-d benchmarks have also shown that the benefit varies with concurrency and workload shape, which is why the project provides tested configurations rather than presenting one universal topology. (llm-d)
What are llm-d’s “well-lit paths”?
Distributed inference has many possible configurations.
For example:

How many prefill workers?
How many decode workers?
Which tensor-parallel size?
Which networking backend?
Which cache policy?
Which routing policy?
Which autoscaling metric?
There is no single answer that works everywhere.
llm-d uses the term:
Well-Lit Paths
for tested and benchmarked deployment recipes.
A well-lit path may include:

deployment manifests
Helm configurations
hardware assumptions
performance settings
sample workloads
benchmark results
observability configuration
The idea is:

Do not start with an empty page.

Start with a tested pattern,
measure it,
then adapt it.
The project documents well-lit paths for patterns such as intelligent scheduling, disaggregated serving, and large multi-node workloads. (GitHub)
How does flow control fit into llm-d?
Suppose every model server maintains its own isolated queue.
The Router sends a request to Replica A.
Immediately afterward, Replica A becomes overloaded.
The request is now stuck behind work already assigned to that server.
Another replica may become free, but the request has already been committed.
Flow control can delay the final endpoint decision until capacity is available.
This is sometimes called:
late-binding scheduling
Instead of:

Request arrives
→ immediately assign replica
→ wait in that replica's queue
the system can use:

Request arrives
→ hold in an inference-aware queue
→ choose the best replica
  when capacity becomes available
This gives the Router more current information when making the decision.
Why is centralized queueing useful?
It can help prevent this situation:

Replica A:
10 requests waiting

Replica B:
0 requests waiting
while another new request is accidentally sent to Replica A.
A cluster-level queue gives the routing system a better view of total demand.
It can also support:

request priorities
tenant fairness
interactive vs batch traffic
admission control
latency SLOs
Current llm-d routing capabilities include policy-aware flow control, priority dispatch, late binding, and guardrails for requests that cannot meet configured latency objectives. (GitHub)
What is admission control?
Admission control asks:
Should this request enter the serving system now?
Suppose every replica is saturated.
The system has several choices:

accept the request and let latency explode

queue the request

reject the request

send it to another model or cluster
Sometimes accepting everything is worse than rejecting some traffic.
If the system keeps admitting requests beyond capacity:

queues grow
KV-cache pressure grows
TTFT increases
inter-token latency increases
timeouts increase
Admission control protects the requests already being served.
How does autoscaling fit into this?
Kubernetes can add or remove model-server replicas.
But traditional autoscaling often looks at:

CPU utilization
GPU utilization
Those signals alone may not describe inference demand well.
A GPU can be highly utilized but still healthy.
Another GPU can look underutilized while its KV cache is almost full.
More useful inference signals may include:

queue depth
request arrival rate
active sequences
KV-cache pressure
TTFT
TPOT
throughput
pending token work
llm-d can expose router-level demand metrics for Kubernetes autoscaling and also supports more advanced workload-variant scaling patterns. (GitHub)
What is a workload variant?
Suppose the same model is available in several forms:

Variant A:
expensive GPU
low latency

Variant B:
cheaper GPU
higher throughput

Variant C:
quantized model
lower cost
Or:

Variant A:
prefill workers

Variant B:
decode workers
Variants allow the platform to distinguish these serving profiles.
An autoscaler or router can then reason about:

which variant should grow
which variant should shrink
which variant can meet the SLO
which variant is most cost-effective
Does llm-d replace Kubernetes?
No.
llm-d builds on Kubernetes.
Kubernetes still manages:

pods
nodes
deployments
networking
health checks
resource requests
scheduling
restarts
scaling primitives
llm-d adds inference-specific intelligence.
A simple mental model is:

Kubernetes
=
manages workloads and infrastructure

llm-d
=
manages distributed inference behavior
Is llm-d limited to Kubernetes?
llm-d was designed as a Kubernetes-native project, and its main architecture uses resources such as Gateways, InferencePools, labels, Deployments, and autoscaling primitives.

However, the project has also introduced a discovery mode that lets its routing intelligence operate outside Kubernetes environments. The central routing ideas—KV-cache awareness, prefix affinity, flow control, and disaggregated routing—do not fundamentally require Kubernetes. (llm-d)
For this series, the most useful starting point is still:

llm-d
=
Kubernetes-native distributed inference
because that is where the architecture is easiest to connect with LLMOps.
Does llm-d only work with vLLM?
No.
vLLM has been a major engine in the llm-d ecosystem, but the architecture is designed to support multiple model servers.
Current project documentation lists engines such as:

vLLM
SGLang
and multiple accelerator platforms. (GitHub)
The key abstraction is:
Model Server
As long as the server exposes the interfaces and signals required by the stack, it can participate in the distributed serving architecture.
Does llm-d make a single request faster?
Not automatically.
If there is:

one model server
one request
no reusable prefix
no queue
no memory pressure
adding a distributed routing layer may not help much.
The main benefits appear when the system has:

multiple replicas
many concurrent requests
repeated prefixes
long prompts
KV-cache pressure
different worker roles
strict latency targets
llm-d is primarily about improving system-level behavior.
It tries to make the whole fleet more efficient.
When might llm-d be unnecessary?
A simple deployment may not need it.
For example:

one local model
one vLLM server
small traffic
no Kubernetes
no scaling requirement
In that case:

Application
  ↓
vLLM
  ↓
GPU
may be enough.
Adding llm-d would introduce:

more components
more configuration
more observability needs
more networking complexity
Distributed systems should solve an actual scaling problem.
They should not be added only because they look advanced.
When does llm-d start becoming useful?
It becomes more relevant when we have:

multiple inference replicas
large or variable workloads
long-context requests
repeated prompt prefixes
many concurrent users
prefill/decode interference
multi-node model deployments
cost or latency SLOs
Kubernetes-based operations
At that point, the problem changes from:
How do I run this model?
to:

How do I operate a fleet
of model-serving systems efficiently?
That is the problem llm-d is designed around.
What does llm-d not solve?
llm-d does not remove the fundamental limits of inference.
It does not eliminate:

autoregressive decoding
model weight memory
KV-cache growth
network latency
GPU saturation
hardware failures
It helps coordinate these constraints.
But operators still need to understand:

workload shape
capacity
memory
network topology
latency targets
cost constraints
There is no distributed system that makes these tradeoffs disappear.
What should we monitor in an llm-d deployment?
At the request level:

TTFT
TPOT / inter-token latency
end-to-end latency
request failures
queueing time
At the inference level:

input tokens/sec
output tokens/sec
active sequences
batch occupancy
prefix-cache hit rate
KV-cache utilization
At the routing level:

requests per endpoint
routing decisions
queue depth
cache-affinity score
request priority
admission failures
At the infrastructure level:

GPU utilization
GPU memory
network throughput
KV-transfer time
pod health
node health
replica count
For disaggregated serving, this metric becomes especially important:
KV-cache transfer time
Because a slow transfer directly affects the time before decode can begin.
What is the full mental model now?
The complete architecture can look like:

User
  ↓
API Gateway
  ↓
Model Router
  ↓
Selected Model Service
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
InferencePool
  ├── Prefill Variant
  │     ├── Prefill Worker A
  │     └── Prefill Worker B
  │
  └── Decode Variant
        ├── Decode Worker A
        ├── Decode Worker B
        └── Decode Worker C
              ↓
         vLLM / SGLang
              ↓
         GPU Workers
For a normal monolithic deployment:

User
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
InferencePool
  ├── vLLM Replica A
  ├── vLLM Replica B
  └── vLLM Replica C
The Router chooses the best replica.
The engine scheduler manages work inside that replica.
What is the simplest way to remember the layers?

Kubernetes
=
keeps the workloads running

llm-d
=
coordinates the inference fleet

vLLM / SGLang
=
runs inference inside each serving unit

CUDA / accelerator runtime
=
executes hardware operations

GPU / accelerator
=
performs the computation
Or:

Kubernetes manages infrastructure.

llm-d manages distributed inference.

vLLM manages local inference.

The accelerator performs the math.
What is the biggest mental shift?
Until now, many of the articles focused on one model-serving system.
We asked:

How does one server manage KV cache?

How does one engine batch requests?

How much memory does one workload need?
llm-d moves the mental model to the cluster level.
Now the questions become:

Where is the useful cache?

Which endpoint has capacity?

Where should prefill run?

Where should decode run?

Should the KV cache move?

Should another replica start?

Can this request meet its latency target?
That is a major shift.
We are no longer only optimizing model execution.
We are optimizing:

placement
routing
memory locality
network transfers
worker specialization
cluster capacity
What is the key intuition?
The easiest summary is:

vLLM makes an inference engine efficient.

llm-d makes a fleet of inference engines
work together intelligently.
A slightly deeper version is:

llm-d connects:

Kubernetes
+
inference-aware routing
+
distributed KV-cache management
+
prefill/decode disaggregation
+
autoscaling
+
model-serving engines
Its goal is not only to add more servers.
Its goal is to use those servers more intelligently.
What comes next?
This article introduced the overall llm-d architecture.
But one idea deserves a much deeper look:
KV-cache-aware routing
How does the Router know which prefixes are cached?
How does it compare cache locality against queue depth?
What happens when two replicas contain parts of the same prefix?
When should the system reuse cache, transfer cache, or recompute?
That leads naturally to:
LLM Inference Challenges (Part 18)
Understanding KV-Cache-Aware Routing
Because once inference becomes distributed, the important question is no longer only:
Do we have enough KV cache?
It becomes:

Where is the KV cache,
and how do we send each request
to the place where it is most useful?

title: Understanding llm-d and Distributed Inference

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 18)
In the previous part, we explored llm-d and how it coordinates distributed inference across model servers, replicas, GPUs, and Kubernetes nodes. We also introduced an important idea:

Once inference becomes distributed,
the question is no longer only:
Do we have enough KV cache?

It becomes:
Where is the useful KV cache,
and which request should go there?

That question deserves a deeper look because KV-cache-aware routing is one of the ideas that makes routing in LLM inference very different from traditional load balancing. At first, the idea sounds simple:

Find the replica with the matching cache.
Send the request there.

But once queue depth, cache eviction, partial matches, memory pressure, and multiple replicas enter the picture, the routing decision becomes much more interesting. This article is my attempt to build that mental model.
Why does KV-cache-aware routing need its own article?
Traditional load balancing usually thinks about:

healthy endpoints
active connections
request counts
CPU utilization
response latency LLM inference needs to consider all of those things. But it may also need to understand:
which prompt prefixes have already been processed
where their KV-cache blocks currently live
how much of a new prompt can be reused
whether that replica has enough KV-cache capacity
whether waiting for that replica is cheaper than recomputing elsewhere So routing is no longer based only on:
Which server is least busy?
It may also be based on:

Which server has already completed
the most useful work for this request?
First, what is a prompt prefix?
A prefix is the beginning portion of a prompt. Suppose two requests look like this:

Request A:
[System Prompt]
[Company Policies]
[Product Documentation]
Question: How do I reset my password?

Request B:
[System Prompt]
[Company Policies]
[Product Documentation]
Question: How do I update my billing address?
The final questions are different. But most of the beginning is identical:

[System Prompt]
[Company Policies]
[Product Documentation]
That shared beginning is the reusable prefix. Other examples include:

the same system prompt used for every request
the same conversation history in a multi-turn chat
the same document queried with different questions
the same agent instructions repeated across tool calls
the same retrieved context used by several RAG requests
What is prefix caching?

When an inference engine processes a prompt, it creates KV-cache entries for the prompt tokens. If another request later begins with the same token sequence, the engine may reuse those KV-cache blocks instead of recomputing that shared portion. This is commonly called:
Prefix Caching
or:
Automatic Prefix Caching
vLLM’s Automatic Prefix Caching stores KV-cache blocks from previous requests and allows a later request with the same prefix to skip computation for the shared portion. (vLLM)
Does prefix caching store the model’s answer?
No. It does not cache the generated answer. It caches the intermediate key and value tensors produced while processing the prompt. The system is not saying:

I have seen this question before,
so I will return the old response.
It is saying:

I have already processed these prefix tokens,
so I do not need to compute them again.
The new request can still:

contain a different final question
generate a different response
use different sampling settings
continue along a different token path
What does prefix caching actually save?
It saves prefill computation. Suppose a request contains:

8000 shared prefix tokens
+
100 new tokens
Without a cache hit:
Process all 8100 tokens
With a reusable prefix:

Reuse 8000 tokens
Process only the new 100 tokens
This can reduce:

prefill work
time to first token
accelerator usage
cost per request
repeated memory traffic But prefix caching does not make the new output tokens generate in parallel. It mainly helps prefill, not decode. vLLM’s documentation specifically notes that Automatic Prefix Caching reduces prompt-processing time but does not reduce the time required to generate new tokens. (vLLM)
What happens on one inference server?
With one model server, the flow is easier:

Request A
  ↓
vLLM processes shared prefix
  ↓
KV-cache blocks remain available

Request B with same prefix
  ↓
vLLM finds matching blocks
  ↓
Shared prefill is skipped
The inference engine manages:

the KV-cache blocks
block hashes
cache lookup
cache eviction
reuse during the next request Everything happens inside one engine.
What changes when we add multiple replicas?
Suppose we now have three replicas:

Replica A
Replica B
Replica C
Each replica has:

its own model weights
its own scheduler
its own active batches
its own GPU memory
its own local KV cache The caches are not automatically identical. For example:

Replica A:
Prefix X
Prefix Y

Replica B:
Prefix Z

Replica C:
No reusable prefix
Now a request arrives containing Prefix X. If it goes to Replica A:
Prefix X can be reused.
If it goes to Replica B or C:
Prefix X must be recomputed.
The model is the same. The hardware may be the same. But the request can behave very differently depending on which replica receives it.
Why can round-robin routing hurt prefix caching?
A round-robin load balancer might route requests like this:

Request 1 → Replica A
Request 2 → Replica B
Request 3 → Replica C
Request 4 → Replica A
That works well when requests are:

short
uniform
independent But LLM requests can be long, multi-turn, and highly repetitive. If related requests are scattered across replicas:
the same prefix may be processed repeatedly
each replica builds a separate copy of the cache
useful cache locality is lost
time to first token may increase
GPU work is duplicated llm-d’s optimized baseline combines prefix awareness with load awareness because ordinary round-robin policies do not understand these LLM-specific request patterns. (llm-d)
What is KV-cache-aware routing?
KV-cache-aware routing means selecting a model-server endpoint partly based on which KV-cache blocks it already contains. A simple flow is:

New Request
  ↓
Examine Prompt Prefix
  ↓
Find Replicas with Matching KV Blocks
  ↓
Compare Cache Locality and Current Load
  ↓
Select Endpoint

In llm-d, this intelligence lives in the Router’s Endpoint Picker, or EPP. The goal is to route a request toward a replica where the shared prefix can be reused, while still considering whether that replica is healthy and has enough capacity. (llm-d)
Does this create one shared KV cache?
Not necessarily. A useful mental model is:

Not one giant shared cache.

Many local caches
+
knowledge of where blocks live
+
routing decisions based on that knowledge
For example:

Replica A → Blocks 1, 2, 3, 4
Replica B → Blocks 1, 2
Replica C → No matching blocks
The Router does not need to merge all GPU memory into one memory space. It needs enough information to understand:

Which replica currently has
the most useful state?
What exactly needs to match?
Prefix caching is based on token sequences, not semantic similarity. These prompts may mean almost the same thing:

Explain KV cache.

Please explain KV cache.
But they begin with different tokens. So they may not share the same cache blocks. Similarly, small differences can break a prefix match:

different whitespace
different system-prompt versions
different chat templates
messages in a different order
different retrieved documents
different tokenizer configurations The important rule is:

Same meaning
does not guarantee
same token prefix.
How does vLLM represent cached prefixes?
vLLM divides KV cache into fixed-size blocks. Each full block represents the KV state for a group of tokens. For prefix caching, vLLM uses a hash-based design. A block key incorporates:

the parent block’s hash
the tokens in the current block
additional identifying values when required Those additional values can include things such as LoRA identifiers, multimodal input hashes, or cache salts used for isolation. Because the parent hash is included, the same token block appearing after a different prefix receives a different identity. vLLM caches full blocks and uses this chained hashing structure to identify reusable prefixes. (vLLM)
What does chained hashing mean?
Imagine a prompt split into four blocks:

Block 1 → [A B C D]
Block 2 → [E F G H]
Block 3 → [I J K L]
Block 4 → [M N O P]
Conceptually:

Hash 1
=
hash(Block 1)

Hash 2
=
hash(Hash 1 + Block 2)

Hash 3
=
hash(Hash 2 + Block 3)

Hash 4
=
hash(Hash 3 + Block 4)
This creates a chain. If another prompt starts with the same blocks:

[A B C D]
[E F G H]
[I J K L]
then its first three block hashes should match. The engine can reuse those blocks. If the fourth block differs, computation continues from that point.
Can a request have a partial cache hit?
Yes. Suppose a request contains eight prompt blocks:
Replica A contains:
Replica B contains:
Replica C contains:
No matching blocks
The approximate match ratios are:

Replica A → 6 / 8 = 75%
Replica B → 2 / 8 = 25%
Replica C → 0 / 8 = 0%
Replica A has the strongest cache affinity. It can reuse six blocks and compute only the remaining suffix.
Does the entire prompt need to match?
No. A full cache hit is useful, but partial reuse can also save substantial work. For example:

10,000-token prompt
6000 tokens cached
4000 tokens uncached
Reusing 6000 tokens may still be valuable. So the Router is not always asking:
Is this prompt cached?
It may be asking:

How much of this prompt
is cached on each endpoint?
Is the match ratio enough?
Not always. Consider these two cases:

Request A:
90% of 100 tokens cached
=
90 cached tokens

Request B:
60% of 10,000 tokens cached
=
6000 cached tokens
Request A has the higher percentage. But Request B may avoid much more computation. This is why a routing policy may consider:

match ratio
absolute matched length The current llm-d prefix-cache scorer supports both the proportion of matched blocks and the absolute number of matched tokens, with configurable weighting between them. (GitHub)
Why not always choose the largest cache match?
Because the replica with the best cache may also be overloaded. Suppose:

Replica A:
90% prefix match
20 requests waiting
High KV-cache pressure

Replica B:
70% prefix match
No queue
Plenty of KV-cache capacity
Replica A saves more prefill work. But the request may wait a long time before running. Replica B needs more computation. But it may start immediately. The real question becomes:

Is waiting for the best cache hit
cheaper than recomputing on a less busy replica?
What is the Router really trying to minimize?
A useful conceptual model is:

Expected latency
≈
queueing delay
+
uncached prefill time
+
decode time
This is not one universal llm-d formula. It is a way to understand the tradeoff. Cache-aware routing reduces:
uncached prefill time
Load-aware routing reduces:
queueing delay
The Router needs both.
What load signals can matter?
Useful signals may include:

queue depth
active requests
token load
KV-cache utilization
predicted TTFT
predicted inter-token latency
prefix-cache match llm-d’s Router supports modular scorers for queue depth, running requests, token load, KV-cache utilization, latency, and prefix affinity. Its optimized baseline also probes endpoint metrics and combines load awareness with prefix awareness to avoid hotspots. (llm-d)
How does the Endpoint Picker make a decision?
The llm-d Endpoint Picker follows a general lifecycle:

Filter
  ↓
Score
  ↓
Pick
Filter
Remove endpoints that should not handle the request. For example:

unhealthy endpoint
wrong model
wrong worker role
insufficient SLO headroom
incompatible LoRA adapter
Score
Assign scores to the remaining endpoints. For example:

higher prefix match → better score
shorter queue → better score
lower KV-cache utilization → better score
more latency headroom → better score
Pick
Select the final endpoint using the combined scores. The EPP supports multiple weighted scorers, so routing can balance cache reuse against load rather than relying on one signal alone. (llm-d)
What would a simplified scoring example look like?
Suppose the Router gives equal importance to:

Prefix Cache Score
Load Score
KV Capacity Score
The candidate scores might look like:

Replica A:
Prefix = 0.9
Load   = 0.2
KV     = 0.3

Replica B:
Prefix = 0.7
Load   = 0.9
KV     = 0.8

Replica C:
Prefix = 0.0
Load   = 1.0
KV     = 1.0
Replica A has the best cache. Replica C has the most capacity. Replica B may provide the best overall balance. The exact weights depend on:

workload shape
latency targets
prompt lengths
traffic volume
hardware
cache behavior There is no universal perfect score.
How does llm-d know what is cached?
This was one of the most interesting questions for me. It is easy to say:
Route to the replica with the cache.
But the Router still needs to know:

What is cached?
Where is it cached?
Has it been evicted?
llm-d currently documents two approaches:

Approximate Prefix-Cache Routing

Precise Prefix-Cache Routing
They solve the same broad problem but obtain cache knowledge differently. (llm-d)
What is approximate prefix-cache routing?

Approximate routing is the lighter approach. The Router does not maintain an exact view reported by every model server. Instead, it builds an estimate based largely on its own routing history. The flow is roughly:

1. Approximate prompt tokens.

2. Split the prompt into logical blocks.

3. Build rolling prefix hashes.

4. Remember which hashes were routed
   to which replicas.

5. Assume the selected replica
   now contains that prefix.

6. Use that history to score
   future requests.

In llm-d’s approximate path, the EPP estimates token boundaries using character-to-token ratios, builds a rolling hash chain, and stores recent prefix-to-pod associations in a local in-memory LRU index. (llm-d)
Why does approximate routing use characters?

The Router may not contain the model’s tokenizer. But the prompt arrives as text. So the approximate implementation estimates how many characters correspond to a token and uses that estimate to create logical blocks. This makes it lightweight because it does not require:

a tokenizer service
exact token IDs
model-server cache events
a live global cache index
What does the approximate Router actually know?
It mainly knows:

I previously sent this prefix
to Replica A.
It then assumes:
Replica A probably still has it.
This can work surprisingly well for:

stable workloads
repeated prompts
low cache churn
simple deployments
Why can the approximate view become wrong?
Because the Router’s history may diverge from the model server’s real memory. For example:

Router believes:
Prefix X → Replica A

But Replica A:
evicted Prefix X
due to KV-cache pressure
Other events can also change reality:

pod restart
cache eviction
model reload
memory pressure
a request not completing as expected The approximate Router may still believe the prefix exists until its local history changes. The llm-d documentation describes this as the main limitation of the lightweight approach: the local estimate can diverge from the model server’s actual cache state. (llm-d)
What is precise prefix-cache routing?
Precise routing uses actual token identities and actual cache events from model servers. The flow is closer to:

Prompt
  ↓
Exact Tokenization
  ↓
Exact Block Keys
  ↓
Global KV-Cache Index Lookup
  ↓
Per-Replica Match Information
  ↓
Cache + Load Scoring
  ↓
Selected Replica
Instead of assuming where the cache probably exists, the system builds a near-real-time view from the model servers themselves. (llm-d)
How does precise tokenization work?

The prompt must be converted into the same token IDs that the model server uses. In llm-d’s precise path, a token-producing component can use vLLM’s render endpoint to obtain exact token IDs. This matters because:

Character approximation
may not equal
actual tokenizer output.
Once the exact tokens are known, the system can derive cache-block identities that match the inference engine’s view. (llm-d)
How does the Router learn about cache changes?
The model servers emit cache events. For example:
BlockStored
means a KV-cache block has been created or placed on a cache tier.
BlockRemoved
means a block has been evicted or removed. The KV-Cache Indexer consumes these events and maintains a mapping similar to:

Block Hash 101 → Replica A, Replica B
Block Hash 102 → Replica A
Block Hash 103 → Replica C
Current llm-d architecture uses event-driven cache tracking so the indexer can maintain a near-real-time block key → pods view across the inference pool. (GitHub)
What does the KV-Cache Indexer do?
The Indexer is the observability layer for precise cache-aware routing. It answers questions such as:

Which replica has Block 1?

Which replica has Blocks 1–6?

Was Block 4 recently evicted?

Is a copy in accelerator memory
or another cache tier?
The Router’s scorer can consult this index when evaluating candidate endpoints. A useful mental model is:

KV-Cache Indexer
=
a directory of reusable inference state
Does the Indexer store the actual KV tensors?
Not necessarily. The index primarily tracks metadata:

which block
lives on
which endpoint or cache tier
The actual KV tensors remain in:

GPU or accelerator memory
CPU memory
an offloaded storage tier The index tells the routing system where the useful state is.
What does a precise routing example look like?
Suppose a new request produces these block keys:

H1
H2
H3
H4
H5
H6
The global index says:

Replica A:
H1, H2, H3, H4, H5

Replica B:
H1, H2, H3

Replica C:
H1
The cache matches are:

Replica A → 5 blocks
Replica B → 3 blocks
Replica C → 1 block
The Router then combines that information with load:

Replica A:
5-block match
High queue

Replica B:
3-block match
Low queue

Replica C:
1-block match
Medium queue
The final choice may still be Replica B. Precise routing improves cache knowledge. It does not remove the need for scheduling judgment.
What is speculative indexing?
There can be a small timing gap:

Router selects Replica A
  ↓
Request begins processing
  ↓
Replica A creates cache blocks
  ↓
KV events reach the Indexer

During that gap, another similar request may arrive before the official cache event appears. Speculative indexing lets the routing layer temporarily assume that the newly routed prefix is being created on the selected replica. This reduces the blind spot between:
routing decision
and:
event-confirmed cache state
llm-d’s precise implementation includes this mechanism to make new state visible sooner. (llm-d)
Is precise routing free?
No. It requires more infrastructure:

exact tokenization
cache-event publication
event transport
a global block index
additional Router memory and processing
model-server integration So the tradeoff is:

Approximate:
simpler and lighter,
but less accurate

Precise:
more accurate and observable,
but more operationally involved
llm-d positions the approximate approach for lighter or simpler workloads and the precise approach for more complex, high-scale serving where exact cache state is more valuable. (llm-d)
What is the simplest difference between the two?
Approximate routing says:

I sent this prefix to Replica A,
so Replica A probably has it.
Precise routing says:

Replica A reported that it stored
these exact token blocks,
and has not reported their removal.
That is the key difference.
What happens after the Router selects a replica?
The request enters the selected inference engine. For example:

llm-d Router
  ↓
Replica B selected
  ↓
vLLM Scheduler
  ↓
Automatic Prefix Cache Lookup
  ↓
Matching KV Blocks Reused
  ↓
Remaining Prompt Tokens Prefilled
  ↓
Decode Begins
The llm-d Router does not perform attention computation. It places the request where reuse is most likely. The inference engine performs the actual block lookup and model execution.
Does the Router itself create the cache hit?
No. The cache hit occurs inside the model server. The Router improves the chance that the request reaches a model server where a hit is possible. So the distinction is:

Router
=
places the request near reusable state

Inference Engine
=
actually reuses that state
How is this different from session affinity?
Session affinity usually means:

Same session ID
→ same replica
KV-cache-aware routing means:

Same or partially shared token prefix
→ replica with matching blocks

These can overlap, but they are not identical. For a multi-turn conversation, session affinity may send the user back to the same replica. That often preserves the conversation cache. But prefix-cache-aware routing can also help across different users. For example:

User A
User B
User C
may all share:

the same system prompt
the same policy document
the same coding-agent instructions
the same RAG context A cache-aware Router can recognize reusable token prefixes even though the session IDs are different.
Is cache-aware routing semantic routing?
No. Semantic routing asks:

What does this request mean?
Which model or service fits it?
KV-cache-aware routing asks:

Which endpoint has already processed
the exact beginning of this request?
Semantic similarity may send two requests to the same model. But KV-cache reuse requires compatible token prefixes.
How does this relate to model routing?
The complete flow may contain both:

User
  ↓
Model Router
  ↓
Choose model or service
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
Choose best replica
  ↓
vLLM Scheduler
  ↓
Choose when request runs
The layers answer different questions:

Model Router:
Which model?

llm-d Router:
Which serving endpoint?

vLLM Scheduler:
Which requests run now?

GPU:
Perform the computation.
How does this relate to PagedAttention?
PagedAttention and KV-cache-aware routing operate at different levels. PagedAttention helps the model server:

store KV cache in blocks
allocate memory dynamically
avoid large contiguous allocations
reuse blocks efficiently
KV-cache-aware routing helps the distributed system:

send requests toward replicas
that already contain useful blocks
The connection is:

PagedAttention
organizes local KV memory.

Prefix Caching
reuses local KV blocks.

KV-Cache-Aware Routing
preserves reuse across replicas.
Can cache-aware routing create hotspots?
Yes. Suppose Replica A contains a very popular system prompt. Thousands of incoming requests share that prefix. A cache-only policy may send all of them to Replica A:

Popular Prefix
  ↓
Replica A
  ↓
Replica A
  ↓
Replica A
The cache hit rate looks excellent. But:

the queue grows
TTFT increases
decode batches become overloaded
other replicas remain underused This is why cache affinity cannot be the only routing signal.
How can the Router balance affinity and distribution?
A routing strategy can:

use cache match as one weighted score
combine it with queue depth and KV utilization
select among several cache-compatible endpoints
break cache stickiness when latency becomes too high
occasionally explore other replicas to seed additional cache copies The current llm-d Router includes a prefix-affinity filter that can preserve cache locality while breaking stickiness when estimated TTFT on cache-heavy endpoints becomes significantly worse. It also supports exploration so cache state does not remain permanently concentrated on one subset of replicas. (GitHub)
What is the deeper tradeoff?
The Router is balancing two opposing goals:

Locality
vs
Distribution
Locality says:

Keep similar requests together
to maximize cache reuse.
Distribution says:

Spread requests out
to avoid overloading one replica.
Too much locality creates hotspots. Too much distribution destroys cache reuse. Good routing lives somewhere between them.
What happens when a cache block is evicted?
KV cache is limited. As new requests enter and active sequences grow, older reusable blocks may be evicted. The state may change like:

Time 1:
Replica A has Prefix X

Time 2:
Memory pressure increases

Time 3:
Prefix X is evicted

Time 4:
New request with Prefix X arrives

With approximate routing, the Router may still believe Replica A has the prefix. With precise routing, a removal event updates the index. This is one reason actual cache events become valuable in high-churn systems.
Does a high cache hit always mean lower latency?
No. A high cache hit reduces prefill computation. But end-to-end latency also depends on:

queueing
active decode load
GPU communication
KV-cache pressure
output length
network latency
scheduling overhead A request with a perfect cache hit can still be slow if the selected replica has a long queue. A request with no cache hit can still start quickly on an idle replica. Cache locality is important. It is not the whole system.
Which workloads benefit most?
KV-cache-aware routing is especially useful for workloads with repeated, long prefixes:

multi-turn conversations
long-document question answering
shared enterprise system prompts
RAG workloads with overlapping retrieved context
coding agents with repeated repository context
tool-using agents with growing conversation histories
batch jobs using the same instruction template vLLM identifies long-document querying and multi-round conversation as major Automatic Prefix Caching use cases. llm-d’s routing guidance also highlights shared prompts, conversations, agentic loops, and overlapping RAG context as strong candidates for prefix affinity. (vLLM)
When does it help less?
It provides less value when:

prompts are short
every request has a unique prefix
output generation dominates total latency
cache entries are evicted before reuse
request volume is too low to produce repeated prefixes
there is only one model-server replica For long-output workloads, decode may dominate the request even when prefill is reduced. For unique prompts, there is simply nothing to reuse. (vLLM)
Why does prompt consistency matter?
Applications can unintentionally destroy cache reuse. For example, suppose every request includes:
Current timestamp: 10:01:01
then:
Current timestamp: 10:01:02
near the beginning of the prompt. Everything after that point may receive different chained block hashes. Similarly, changing:

system-prompt wording
message ordering
document ordering
dynamic metadata placement can reduce prefix reuse. A cache-friendly prompt structure often places:

stable shared content first
dynamic request-specific content later
This allows more leading blocks to remain identical.
What about multi-tenant isolation?

Two tenants may use identical prompt text. But a platform may not want their cache identities to overlap. vLLM’s block-hash design can include extra values such as cache salts, allowing otherwise identical prefixes to be separated when stronger isolation is required. It can also include LoRA and multimodal identifiers so blocks are not incorrectly reused across incompatible model states. (vLLM) The broader lesson is:

Cache identity must represent
all state that affects the computation.
Text alone may not be enough.
What should we measure?
For a cache-aware routing experiment, I would track:

prefix-cache hit ratio
matched blocks or matched tokens
TTFT
prefill tokens actually computed
queueing time
per-endpoint queue depth
active requests per endpoint
KV-cache utilization
cache eviction rate
request distribution across replicas
Router scheduling latency
output tokens/sec The llm-d EPP exposes metrics for prefix-index hit ratio and matched bytes, along with per-endpoint queue size, average KV-cache utilization, running requests, and scheduling latency. (llm-d)
Why is hit rate alone not enough?
Suppose an experiment shows:

Cache hit rate:
95%
That sounds excellent. But if:

Replica A receives 90% of traffic
and develops a huge queue
then user latency may still become worse. A good experiment should compare:

Cache Reuse
+
Load Balance
+
User-Facing Latency
The goal is not to maximize one metric in isolation. The goal is to improve the whole serving system.
What would a useful experiment look like?
A simple experiment could compare three routing policies:
Policy 1 — Round Robin

Ignore cache state.
Spread requests evenly.
Policy 2 — Cache Only

Always choose the replica
with the strongest prefix match.
Policy 3 — Cache + Load

Combine prefix match,
queue depth,
and KV-cache utilization.
Then run a workload containing:

a shared long system prompt
repeated multi-turn conversations
some completely unique requests Measure:
TTFT
throughput
cache hit ratio
queue imbalance
GPU utilization
p95 and p99 latency That would make the routing tradeoff visible rather than only theoretical.
What is the full request flow now?
The complete mental model looks like this:

User sends request
  ↓
Prompt is parsed
  ↓
Prefix blocks are approximated
or tokenized exactly
  ↓
Router evaluates candidate endpoints
  ↓
Cache match is calculated
  ↓
Load and memory signals are added
  ↓
Best endpoint is selected
  ↓
Inference engine checks local cache
  ↓
Matching KV blocks are reused
  ↓
Uncached suffix is prefilled
  ↓
Decode begins
  ↓
New KV blocks are stored
  ↓
Cache state is updated
What is the most important distinction?
I would separate the pieces like this:

Automatic Prefix Caching
=
Can this engine reuse previous prompt work?

KV-Cache Indexing
=
Where does that reusable work currently exist?

KV-Cache-Aware Routing
=
Which endpoint should receive this request?

Load-Aware Scheduling
=
Is that endpoint still a good choice right now?
These ideas work together. None of them alone solves the complete distributed routing problem.
What is the biggest mental shift?
In traditional systems, routing often feels like:

Send the request
to a healthy server
with available capacity.
In LLM inference, routing can become:

Send the request
to a healthy server
with available capacity
that also contains the most useful
intermediate model state.

That extra condition changes a lot. The request is no longer stateless from the routing layer’s point of view. Its prompt history may have already created valuable work somewhere in the cluster. The Router is trying to preserve that work.
What is the key intuition?
The simplest summary is:

Prefix caching saves repeated prefill work.

KV-cache-aware routing preserves
that saving when we add more replicas.
Or:

Without cache-aware routing,
scale-out can destroy locality.

With cache-aware routing,
the system tries to scale
without throwing useful computation away.
What comes next?
KV-cache-aware routing works naturally when one model server performs both:

Prefill
and
Decode
The request reaches the replica. The prefix is reused or computed. Then decode continues on that same server. But what happens when prefill and decode run on different workers? Now the system must:

choose a prefill worker
choose a decode worker
create or find the KV cache
move that cache between workers
keep the transfer from hurting TTFT
That leads naturally to: Understanding Prefill/Decode Disaggregation and KV-Cache Transfer
Because once prefill and decode are separated, the question is no longer only:
Where is the KV cache?
It also becomes:

How do we move it
to the worker that needs it
without losing the performance
we were trying to gain?

title: Understanding KV-Cache-Aware Routing

blocks.text: Why I Created an Open Atlas of the LLM Inference Ecosystem
Over the last few months, I have been writing this LLM Inference Challenges series to understand how modern inference systems work.
We started with concepts like KV cache, batching, GPU utilization, distributed inference, vLLM, llama.cpp, llm-d, routing, and many other topics.
One thing I noticed while learning was that understanding the concepts was only half the challenge.
The other half was simply keeping up.
Every week, I would come across:

a new inference engine
a new serving framework
another optimization paper
a new benchmark
another routing project
a model release
a hardware announcement
or an interesting blog explaining something I hadn't seen before.
The pace of innovation in this space is incredible.
It is also overwhelming.
After a while, I found myself asking the same question repeatedly:
"Where did I see that project?"
or
"What category does this tool belong to?"
or
"How does this fit into everything else?"
That question eventually became Inference Atlas.
What is Inference Atlas?
Inference Atlas is an open-source, community-driven directory of the LLM inference ecosystem.
GitHub: https://github.com/aruanurag/inference-atlas
Website: https://www.inferenceatlas.org/
The goal is intentionally simple.
Instead of trying to become another benchmark or another search engine, I wanted one place where I could quickly understand:

what a project does
where it fits in the inference stack
why it exists
and what related projects I should explore next.
Think of it as a map rather than a ranking.
Why build another directory?
There are already many excellent resources.
The problem isn't that information doesn't exist.
The problem is that it is scattered.
One day I am reading:
a GitHub repository
The next day:
a research paper
Then:
an NVIDIA blog
Then:
a LinkedIn post
Then:
documentation
Then:
a conference talk
After a few weeks, I realized I was spending more time trying to remember where something lived than actually learning it.
Inference Atlas became my way of organizing that knowledge.
The ecosystem is much larger than I expected
When I first started this series, I thought LLM inference mostly meant running a model.
Now I see an ecosystem that spans many layers.
For example:
Inference Engines

vLLM
llama.cpp
TensorRT-LLM
SGLang
TGI
Serving & Distributed Inference

llm-d
Ray Serve
Kubernetes-based serving
Model routers
Optimization

Continuous batching
PagedAttention
Speculative decoding
Prefix caching
Quantization
Hardware

CPUs
GPUs
NPUs
AI accelerators
Observability

Metrics
Benchmarking
Profiling
Monitoring
Model Formats

GGUF
Safetensors
ONNX
TensorRT engines
And that's only a small part of it.
Every week, new projects appear.
Keeping track of all of them has become a challenge in itself.
Why call it an Atlas?
An atlas doesn't try to tell you where to go.
It simply helps you understand the landscape.
That is exactly what I wanted.
I don't want Inference Atlas to say:
"This is the best project."
Instead, I want it to answer:

What problem does this solve?
Where does it fit?
What should I learn next?
What are similar projects?
Sometimes, simply knowing that a project exists is enough to start learning.
Built for learners first
Although anyone can use it, I built it primarily for people like me.
People who are trying to understand LLM inference one concept at a time.
If you've followed this series, you'll know I like building mental models.
Inference Atlas follows the same philosophy.
Instead of remembering hundreds of project names, I want to understand how they connect.
It will keep evolving
This isn't meant to be a static website.
As the ecosystem evolves, the Atlas should evolve too.
Some categories will grow.
Some projects will disappear.
New inference techniques will emerge.
That is completely expected.
In many ways, the Atlas is another learning project.
As I learn, it grows.
This is where I need your help
One of the reasons I made the project open source is because there is no way one person can keep up with everything happening in LLM inference.
If you know about:

an interesting inference project
a serving framework
an optimization library
a benchmarking tool
a deployment platform
a useful paper
or anything else that belongs in this ecosystem,
I would love your help.
You can:

⭐ Star the repository
Fork it and submit a Pull Request
Open a GitHub Issue with enough context for me to review and add it
My hope is that over time this becomes something the community helps build together.
Why this fits into the series
Although this article is a little different from the previous ones, I think it belongs here.
Learning LLM inference is no longer just about understanding transformers or GPUs.
It is also about navigating a rapidly evolving ecosystem.
Inference Atlas is my attempt to make that journey a little easier—for myself first, and hopefully for others too.
If it saves someone an hour of searching, or helps them discover a project they wouldn't have found otherwise, then it has already done its job.
Useful Links
Inference Atlas GitHub https://github.com/aruanurag/inference-atlas
Inference Atlas Website https://www.inferenceatlas.org/

title: Building Inference Atlas

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 19)
In the previous part, we explored KV-cache-aware routing.
The main idea was:

Do not route only based on load.

Also consider where useful
KV-cache state already exists.
That works naturally when one model server handles both phases of inference:

Prefill
+
Decode
The request reaches one server, the prompt is processed, the KV cache is created, and token generation continues on the same server.
But modern distributed inference systems may separate these two phases.
Now the request may begin on one worker and finish on another.
That creates a new problem:

How do we move the KV cache
from the prefill worker
to the decode worker
without losing the performance
we were trying to gain?
This is where prefill/decode disaggregation and KV-cache transfer become important.
Why separate prefill and decode?
We previously learned that prefill and decode behave very differently.
Prefill processes the prompt:

many input tokens
large matrix operations
high parallelism
compute-heavy work
Decode generates the response:

one token per sequence per step
repeated access to model weights
repeated access to KV cache
latency-sensitive work
A useful simplification is:

Prefill
=
compute-heavy

Decode
=
memory-bandwidth and latency-sensitive
When both phases run on the same workers, they compete for the same resources.
A long prompt may begin prefill while several other requests are actively decoding.
The flow can look like:

Active users are decoding
  ↓
A long prompt arrives
  ↓
Large prefill workload enters
  ↓
Decode steps receive less predictable access
to compute and memory bandwidth
  ↓
Inter-token latency increases
In other words, a new user waiting for the first token can disturb users who are already receiving tokens.

vLLM describes one motivation for disaggregated prefilling as the ability to tune time to first token and inter-token latency separately, while also controlling decode tail latency caused by prefill work entering the same engine.
What is prefill/decode disaggregation?
In a normal deployment:

Model Server
├── Prefill
└── Decode
In a disaggregated deployment:

Prefill Workers
+
Decode Workers
The prefill workers process prompts and create KV cache.
The decode workers receive that KV cache and generate output tokens.
The request flow becomes:

User Request
  ↓
Router
  ↓
Prefill Worker
  ↓
Prompt Processing
  ↓
KV Cache Created
  ↓
KV Cache Transferred
  ↓
Decode Worker
  ↓
Token Generation
  ↓
Response Streamed

llm-d describes this as splitting one inference request across specialized workers, with the Router selecting both a prefill endpoint and a decode endpoint and coordinating the KV-cache transfer between them.
How is this different from the parallelism we already learned?
It helps to keep the layers separate:

Tensor Parallelism
=
split tensors across GPUs

Pipeline Parallelism
=
split model layers across stages

Data Parallelism
=
create multiple model replicas

Prefill/Decode Disaggregation
=
split runtime phases across workers
These techniques can still be used together.
For example:

Prefill Worker Group
→ 4 GPUs using tensor parallelism

Decode Worker Group
→ 8 GPUs using tensor parallelism
Disaggregation does not replace multi-GPU parallelism.
It changes where different phases of the request execute.
Why is independent scaling useful?
Different applications create different workload shapes.
Consider a document-analysis application:

Very long prompts
Short answers
This workload may need:

more prefill capacity
less decode capacity
Now consider a creative-writing application:

Short prompts
Very long answers
This may need:

less prefill capacity
more decode capacity
With combined workers, every replica contains both capabilities, even when the workload needs more of one than the other.
With disaggregation, the system can use ratios such as:

4 Prefill Workers
+
8 Decode Workers
or:

8 Prefill Workers
+
4 Decode Workers
This allows the infrastructure to match the actual workload rather than treating every request phase identically.
What must move between the workers?
The decode worker cannot continue with only the original prompt text.
It needs the KV cache produced during prefill.
The KV cache contains the key and value tensors created for the prompt across the model’s transformer layers.
Without that state, the decode worker would need to process the entire prompt again.
That would defeat the purpose.
So after prefill:

Prefill Worker
has:
- prompt KV-cache blocks
- information describing those blocks
- the position where generation should continue
The decode worker needs enough information to place those blocks correctly in its own KV-cache memory.
Is only the KV-cache data transferred?
There are really two related transfers:

Control information
+
KV-cache data
The control information may describe:

which prefill worker produced the cache
which decode worker should receive it
which memory regions or blocks are involved
how the receiver can locate the transferred state
when the transfer has completed
The actual data plane moves the large KV tensors.
A useful mental model is:

Control plane:
Where should the cache go,
and how should the workers coordinate?

Data plane:
Move the actual KV-cache bytes.
Current llm-d and vLLM integrations exchange transfer metadata between the prefill and decode sides, while the inference runtime’s KV connector performs the cache movement.
Why can the transfer be expensive?
KV-cache size grows with:

prompt length
number of model layers
number of KV heads
head dimension
KV-cache precision
So a short prompt may create a relatively small transfer.
A long-context request may create a much larger one.
The new critical path becomes:

Queue for Prefill
+
Prefill Computation
+
KV-Cache Transfer
+
Queue for Decode
+
First Decode Step
This means time to first token is no longer controlled only by prefill compute.
It also depends on how quickly the cache reaches the decode worker.
The longer the prompt and the larger the model, the more important the network becomes.
Why not just send the cache through a normal network request?
KV caches can be large, and copying them through multiple intermediate locations would create overhead.
An inefficient path might look like:

Prefill GPU
  ↓
Prefill CPU Memory
  ↓
Application Process
  ↓
Network
  ↓
Decode Application Process
  ↓
Decode CPU Memory
  ↓
Decode GPU
Every extra copy increases:

latency
CPU overhead
memory bandwidth usage
High-performance systems try to make the path more direct:

Prefill GPU Memory
  ↓
High-Speed Interconnect
  ↓
Decode GPU Memory

NVIDIA NIXL is one transport layer used in current distributed serving systems to move KV cache directly between workers. It can use technologies such as NVLink, PCIe, or RDMA-capable networking depending on the topology.
Why does RDMA matter?
When prefill and decode run on different nodes, the cache must cross the network.
Traditional networking often involves more CPU participation and memory copying.
RDMA allows data to move between registered memory regions with much less CPU involvement.
The important intuition is:

Normal networking:
more software and CPU involvement

RDMA:
more direct memory-to-memory transfer

llm-d’s deployment guidance recommends high-performance RDMA interconnects for production disaggregated serving. Without RDMA, its NIXL path can fall back to TCP, but that path is positioned mainly for testing rather than efficient production transfer.
Can KV transfer overlap with other work?
Ideally, yes.
The system does not want the entire GPU to remain idle while one request’s KV cache is moving.
A transfer layer may perform asynchronous or non-blocking movement so workers can continue handling other requests.
Conceptually:

Request A KV cache is transferring

Meanwhile:

Prefill Worker
→ processes Request B

Decode Worker
→ generates tokens for Request C
This does not make the transfer free.
But it can hide some of the transfer time behind useful computation.
The final request still cannot start its own decode phase until the required KV state is available.
Who selects the prefill and decode workers?
A disaggregated router now makes two placement decisions:

Which prefill worker should process the prompt?

Which decode worker should continue generation?
For the prefill worker, it may consider:

prefill queue depth
compute capacity
existing prefix cache
prompt length
For the decode worker, it may consider:

active decode sequences
KV-cache capacity
expected output length
inter-token latency
network distance from the prefill worker
The choices are connected.
A decode worker may look lightly loaded, but if it is far from the selected prefill worker, the cache transfer may be expensive.
So routing may become topology-aware:

Do not only choose good workers.

Choose a good worker pair.
Why does topology matter?
Suppose there are two possible decode workers:

Decode A:
same rack as Prefill Worker
moderate queue

Decode B:
different zone
empty queue
Decode B has less work.
But transferring a large KV cache to it may take longer.
The Router must balance:

queue delay
vs
transfer delay
A useful conceptual formula is:

Expected TTFT
≈
Prefill Queue
+
Prefill Compute
+
KV Transfer
+
Decode Queue
+
First Decode Step
The best endpoint is not always the emptiest one.
It may be the endpoint that gives the lowest total path.
Why must the prefill and decode workers be compatible?
The decode worker must understand the KV-cache layout produced by the prefill worker.
Compatibility can depend on:

model version
KV-cache precision
block size
attention implementation
tensor-parallel configuration
runtime version
If the two workers organize KV memory differently, directly transferring the blocks may not work correctly.
Current llm-d operational guidance specifically warns that prefill and decode pairs must use compatible KV-cache layouts, including during rolling upgrades or configuration changes.
This makes deployments more operationally sensitive.
A normal stateless service can sometimes roll out one replica at a time with few concerns.
Disaggregated inference workers are cooperating on the same request state.
Their compatibility matters.
Does disaggregation always make inference faster?
No.
This is probably the most important limitation.
Disaggregation adds:

routing complexity
another queue
transfer coordination
network dependency
KV-cache movement
more operational components
For short prompts, the cache transfer may cost more than the prefill interference it prevents.
For a small deployment with low traffic, combined workers may be simpler and faster.
Disaggregation becomes more attractive when:

prompts are long
traffic is high
prefill disrupts decode latency
the workload has an uneven prefill/decode ratio
high-speed networking is available
The correct question is not:
Is disaggregation better?
It is:

Does separating the phases save
more time than the transfer adds
for this workload?
What should we measure?
A useful experiment should compare a combined deployment with a disaggregated one.
Track:

time to first token
inter-token latency
p95 and p99 latency
prefill queue time
decode queue time
KV-cache transfer time
input tokens per second
output tokens per second
GPU utilization
network throughput
The most important comparison is not only average throughput.
We should also ask:

Did long prefill requests stop disturbing
users who were already decoding?
That is one of the main reasons to consider the architecture.
What is the key mental model?
I would summarize it like this:

Prefill/Decode Disaggregation
separates two very different workloads.

KV-Cache Transfer
reconnects the request state
between those workloads.
Or:

Disaggregation gives us
independent scaling and isolation.

KV transfer introduces
a new network-dependent critical path.
The system wins only when:

benefit from specialization
>
cost of transferring state
What is the biggest mental shift?
Until now, networking mostly helped multiple GPUs collaborate.
Here, networking becomes part of one user request’s latency.
The first token may depend on:

a prompt processed on one GPU
a large cache transferred across the network
and generation beginning on another GPU
So the infrastructure is not only transporting requests.
It is transporting the model’s intermediate state.
That makes KV-cache movement one of the most important data-plane problems in distributed inference.
What comes next?
Now that the overall disaggregated flow is clearer, one component deserves a closer look:
NIXL
What exactly does a KV-transfer layer do?
How does it move data across GPU memory, CPU memory, networks, and storage?
How does it work with systems such as vLLM, llm-d, and NVIDIA Dynamo?
That could lead to:
LLM Inference Challenges (Part 21)
Understanding NIXL and the KV-Cache Data Plane
Because once inference state starts moving between workers, routing tells us where it should go.
The data plane determines:
how quickly it gets there.

title: Understanding Prefill/Decode Disaggregation and KV-Cache Transfer

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges - Hands-on Lab 03
In my earlier hands-on labs, the request path was relatively simple.
The first lab ran llama.cpp locally. The second moved to vLLM on an OCI GPU instance.
In both cases, the mental model was mostly:

Client
  ↓
Model server
  ↓
Model inference
Lab 3 changed that topology.
Instead of sending requests directly to one model server, I deployed a routed, Kubernetes-native inference service:

Client / Benchmark
        ↓
llm-d Router / EPP
        ↓
Healthy CPU vLLM replica
That extra routing layer may look like a small change, but it introduced a much larger set of questions:

Which replica receives the request?
How much work can each replica admit?
What happens when concurrency increases?
Where does the KV cache live?
What happens when the cluster has no room for another pod?
Which metric changes when I tune a serving parameter?
This is where the lab became much more interesting.
Is this llm-d versus vLLM?
No.
This was the first distinction I wanted the lab to make clear.
vLLM is still performing the model inference. It processes the prompt, manages the local KV cache, schedules sequences, and generates tokens.

llm-d provides the routing layer around the model-server pool. Its Router combines a proxy with the Endpoint Picker, or EPP. The EPP evaluates eligible endpoints and tells the proxy which model-server pod should receive the request. (LLM-D)
So the relationship is:

llm-d
=
routes and coordinates requests

vLLM
=
runs the model inference
The purpose of this lab was not to compare them. It was to observe what changes when inference becomes a routed service instead of one directly accessed server.
What did I build?
I added a new experiment type to my OCI Inference Cloud workbench.
The app:

validates the selected kubeconfig context and namespace
inspects available Kubernetes nodes, CPU, memory, and versions
renders a deployment plan before changing the cluster
deploys the llm-d standalone Router and CPU vLLM pool
waits for the components to become ready
starts a local port-forward
exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint
sends test inference requests
runs repeatable benchmark presets
stores benchmark history for comparison
The initial model is Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. It is public, small enough for the first CPU experiment, and does not require a Hugging Face token. (GitHub)
I also wanted the safety boundary to be very clear:

The app does not create the Kubernetes cluster.

The app does not delete the Kubernetes cluster.

It operates only inside the selected
namespace and Helm release.
That made the automation useful without hiding what it was doing.
Why change only one setting at a time?
The workbench exposes many parameters:

replica count
CPU and memory per replica
CPU KV-cache size
maximum model length
maximum concurrent sequences
maximum batched tokens
reserved CPU cores
optional CPU thread binding
prefix caching
benchmark concurrency, request count, and output length
Changing everything together can produce a different benchmark result, but it does not teach me much.
