The more useful loop is:

Establish baseline
  ↓
Change one setting
  ↓
Redeploy
  ↓
Repeat the same workload
  ↓
Compare the metrics
  ↓
Write down why they may have changed
The repository was built around this idea: inference concepts become easier to understand when they are measured rather than only described. (GitHub)
Which mental model made the metrics clearer?
The most useful one was separating inference into two phases:

Prefill
and
Decode
During prefill, the model processes the input prompt and builds the KV cache.
During decode, it generates new tokens one at a time.
This immediately helped me understand why one benchmark number is never enough.
A longer prompt increases prefill work. I should therefore expect it to affect time to first token, especially TTFT p95.
A longer response spends more time in decode. In that case, inter-token latency, end-to-end latency, and output tokens per second become more important.

vLLM exposes these as separate concepts: TTFT measures the time until the first token, inter-token latency measures intervals between generated tokens, and end-to-end latency measures the full request. (vLLM)
What do the main tuning knobs really control?
I started grouping the parameters into four categories.
Compute
CPU per replica controls how much processing capacity the model server receives.
If decode is CPU-bound, increasing CPU may improve inter-token latency and output speed. But that only helps when the cluster has those CPUs available.

Reserved CPU cores and thread binding are more advanced controls. vLLM recommends leaving CPU capacity for the serving framework and supports explicit OpenMP thread placement, including NUMA-aware automatic binding. (vLLM)
Capacity
CPU KV-cache size controls how much memory vLLM can use for active sequence state.
A larger cache may allow more parallel requests, but it also consumes more host memory.
Maximum model length limits how much context one sequence can use. Increasing it provides more context capacity, but it also increases the amount of KV-cache space that a request may require.
These are not simple speed settings. They are capacity-planning settings.
Scheduling
Maximum concurrent sequences controls how many sequences the engine may keep active.
Maximum batched tokens controls how much token work can be admitted into a scheduling step.
Increasing either value can improve aggregate throughput, but it can also create more competition for CPU, batching capacity, and KV-cache memory.
So the tradeoff can look like:

Higher concurrency
  ↓
More aggregate throughput
  +
More queueing and competition
  ↓
Higher TTFT or p95 latency
“Higher” is not automatically “better.”
Topology
Replica count changes how many independent model servers can handle requests.
More replicas can improve aggregate requests per second, but only when Kubernetes has enough unused CPU and memory to schedule them.
A desired replica count is not the same thing as available cluster capacity.
Why was prefix caching my favorite experiment?
Prefix caching is a very clean way to connect prefill, KV cache, routing, and metrics.
Suppose many requests share a long beginning:

[Large system prompt]
[Company policies]
[Product documentation]
[Small changing question]
The first request processes the entire prefix and builds its KV cache.
Later requests can reuse the cached prefix and avoid repeating that prefill work.
That should most directly affect:

TTFT
and
requests per second

It should not materially accelerate the decode phase. The new output tokens still need to be generated one at a time. vLLM’s documentation makes the same distinction: automatic prefix caching reduces repeated prompt processing, but it does not reduce the time required to generate new tokens. (vLLM)
This also explains why my first instinct would have produced a poor benchmark.
A short prompt followed by a 128-token response mostly measures decode.
A better prefix-cache test uses:

a shared 2,000–4,000-token prefix
a small changing question at the end
short outputs of roughly 16–32 tokens
at least 30–50 requests
identical concurrency in both runs
Then I can enable prefix caching, run the workload, disable it, redeploy, and repeat exactly the same test.
The first request is still a cache miss. Later requests benefit only when the relevant prefix remains cached. (GitHub)
With multiple replicas, another question appears:

Did the request reach the replica
that already has the prefix?
That is where prefix caching and inference-aware routing start connecting.
What happened during the Kubernetes rollout?
One of the most useful lessons came from a deployment that did not behave as expected.
On a one-node CPU cluster, the vLLM pod may consume most of the allocatable CPU.

When I changed a serving parameter, Kubernetes started a rolling update. A normal rolling update can create an additional pod before terminating the old one, depending on maxSurge and maxUnavailable. (Kubernetes)
But the node did not have enough CPU for both model-server pods.
The new pod stayed Pending with:
Insufficient CPU
This was not a model error.
It was not an llm-d routing error.
It was a cluster-capacity and rollout-strategy problem.
The lab now uses:

maxSurge: 0
maxUnavailable: 1
That briefly terminates the old decoder pod so the newly configured pod can schedule.
The cluster, namespace, llm-d Router Service, and release remain in place, but inference is briefly interrupted while the model-server pod is replaced. (GitHub)
It is not a zero-downtime solution.
It is an honest solution for a capacity-constrained learning cluster.

The same lesson applies to scaling from one replica to two. If the first replica already consumes nearly all available CPU and memory, the second replica cannot appear simply because I changed a number in the UI.
To test scale-out properly, the cluster needs real spare capacity or another worker node.
What experiments can readers run?
The full instructions are in Lab 3, but these are the experiments I would begin with:

Concurrency sweep: Keep the model and prompts fixed. Increase only benchmark concurrency and compare requests per second, TTFT p95, latency p95, and failures.
Prefix caching on versus off: Use one long shared prefix, short changing questions, and short outputs. Compare TTFT p95 and requests per second more closely than decode tokens per second.
CPU experiment: Keep everything else fixed and change CPU per replica. Observe whether ITL and output throughput improve, or whether another bottleneck remains.
Scheduling experiment: Change only maximum concurrent sequences or maximum batched tokens. Look for the point where throughput improves but tail latency begins to deteriorate.
Replica experiment: Move from one to two replicas only on a cluster with enough unused capacity. Compare aggregate throughput, request distribution, readiness time, and behavior during scale-out.
For every run, I would save:

Configuration
Workload
Successful and failed requests
TTFT p95
Latency p95
Approximate ITL
Requests/sec
Output tokens/sec
Observations
A benchmark with zero successful requests is a connectivity failure, not a performance result. The endpoint must work before its numbers are compared with successful runs. (GitHub)
What was the main learning?
The biggest lesson from this lab was that inference performance is not one speed number.
It is the interaction between:

Prefill
Decode
CPU capacity
KV-cache capacity
Batching
Queueing
Concurrency
Routing
Replica placement
Cluster capacity
A setting can improve throughput and hurt TTFT.
A larger cache can support more active work but consume the memory needed elsewhere.
A second replica can improve throughput, but only when Kubernetes can actually schedule it.
Prefix caching can dramatically reduce repeated prefill work, but it does not make decode tokens appear faster.
That is why I enjoyed this experiment.
I was not looking for one “best” configuration.
I was trying to make the system’s behavior visible.
The complete deployment steps, benchmark workflow, experiment suggestions, and observation template are available in Lab 3 of the LLM Inference Lab repository. (GitHub)

title: From One Model Server to llm-d and CPU vLLM on Kubernetes

blocks.text: Understanding LLM-D Autoscaling, Observability, and Workload Behavior on OKE
Github : Lab 4
What happens when an LLM inference service receives:

longer prompts
repeated context
longer outputs
more concurrent users

Do all of these workloads affect the system in the same way? And when performance starts degrading, should we simply add another replica based on CPU utilization? That is what I wanted to understand in Lab 4. In the previous lab, I deployed LLM-D with a CPU-based vLLM model server on an existing Oracle Kubernetes Engine cluster. Lab 4 extends that setup with:

Prometheus
Grafana
KEDA
LLM-D demand metrics
OKE Cluster Autoscaler
repeatable workload experiments
The goal was not only to autoscale the deployment. The bigger goal was to make the inference system observable enough to understand why it should scale.
What was the main question behind this lab?
The main question was:

Can we scale an inference service
based on actual inference demand
instead of only infrastructure utilization?
Traditional application autoscaling often starts with CPU utilization. For example:

CPU above 70%
→ add another pod
That can be useful, but LLM inference has more direct signals:

How many requests are running?
How many requests are waiting?
Is TTFT increasing?
Is KV cache being reused?
Are model servers running out of capacity?

A model server may already have high active concurrency or user-visible queueing before an average CPU metric tells a useful story. So this lab intentionally used LLM-D EPP demand metrics as the primary autoscaling signals. The simplified architecture was:

Client / Benchmark Workload
        ↓
LLM-D EPP / Routing Layer
        ↓
CPU vLLM Model-Server Pods
        ↓
Prometheus collects metrics
        ↓
Grafana shows system behavior
        ↓
KEDA queries Prometheus
        ↓
Generated HPA scales model pods
        ↓
If a new pod cannot fit:
OKE Cluster Autoscaler adds a node
The important point is that this contains two different scaling layers.

KEDA
=
scales model-server pods

OKE Cluster Autoscaler
=
adds cluster nodes

KEDA can request another vLLM replica, but it cannot create CPU or memory capacity. OKE Cluster Autoscaler only becomes involved when Kubernetes has created a pod that cannot be scheduled on the existing nodes.
What observability stack did I use?
The lab installed a dedicated monitoring stack containing:

Prometheus through kube-prometheus-stack
Grafana
KEDA
ServiceMonitor-based metric discovery
LLM-D Grafana dashboards: Grafana remained internal to the cluster. Instead of exposing it through a public ingress, the workbench opened a local kubectl port-forward connection:

kubectl --context <context> -n llm-d-monitoring \
  port-forward service/llmd-grafana 3000:80
This made the dashboards available on:

The lab intentionally kept Grafana private and accessed it only through the local tunnel. which metrics did I watch? One of the biggest lessons was that inference performance cannot be understood through one metric. I watched:

Time to First Token
Inter-token latency
End-to-end request latency
Requests per second
Generated tokens per second
Prompt-token throughput
KV-cache hit rate
KV-cache usage
Active requests
Waiting requests
EPP queue depth
Ready and Pending replicas
Node count
Each metric describes a different part of the request lifecycle.

TTFT
=
How long before generation begins?

Inter-token latency
=
How quickly tokens continue after the first token?

End-to-end latency
=
How long does the full request occupy the system?

KV-cache hit rate
=
How much prompt processing is being reused?

Queue depth
=
How much work cannot currently enter a backend?

Running requests
=
How much active serving demand exists?
Looking at only one of them can lead to the wrong conclusion.
How did I keep the experiments meaningful?
The lab used five repeatable workload recipes. The important rule was:
Change one workload characteristic at a time.
Before the cache experiments, I restarted the model-server deployment to clear the in-memory prefix cache and reset cumulative counters. I then ran:

1. Short unique prompts
2. Long unique prompts
3. Long shared-prefix prompts
4. Long outputs
5. Sustained concurrent traffic
This made it easier to connect each workload change with the dashboard behavior.
Experiment 1 — What happens with short, unique prompts?
The first experiment established the baseline. It used:

100 short prompts
concurrency 1
maximum output 128 tokens
no intentional shared prefix
The approximate endpoint-level results were:

Generated throughput: 41.5 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 144 ms
Approximate ITL: 34 ms
The dashboards showed:

low TTFT
stable inter-token latency
almost no queueing
near-zero prefix-cache hit rate
little persistent KV-cache use after completion This became the control case. Short unique prompts require relatively little prefill work and provide almost nothing for prefix caching to reuse.
Experiment 2 — What changes with long, unique prompts?
The second experiment increased prompt length but intentionally kept every prompt unique. The approximate results were:

Generated throughput: 32.4 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 764 ms
Approximate ITL: 36 ms
TTFT increased dramatically:
But inter-token latency stayed close to the baseline:

34 ms
→
36 ms

This made the prefill/decode distinction visible. The model had much more prompt context to process before producing the first token. That increased TTFT. But once decoding started, the cadence between generated tokens remained comparatively stable. The lesson was:

Long input
primarily stresses prefill.
Experiment 3 — What changes when the long prefix is reused?
The third experiment used long prompts again, but this time every prompt shared the same large initial prefix. Only the final suffix changed. The approximate results were:

KV-cache hit rate: 53%
Generated throughput: 39.9 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 172 ms
Approximate ITL: 36.5 ms
Compare the two long-prompt workloads:

Cold long unique:
p95 TTFT ≈ 764 ms

Warm shared prefix:
p95 TTFT ≈ 172 ms

The prompt was still long. But the model no longer needed to repeat all of the prefill computation. The shared KV state could be reused. Inter-token latency remained broadly stable because prefix caching mainly improves:

prompt processing
and
time to first token
It does not create the same dramatic improvement in decode speed. This is why prefix caching can be useful for:

repeated system prompts
policy instructions
RAG instruction blocks
long shared documents
multi-turn conversation history The first uncached request could still appear in p99 TTFT, but once the cache warmed, the following requests became much faster.
Experiment 4 — What happens when outputs become much longer?
The fourth experiment kept concurrency at one but increased the maximum output to approximately 512 tokens. The approximate results were:

50 successful requests
Generated throughput: 41.7 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 146 ms
Approximate ITL: 35.6 ms
p95 end-to-end latency: 16 seconds

TTFT and inter-token latency remained close to the original baseline. But the complete request took much longer. Why? Because each request occupied the model server for many more decode iterations. The model was not necessarily generating each token more slowly. It was simply generating many more tokens. The lesson was:

Long output
=
more decode work
+
longer request residence time
This reduces completed requests per second and increases the chance of contention when multiple users arrive.
Experiment 5 — What changes when concurrency increases?
The final experiment used sustained mixed traffic with:

concurrency 8
maximum output 128 tokens
At the captured moment, Grafana showed:

Running requests: 8
Waiting requests: 0

TTFT p50: approximately 112 ms
TTFT p95: approximately 236 ms
TTFT p99: approximately 247 ms

ITL p50: approximately 38 ms
ITL p95: approximately 50 ms

Request throughput: approximately 0.74 requests/sec
KV-cache hit rate: approximately 52%
Even without a persistently non-zero queue, the active-request count was high enough to request more capacity. This was an important observation:
Queue depth is not the only demand signal.
Eight active requests already represented enough concurrent work for KEDA to scale the deployment.
Which autoscaling metrics did KEDA use?
The KEDA policy used two LLM-D EPP metrics:

llm_d_epp_flow_control_queue_size

llm_d_epp_request_running
The first measured requests waiting because backend capacity was unavailable. The second measured active in-flight requests. The default policy was:

Minimum replicas: 1
Maximum replicas: 3
Queue threshold: 1 per replica
Running-request threshold: 4 per replica
Polling interval: 15 seconds
Scale-down stabilization: 5 minutes
KEDA evaluated both signals and used the larger desired replica calculation. The active-request calculation was:

Active requests = 8

Threshold
= 4 requests per replica

Desired replicas
= ceil(8 / 4)
= 2

KEDA’s generated HPA therefore requested a second CPU vLLM pod. This was the pod-scaling event. But the cluster did not have enough available CPU and memory to schedule that pod. So the second replica stayed:
Pending
That Pending pod was not a failed autoscaling result. It was the next signal in the scaling chain.
How did node scaling happen?
Once the pod was Pending because its resource requests could not fit, OKE Cluster Autoscaler had a legitimate reason to add capacity. The full sequence was:

1. Concurrent traffic increases.

2. LLM-D reports active requests
   and/or queue depth.

3. Prometheus stores the metrics.

4. KEDA queries Prometheus.

5. The generated HPA requests
   another vLLM pod.

6. Kubernetes creates the pod.

7. The pod cannot fit
   and remains Pending.

8. OKE Cluster Autoscaler
   adds a managed node.

9. The pod moves:
   Pending
   → ContainerCreating
   → Running
   → Ready
This distinction is important:

KEDA responds to inference demand.

OKE Cluster Autoscaler responds
to unschedulable Kubernetes capacity demand.

They solve two related but different problems. Why not scale nodes immediately? Because additional pods may already fit on existing nodes. If every pod scale-out directly created a new node, the cluster could add unnecessary infrastructure. Kubernetes first tries to place the new replica using available capacity. Only when the requested CPU and memory cannot fit does node autoscaling become necessary. So the correct sequence is:

Demand
→ Pod
→ Scheduling decision
→ Node, only when needed
Why did the endpoint and Grafana show different values?

Another useful lesson was that the workbench and Grafana did not always report identical latency numbers. The workbench measured requests at the local OpenAI-compatible endpoint. That measurement included:

router overhead
network overhead
streaming behavior
client-side timing
The vLLM Grafana metrics were emitted closer to the model server. So both measurements were valid, but they represented different parts of the request path. The lesson was:

Before comparing two metrics,
understand where each one is measured.
The same name does not always mean the same measurement boundary. What did this lab teach me? The first lesson was:

TTFT and inter-token latency
tell different stories.
Long prompts increased TTFT because they increased prefill work. They did not create the same increase in inter-token latency. The second lesson was:
Prefix caching primarily improves prefill.
The warm shared-prefix workload reduced TTFT significantly, while decode cadence remained relatively stable. The third lesson was:
Output length is an occupancy problem.
Long outputs keep requests inside the model server for longer, even when tokens continue arriving at a stable rate. The fourth lesson was:

Concurrency connects benchmarking
to autoscaling.
A system that looks healthy at concurrency one may behave very differently when eight requests are active. The fifth lesson was:

Autoscaling should use signals
that represent actual inference demand.
CPU utilization remains useful for diagnosis, but active requests and queue depth are closer to the user-facing serving problem. And finally:

Pod scaling and node scaling
must be understood as one chain.
A model-serving platform is not fully elastic if it can request a pod but cannot create the infrastructure required to run it.
What is the biggest mental shift?
Before this lab, it was easy to think about autoscaling as:

Load increases
→ Add more servers
The real system is more layered:

Workload shape
changes inference behavior.

Inference behavior
changes TTFT, ITL, cache usage,
queueing, and active concurrency.

Inference metrics
drive pod scaling.

Unschedulable pods
drive infrastructure scaling.
So autoscaling is not a separate infrastructure feature sitting outside inference. It is connected directly to:

prefill
decode
KV-cache reuse
request residence time
concurrency
routing
capacity
What is the key intuition?
The simplest summary is:

Prompt length changes prefill.

Shared context changes cache economics.

Output length changes decode occupancy.

Concurrency changes the scaling story.
Lab 4 made these relationships visible on a real Kubernetes deployment. It also showed how:

LLM-D
+
vLLM
+
Prometheus
+
Grafana
+
KEDA
+
OKE Cluster Autoscaler
can work together as one observable and demand-driven inference platform.
What comes next?
Now that the scaling sequence is visible, the next question becomes:

How do we turn these experiments
into an actual capacity plan?
That means connecting:

prompt distribution
output distribution
concurrency
TTFT targets
replica count
node size
scale-up time
cost
Because autoscaling can react to demand. But good capacity planning decides how much warm capacity should already exist before that demand arrives.

title: Understanding LLM-D Autoscaling, Observability, and Workload Behavior on OKE

blocks.text: In the previous part, I explored autoscaling, observability, and workload behavior using LLM-D, vLLM, Prometheus, Grafana, KEDA, and OKE Cluster Autoscaler.
The experiments made one thing very clear:

Prompt length changes prefill.

Shared context changes cache economics.

Output length changes decode occupancy.

Concurrency changes the scaling story.
The lab also showed the complete scaling chain:

Inference demand
→ more model-server pods
→ Pending pod
→ more cluster nodes
→ additional serving capacity
But that led me to another question:

How much capacity should already exist
before the traffic arrives?
Autoscaling can react to demand.

links.text: Understanding LLM-D Autoscaling, Observability, and Workload Behavior on OKE

blocks.text: Capacity planning decides how much capacity should already be available while autoscaling reacts. That was the natural handoff from Understanding LLM-D Autoscaling, Observability, and Workload Behavior on OKE.
What did I initially think capacity planning meant?
At first, I thought the calculation would be simple:

Expected traffic
÷
throughput per replica
=
number of replicas
For example:

Expected traffic = 3 requests/sec

One replica = 1 request/sec

Required replicas = 3
That sounds reasonable.
But after the experiments in Part 22, this started feeling incomplete.
One request may contain:

50 input tokens
+
50 output tokens
Another request may contain:

8000 input tokens
+
500 output tokens
Both count as:
one request
But they create completely different amounts of work.
So capacity planning for LLM inference cannot begin with request count alone.
What is capacity planning?
The mental model I am building is:

Capacity Planning
=
understand the workload
+
measure safe serving capacity
+
estimate peak demand
+
keep enough warm capacity
+
leave room for failures and scaling
The word safe is important.
The goal is not to find the maximum amount of traffic the system can accept before it crashes.
The goal is to find how much traffic it can serve while still meeting the expected user experience.
What is the difference between capacity planning and autoscaling?
Capacity planning answers:
How much capacity should already exist?
Autoscaling answers:
When should we add or remove capacity?
They work together, but they solve different problems.
A simplified flow is:

Capacity Planning
→ choose minimum warm replicas

Autoscaling
→ add replicas when demand grows

Cluster Autoscaling
→ add nodes when replicas cannot fit
In my Lab 4 setup, KEDA could request another model-server pod.
But if the cluster did not have enough CPU or memory, that pod remained Pending until OKE Cluster Autoscaler added a node.
That entire process takes time.

The Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler itself runs as a periodic control loop rather than responding continuously; the default synchronization period is 15 seconds. After that decision, Kubernetes may still need to schedule a pod, provision a node, pull an image, load the model, and wait for readiness. (Kubernetes)
So the new capacity does not appear instantly.
That is why some capacity must already be warm.
What does warm capacity mean?
Warm capacity means model-serving replicas that are:

already running
already holding model weights
already connected to the router
already ready to accept requests
For example:

Minimum replicas = 2

Current demand needs only 1 replica

Second replica remains ready
for a burst or failure
That second replica may look idle during quiet periods.
But it is also reducing the risk that users wait through the full scale-up process.
So warm capacity is not simply wasted capacity.
It is partly:

latency protection
+
failure protection
+
scale-up protection
What exactly are we planning capacity for?
This was one of the biggest clarifications for me.
We are not planning capacity for:
a model
We are planning capacity for:

a model
+
a runtime
+
a hardware configuration
+
a workload profile
+
a performance target
The same model may have very different capacity depending on:

CPU or GPU
quantization
tensor-parallel size
context length
batching configuration
prefix-cache behavior
input-token distribution
output-token distribution
request concurrency
So asking:
How many requests can this model handle?
is still not enough.
The better question is:

How many requests of this workload type
can this serving configuration handle
while meeting this latency target?
What is a workload profile?
A workload profile describes the traffic the inference service receives.
The most useful dimensions appear to be:

request arrival rate
concurrent requests
input-token length
output-token length
prefix-cache reuse
traffic burstiness

These dimensions are also reflected in modern inference benchmarking tools. For example, vLLM’s serving benchmark supports controls for request rate, maximum concurrency, input length, output length, and burstiness. (vLLM)
A useful profile may look like:

Request rate:
2 requests/sec

Prompt length:
p50 = 500 tokens
p95 = 4000 tokens

Output length:
p50 = 100 tokens
p95 = 500 tokens

Prefix-cache hit rate:
approximately 40%

Peak concurrency:
12 requests
That tells us much more than:
We expect 2 requests/sec.
Why can’t I use one throughput number?
Lab 4 made this especially visible.
With short, unique prompts, I observed approximately:

Generated throughput: 41.5 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 144 ms
With long, unique prompts:

Generated throughput: 32.4 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 764 ms
With a long reusable prefix:

KV-cache hit rate: 53%
Generated throughput: 39.9 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 172 ms
And with longer outputs:

Generated throughput: 41.7 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 146 ms
p95 end-to-end latency: 16 seconds
The same model server produced very different user-facing behavior depending on the workload.
This means:

Tokens/sec alone
does not describe capacity.
It needs to be interpreted together with:

TTFT
ITL
request latency
queue depth
concurrency
input length
output length
cache behavior
What should define acceptable capacity?
This leads to Service Level Objectives, or SLOs.
An example SLO might be:

p95 TTFT < 500 ms

p95 ITL < 60 ms

Error rate < 1%
These are only example values.
The correct targets depend on the application.
For an interactive chatbot, TTFT and ITL may be very important.
For an offline batch summarization workload, total throughput may matter more.
For a coding agent, long context and repeated prefixes may dominate.
So capacity should be measured against the application’s actual goal.
What is goodput?
This helped me separate two ideas.
Throughput measures:
How much work completed?
Goodput measures:

How much work completed
while still meeting the SLO?
For example:

System throughput:
2 requests/sec

Requests meeting TTFT and ITL targets:
1.5 requests/sec

Goodput:
1.5 requests/sec
NVIDIA’s GenAI-Perf documentation defines goodput as the number of completed requests per second that meet configured service-level constraints such as TTFT or inter-token latency. (NVIDIA Docs)
That means the replica’s real usable capacity is not necessarily its maximum throughput.
It is closer to:
maximum sustainable goodput
How do we find the safe capacity of one replica?
The simplest approach I understand so far is:

Fix the model, hardware, runtime configuration, and number of replicas.
Create a realistic workload profile.
Start at a low request rate or concurrency.
Increase demand gradually.
Track TTFT, ITL, queueing, errors, memory, and throughput.
Find the point where the SLO begins to degrade.
Choose an operating point below that limit.
This gives us:

Safe capacity per replica
=
highest sustained demand
that still meets the SLO
with enough operating headroom
The objective is not to reach the largest possible number.
It is to identify the region where the system remains predictable.

Performance guidance for generative-AI serving follows this same general method: benchmark representative input and output lengths, increase concurrency, and identify the point where latency begins degrading beyond the acceptable target. (NVIDIA Docs)
What is the capacity knee?
As load increases, performance may initially remain stable.
For example:

Concurrency 1:
p95 TTFT = 140 ms

Concurrency 2:
p95 TTFT = 150 ms

Concurrency 4:
p95 TTFT = 180 ms
Then the system may reach a point where latency rises much faster:

Concurrency 6:
p95 TTFT = 300 ms

Concurrency 8:
p95 TTFT = 700 ms

Concurrency 10:
p95 TTFT = 1500 ms
That sharp change is sometimes described as the knee of the curve.
Before the knee:

the system absorbs more demand
without severe degradation
After the knee:

queueing grows
latency rises quickly
the system becomes less predictable
Capacity planning should normally operate before that knee, not directly on it.
Did Lab 4 prove that one replica supports four requests?
No.
This distinction is important.
In Lab 4, the KEDA policy used:

Running-request threshold:
4 per replica
So when the system observed:
8 active requests
the calculation became:

ceil(8 / 4)
=
2 replicas
That showed that the autoscaling policy worked.
It did not prove that four active requests were the true maximum or optimal capacity of one replica.
The value was a configured scaling target.
KEDA’s AverageValue metric type works in this way: it treats the target as the desired average metric value per replica and calculates the replica count from the total metric value. (KEDA)
To validate whether 4 is a good target, I would still need to benchmark:

1 active request
2 active requests
4 active requests
6 active requests
8 active requests
...
Then observe where the selected TTFT and ITL targets begin to fail.
How are request rate and concurrency connected?
A useful approximation is:

Concurrency
≈
request arrival rate
×
average request duration
Suppose:

Arrival rate = 2 requests/sec

Average request duration = 5 seconds
Then the system may have approximately:

2 × 5
=
10 active requests
This explains why output length matters so much.
Suppose the arrival rate stays the same, but responses become longer:

Before:
2 requests/sec × 5 seconds
= 10 active requests

After:
2 requests/sec × 15 seconds
= 30 active requests
Traffic did not increase in requests per second.
But active concurrency tripled because every request stayed in the system longer.
That creates:

more decode work
more KV-cache occupancy
more active sequences
greater probability of queueing
How do we calculate the number of replicas?
Once safe capacity per replica is measured, the first estimate becomes:

Required replicas
=
ceil(
peak demand
÷
safe capacity per replica
)
For example, suppose a benchmark shows:

Safe goodput per replica:
0.8 requests/sec

Expected peak demand:
2 requests/sec
Then:

ceil(2 / 0.8)
=
ceil(2.5)
=
3 replicas
We can also calculate using validated active concurrency:

Required replicas
=
ceil(
expected peak active requests
÷
safe active requests per replica
)
Suppose:

Peak active requests = 10

Validated safe active requests
per replica = 4
Then:

ceil(10 / 4)
=
3 replicas
These are starting estimates.
They do not yet include failures, bursts, or scale-up delay.
Why do we need headroom?
Running at 100% of measured capacity leaves no room for variation.
Real traffic contains:

long-tail prompts
longer-than-expected outputs
cache misses
temporary traffic bursts
replica failures
node failures
model reloads
routing imbalance
forecasting errors
So I now think about several types of headroom:

Performance headroom
=
avoid operating at the capacity knee

Burst headroom
=
absorb short traffic spikes

Failure headroom
=
continue serving when a replica fails

Scale-up headroom
=
serve traffic while new capacity starts
The exact amount is a business and engineering decision.
There is no universal percentage that works for every inference service.
What is N+1 capacity?
One simple availability policy is:

Required for demand = N replicas

Keep one additional replica = N + 1
For example:

Normal peak requires 3 replicas.

Warm capacity = 4 replicas.
If one replica fails:
3 replicas remain
and the expected peak workload can still be served.
But N+1 is only one policy.
For larger deployments, operators may plan for:

one node failure
one availability-domain failure
multiple replica failures
regional failover
The capacity model should reflect the actual failure scenario the system needs to tolerate.
How do replicas translate into nodes?
Once the replica count is known, I still need to determine where those replicas will run.
A simplified calculation is:

Pods per node
=
minimum of:

allocatable CPU ÷ pod CPU request

allocatable memory ÷ pod memory request

available accelerators ÷ accelerators per pod
Then:

Required nodes
=
ceil(
required replicas
÷
pods per node
)
Suppose one node can safely fit:
2 model-server replicas
And warm capacity requires:
5 replicas
Then:

ceil(5 / 2)
=
3 nodes
This calculation should use allocatable resources, not the node’s full advertised resources.
Kubernetes, networking components, monitoring agents, and other system workloads also need capacity.
For GPU deployments, topology may become another constraint.
A replica may require:

1 GPU
4 GPUs using tensor parallelism
or
multiple nodes
So the scheduling unit may be much larger than one pod on one GPU.
How does scale-up time affect capacity?
Suppose the service currently has warm capacity for:
1 request/sec
Traffic suddenly rises to:
2 requests/sec
And additional capacity takes:
60 seconds
to become ready.
A simplified estimate of temporary backlog growth is:

Backlog
≈
(incoming rate - warm service rate)
×
scale-up time
So:

(2 - 1) requests/sec
×
60 seconds
=
approximately 60 queued requests
This is a simplified model.
Real systems also have variable request duration, batching, and partial completions.
But it makes the basic risk visible.
Even if autoscaling eventually adds enough capacity, users arriving during that minute may already experience poor TTFT or timeouts.
How much warm capacity should we keep?
The answer depends partly on how much queueing the application can tolerate.
An interactive assistant may need:

more warm capacity
faster scale-up
stricter TTFT protection
A batch-processing service may tolerate:

more queueing
slower scale-up
higher utilization
The basic tradeoff is:

More warm capacity
=
higher cost
+
lower latency risk

Less warm capacity
=
lower idle cost
+
greater scale-up and queueing risk
Capacity planning is therefore not purely a performance calculation.
It is also a cost and reliability decision.
How do capacity planning and autoscaling fit together?
The mental model I now have is:

Warm capacity
handles immediate expected demand.

Pod autoscaling
handles sustained demand growth.

Node autoscaling
creates infrastructure for new pods.

Admission control
protects the service
when demand exceeds all available capacity.
These layers should not be treated as independent features.
They are parts of one capacity system.
Can one model have multiple capacity profiles?
Yes.
This may be one of the most important lessons.
The same model can have different capacity profiles for:

Interactive chat

Long-context RAG

Coding assistants

Agentic workflows

Offline batch processing
For example:

Interactive chat:
short prompts
medium outputs
strict TTFT

RAG:
long prompts
short outputs
possible prefix reuse

Creative writing:
short prompts
very long outputs
decode-heavy

Document summarization:
long prompts
long outputs
high total occupancy
Trying to combine all of these into one average request can hide the real bottlenecks.
It may be better to create:

separate workload classes
separate benchmark profiles
possibly separate serving pools
What would a practical capacity-planning process look like?
The process I would follow now is:

1. Define workload classes.

2. Measure prompt-length distributions.

3. Measure output-length distributions.

4. Measure arrival rate,
   concurrency, and burstiness.

5. Define TTFT, ITL,
   error-rate, and throughput targets.

6. Benchmark one replica
   with realistic workloads.

7. Find the SLO-safe capacity point.

8. Forecast normal and peak demand.

9. Calculate required replicas.

10. Add burst, failure,
    and scale-up headroom.

11. Map replicas to nodes.

12. Measure real pod and node
    scale-up times.

13. Run a full-system load test.

14. Compare prediction
    with production measurements.
The last step matters.
Capacity planning is not something we calculate once and finish.
The estimates should be compared with real behavior and adjusted continuously.
How does this change how I interpret Lab 4?
During the concurrent workload, I observed approximately:

Running requests: 8
Waiting requests: 0

p95 TTFT: 236 ms
p95 ITL: 50 ms

Request throughput:
0.74 requests/sec
KEDA requested another replica because the configured threshold was:
4 running requests per replica
This was a successful autoscaling experiment.
But it was only one point on the performance curve.
To turn that experiment into a real capacity plan, the next step would be:

Choose an SLO.

Hold the deployment at one replica.

Increase request rate gradually.

Repeat across:
- short unique prompts
- long unique prompts
- shared-prefix prompts
- long outputs
- realistic mixed traffic

Find where p95 TTFT,
p95 ITL, queue depth,
or errors cross the target.

Set the scaling threshold
before that point.
That would turn:
4 active requests per replica
from a configured assumption into a measured operating target.
What is the biggest mental shift?
Before exploring this, I thought capacity planning was mainly:

Peak requests
÷
maximum throughput
=
replicas
Now the picture looks more like:

Workload shape
determines per-request work.

SLO
defines acceptable performance.

Benchmarking
finds safe replica capacity.

Demand forecasting
estimates required replicas.

Scale-up time and failures
determine headroom.

Cost
influences how much capacity stays warm.
So the final number is not simply a hardware calculation.
It is the result of several connected decisions.
What is the key intuition?
The simplest summary is:

Benchmarking tells me
what one replica can safely do.

Capacity planning tells me
how many replicas should already exist.

Autoscaling tells the system
when to add or remove replicas.

Cluster autoscaling tells Kubernetes
where those replicas can run.
And the deeper lesson is:

Capacity is not the maximum load
the system can survive.

Capacity is the load
the system can serve reliably
while meeting the user experience target.
What comes next?
Now that the capacity-planning mental model is clearer, the next question becomes:

Which live metrics should trigger scaling
before users experience a problem?
Should we scale on:

active requests
queue depth
TTFT
ITL
KV-cache pressure
token backlog
goodput
And which of these are early signals versus signals that tell us the system is already unhealthy?
That leads naturally to:
LLM Inference Challenges
Understanding SLO-Driven Autoscaling for LLM Inference
Because capacity planning decides the starting point.
The next challenge is making the system react early enough to protect that capacity plan when real traffic behaves differently from the forecast.

title: Understanding Capacity Planning for LLM Inference

blocks.text: As I have been learning more about LLM inference, NVIDIA has kept appearing everywhere.

At first, it was easy to put everything in one bucket: NVIDIA means GPUs. Then I started seeing terms like TensorRT-LLM, Triton, NIM, NVLink, NVSwitch, InfiniBand, DGX, and HGX. I knew they were all related to AI infrastructure, but I did not have a clear picture of how they fit together.
More importantly, I did not understand why I should care about all of them while learning inference.

After spending time with topics like KV cache, routing, prefill/decode behavior, batching, distributed inference, and hyperscaler infrastructure, the picture is becoming clearer. NVIDIA is not only providing the compute where an LLM runs. It has pieces across the path from a GPU inside a server to a model exposed as an API.
This article is my attempt to build that mental model.
The question I started with
When we say that a model is running on an NVIDIA GPU, what does that really tell us?
It tells us something important about the compute, but it does not explain:
- whether the model fits in memory;
- how multiple GPUs communicate;
- how multiple servers communicate;
- where the model is stored before it is loaded;
- how the model is optimized for inference; or
- how it becomes a service that an application can call.
That is the gap this stack fills.
The simplest way I now think about it is:
NVIDIA’s LLM inference stack goes from storage, to compute and memory, to GPU and cluster communication, to systems, to software, and finally to a deployable inference service.
First, separate memory, storage, and communication
One source of confusion for me was treating terms such as HBM, NAND, NVLink, and InfiniBand as if they described competing kinds of memory. They do not.
Here is how I separate them:
- GPU HBM is fast, volatile memory attached to a GPU. During inference, it holds the active model weights, KV cache, and intermediate data.
- NAND or NVMe SSD is persistent flash storage. It stores model files, containers, checkpoints, and cached artifacts.
- NVLink and NVSwitch are scale-up GPU interconnects. They move data between tightly connected GPUs.
- InfiniBand, RoCE, and EFA are examples of scale-out cluster fabrics. They move data between servers or GPU nodes.

HBM is where the active inference working set needs to live. NAND is slower, but it is persistent, much larger, and less expensive per unit of capacity. NVLink and InfiniBand do not store the model at all; they transport data between compute devices.

That distinction explains why the fastest technology cannot simply be used everywhere. HBM is expensive and capacity-limited. NVLink is designed for tightly coupled GPU domains and has physical, topology, power, and cost constraints. NAND provides durability. A scale-out network provides the reach and fan-out required to connect racks or entire clusters.
1. GPUs: where the model runs
The GPU is still the starting point.
LLMs involve a huge amount of matrix multiplication. NVIDIA GPUs provide highly parallel compute, and Tensor Cores are designed to accelerate the lower-precision math commonly used for AI workloads.
But while looking at inference, I realized that compute is only one part of the story.

An inference system also needs memory for the model weights and for the KV cache. The KV cache keeps growing as context length and concurrent requests increase. During decode, every new token needs to work with the model weights and the relevant cache again.
That gives us three different things to think about:
- Compute capability helps process model operations quickly.
- GPU memory capacity affects whether the weights and KV cache can fit.
- Memory bandwidth affects how quickly data can be moved while generating tokens.
This connects directly to the prefill/decode split I wrote about earlier.

Prefill processes many input tokens together and can make very effective use of parallel compute. Decode generates one token at a time, so memory movement, scheduling, and cache behavior become much more visible. A GPU is not simply “fast” or “slow” for inference; the workload shape matters.

So, when I look at a GPU now, I do not only think about FLOPS. I also ask: How much memory does it have? What precision will the model use? How large can the KV cache become? Is this workload mainly prompt-heavy, generation-heavy, or both?
One GPU may not be enough. A larger model may not fit on it, or a workload may need more throughput than one GPU can provide.
The immediate answer sounds simple: add more GPUs.
But then another question appears: how do those GPUs communicate?

If a model is split across GPUs using tensor parallelism, the GPUs need to exchange information while processing the model. During token generation, that communication can happen repeatedly. If the communication path is slow, GPUs spend time waiting for one another.
This is where NVLink and NVSwitch come in.
- NVLink is a high-bandwidth connection between GPUs.
- NVSwitch expands this into a fabric that can connect multiple GPUs at high bandwidth.
The key insight for me was that multi-GPU inference is not just about adding compute. It is also about reducing the cost of coordination.
That is why two machines with the same number of GPUs can behave very differently for a large model. The topology and interconnect can matter just as much as the GPU count.

NVLink has traditionally described scale-up communication within a tightly integrated multi-GPU system. Newer rack-scale designs, such as NVLink 72 memory fabrics, can extend that scale-up domain across multiple compute hosts in a rack. Even then, a broader scale-out network is still needed to connect multiple memory fabrics or racks.
3. Networking: moving from one server to a cluster
NVLink and NVSwitch help GPUs collaborate inside a tightly connected system or memory fabric. But real inference platforms often extend beyond that domain.

We may need more replicas to handle traffic. We may need model-parallel workers across nodes. Or we may decide to separate prefill and decode into different pools, which is one of the ideas I have been trying to understand through llm-d and disaggregated serving.
Now the network becomes part of the inference design.

NVIDIA’s networking portfolio includes InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet for high-performance AI networking. There are also BlueField DPUs, which can offload infrastructure work related to networking, storage, and security.

I do not think of these as “extra infrastructure” anymore. For distributed inference, they influence how effectively the system can move data, synchronize workers, and keep latency predictable under load.
The distinction that helped me was this:
- Scale up: GPUs communicate inside one tightly connected system or memory fabric. The building blocks include NVLink, NVSwitch, and newer rack-scale NVLink fabrics such as NVLink 72.
- Scale out: Servers, racks, or separate GPU memory fabrics communicate across a cluster. The building blocks can include InfiniBand, RoCE, Spectrum-X Ethernet, AWS EFA, and DPUs.

The phrase “GPU-to-GPU networking” is useful shorthand, but the remote GPUs are not normally joined by one giant direct cable. Traffic leaves a GPU through a high-speed network adapter. Technologies such as GPUDirect RDMA allow that adapter to move data directly between GPU memory and the network while avoiding unnecessary CPU and host-memory copies.
Hyperscalers do not all use the same scale-out fabric
I originally assumed that every large GPU cloud cluster must be using InfiniBand. That is not the case.
Microsoft Azure ND H100 v5
Inside one VM, the GPUs communicate through NVLink. Across VMs, Azure uses NVIDIA Quantum-2 InfiniBand with GPUDirect RDMA.
AWS P5 and P5e
Inside one instance, the GPUs communicate through NVSwitch. Across instances, AWS uses its Elastic Fabric Adapter, or EFA, with GPUDirect RDMA.
OCI H100-style compute clusters
Inside one bare-metal node, the GPUs communicate through NVLink. Across nodes, OCI uses its RDMA cluster network with RoCEv2.
OCI GB200 and GB300 memory-fabric designs
Within a rack-scale GPU memory fabric, GPUs and hosts communicate through NVLink. Separate GPU memory fabrics can be connected through RoCE or InfiniBand, depending on the OCI shape and deployment.
The common architecture is not “every hyperscaler uses InfiniBand.” The common architecture is:
1. use the fastest local GPU fabric for scale-up;
2. use a high-performance RDMA-capable network for scale-out; and
3. make collective-communication libraries such as NCCL understand the topology.

AWS exposes EFA rather than InfiniBand as its customer-facing interconnect for P5 clusters. Azure uses InfiniBand on specific high-end ND offerings, but not every Azure GPU VM supports it. OCI has historically emphasized a custom RoCEv2 cluster network for its GPU Superclusters, while newer GB200 shape variants document both InfiniBand and RoCEv2 options.
This is also why large-scale inference architecture becomes more interesting than simply choosing the biggest possible GPU.
4. HGX and DGX: from components to actual AI systems
Another thing I initially mixed up was GPUs, HGX, and DGX.
The distinction that now makes sense to me is:
NVIDIA GPU: the accelerator engine
NVIDIA supplies the compute device that performs the model operations and holds the active data in GPU memory.
NVIDIA HGX: the multi-GPU platform

HGX combines GPUs, NVLink or NVSwitch, CPUs, networking, and an optimized software stack into a system architecture. OEMs, ODMs, NVIDIA partners, and cloud providers can use that platform to build AI servers.
NVIDIA DGX: NVIDIA’s integrated AI system

DGX packages the hardware with optimized software, management, support, and reference architectures such as BasePOD and SuperPOD. NVIDIA delivers it as an integrated solution rather than only supplying the underlying platform design.
Hyperscaler infrastructure: the complete cloud environment
AWS, Azure, OCI, and other providers combine racks of GPU systems with cluster networking, storage, scheduling, security, tenant isolation, and cloud operations.

A rough analogy is that HGX is the high-performance platform or chassis design, while DGX is NVIDIA’s fully assembled and supported vehicle. A hyperscaler then builds the roads, fleet-management system, storage depots, and dispatch layer around thousands of those compute engines.

Hyperscalers may use HGX-based systems, other NVIDIA reference designs, or their own custom server designs. They do not have to expose the underlying system as a product called “HGX” or “DGX.” For example, AWS exposes P5 instances, Azure exposes ND-series VMs, and OCI exposes bare-metal GPU shapes and Superclusters. OCI also explicitly lists HGX B200 among its infrastructure options.

DGX is therefore part of the infrastructure landscape, but it is not a mandatory ingredient in every cloud GPU service. A provider might offer DGX Cloud or operate DGX-based infrastructure, while its native GPU instances remain cloud-specific products.
This matters because a production inference platform is a system, not a collection of GPU cards.

Power and cooling, GPU topology, drivers, firmware, storage paths, network design, and operational support all affect what the system can actually deliver. This is why an inference benchmark should never be read as a comparison of GPU names alone.
The model, precision, context length, runtime, batching policy, and full system configuration all contribute to the result.
5. CUDA, TensorRT-LLM, and Triton: the software layer
Hardware is useful only when software can use it efficiently.
At the base is CUDA, NVIDIA’s software platform for GPU-accelerated computing. Frameworks and inference engines build on top of it to use the GPU.

For LLM inference, TensorRT-LLM is the name I wanted to understand more. It is an open-source library focused on optimizing LLM inference on NVIDIA GPUs. It includes capabilities around optimized kernels, quantization, KV-cache management, parallelism, and decoding optimizations.

Then there is Triton Inference Server. I think of Triton as the serving layer: it helps expose models as endpoints, manage concurrent requests and batching, and surface operational metrics. TensorRT-LLM can be deployed with Triton as a backend.
The roles become clearer when I describe them this way:
- CUDA helps software use the GPU.
- TensorRT-LLM helps an LLM run efficiently on the GPU.
- Triton helps serve that model in a more production-oriented way.

This is not the only inference path. Tools such as vLLM and SGLang are also important in the broader ecosystem. But this separation helped me understand that an optimized model runtime and an inference server solve different parts of the same problem.
6. NIM: moving closer to a deployable service
Finally, there is NVIDIA NIM.

NIM packages optimized model-serving software into deployable microservices. It does not make hardware, memory, networking, or inference fundamentals disappear. Those layers still determine what performance is possible.

What NIM changes is the amount of assembly required to get to a supported, optimized service. Instead of putting together every runtime, container, dependency, and serving component ourselves, we can start with a packaged microservice for a model or AI capability.
That is why NIM feels particularly relevant to LLMOps.
It shifts part of the problem from How do I build the serving stack from scratch? to questions such as:
- How do I deploy it in my environment?
- How do I configure it for my traffic pattern?
- How do I monitor, secure, scale, and integrate it?
- When do I use a packaged path, and when do I need more control over the runtime?

For containerized and Kubernetes-based deployments, the surrounding tooling matters as well. The NVIDIA Container Toolkit, for example, enables containers to use GPUs. That may sound like a small implementation detail, but it is one of the pieces that connects a GPU-powered model server to a real deployment workflow.

NIM and Triton belong in the same general serving layer, but they are not simply two consecutive mandatory boxes in every deployment. Triton is an inference server that can host TensorRT-LLM and other backends. NIM is a packaged microservice approach that selects and assembles optimized serving components for a supported model or capability.
7. What actually happens when this is deployed
The deployment path becomes easier to visualize as a movement from cold, durable storage to hot, local GPU memory:
1. The model begins in a model registry or object-storage service.
2. A local NVMe or NAND cache may keep a nearby copy for faster loading.
3. The model weights are loaded into GPU HBM, where the active KV cache also lives.
4. NVLink or NVSwitch coordinates work inside the local scale-up domain.
5. InfiniBand, RoCE, Spectrum-X, or EFA coordinates work across nodes when distributed execution is required.
6. NIM, Triton, or another serving layer exposes the running model through an API.

When a serving replica starts, it loads the model from durable storage, possibly through a local NVMe cache, into GPU memory. During inference, the weights and active KV cache stay in GPU memory because returning to NAND for each token would be far too slow.
The way the workload is distributed then depends on the model and traffic pattern:
- Independent replicas: Each worker has its own copy of the model and serves different requests. This is often the simplest way to increase throughput.
- Tensor or model parallelism: One request uses multiple GPUs because the model is too large or because lower latency requires more aggregate compute. NVLink is especially valuable here.
- Multi-node parallelism: A model or expert set extends across servers, so the scale-out RDMA fabric becomes part of the token-generation path.
- Disaggregated prefill and decode: Prompt processing and token generation run in different pools. KV-cache state or related metadata may need to move between those pools.
Request routing also matters. Once a worker has created a request’s KV cache, keeping subsequent decode work on that worker avoids moving or rebuilding that state unnecessarily.
The updated mental model I am keeping
This is the picture I am taking forward:
NAND, NVMe, object storage, and file systems store models durably.
GPU HBM holds the active weights and KV cache.
GPU compute and memory bandwidth determine how efficiently tokens can be generated.
NVLink and NVSwitch determine how well GPUs collaborate within a tightly connected scale-up domain.
InfiniBand, RoCE, Spectrum-X, or EFA determine how systems collaborate across a scale-out cluster.
HGX provides a multi-GPU platform that partners and hyperscalers can build into servers.
DGX packages NVIDIA hardware, software, management, and support into an integrated system.
CUDA and TensorRT-LLM determine how effectively software uses the hardware.
Triton and NIM help turn those capabilities into a deployable inference service.
The more I learn about inference, the more I see that “run the model on a GPU” hides a lot of meaningful decisions.

NVIDIA is a big part of that picture not only because of its GPUs, but because it has offerings across the entire path—from the hardware that generates tokens to the software and infrastructure that help serve them at scale. The hyperscalers then combine those NVIDIA building blocks with their own network fabrics, storage systems, schedulers, and cloud operating models.

My next step is to explore some of these pieces more deeply, especially TensorRT-LLM, NIM, Kubernetes-based serving, and how request routing changes when prefill and decode are separated. That should also make the trade-offs between an opinionated packaged deployment and a more customizable open-source stack much easier to understand.

title: From GPUs to NIM: Understanding NVIDIA’s LLM Inference Stack

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges
Model Routing: Choosing the Right LLM for Each Request
Routing has become one of the most recurring themes in my LLM inference learning.

I have already explored routing at the distributed inference layer: how requests reach the right replica, why KV-cache-aware routing matters, and how systems such as LLM-d try to avoid unnecessary prefill work while keeping inference efficient at scale.
Those discussions focused on a question like this:
A request already has a model. Where should that request run?
Model routing asks a different question:
Before inference even begins, which model should receive this request?

At first, this may sound like an application-layer decision rather than an inference topic. But the more I looked into it, the more I realized that the model choice shapes almost everything that happens afterward.
Choosing a model determines:

Which weights need to be loaded and served
How much accelerator memory and compute the request is likely to consume
The prefill and decode behaviour of that request
Which KV cache can be reused
Which provider, deployment, and replica become eligible
The latency, cost, and quality trade-off the user will experience
So, model routing is not separate from inference. It is the decision that sets the path for inference.
request → choose model → choose provider/deployment → choose replica → reuse or build KV cache
Each stage is a routing decision, but each solves a different problem.
THE THREE ROUTING DECISIONS
Model routing answers: “Which model should answer this request?” It determines the model’s capabilities, cost, context window, tool support, and expected quality.
Provider or deployment routing answers: “Where can this selected model be served?” It considers availability, region, price, and operational constraints.
Replica routing answers: “Which instance should receive the request?” It considers load distribution, latency, and KV-cache locality.
The previous routing articles were mainly about the final stage: efficiently serving a request after its model had already been selected.

This article moves one step earlier in the lifecycle. It explores what happens when the router can change the model itself—and why that can improve cost and quality for an isolated request while also creating new challenges around KV cache reuse, session affinity, and multi-turn conversations.
Why one model is rarely enough
Consider an internal assistant that receives all of these requests:

“Extract the invoice number and total from this text.”
“Summarize this meeting transcript in five bullets.”
“Answer this question using the retrieved policy documents.”
“Help me debug this Kubernetes networking issue.”
“Create a migration plan with risks, dependencies, and rollback steps.”
They do not need the same capabilities.

A simple extraction request may need a fast, lower-cost model with reliable structured output. A difficult debugging or planning request may justify a stronger reasoning model. A RAG request may depend more on retrieval quality, grounding, and citation behaviour than on using the largest model available.
A model router can use signals such as:

Task type or intent
Estimated complexity
Context length
Tool-calling or structured-output requirements
Retrieval confidence
Latency and cost budget
Privacy, provider, or region constraints
The goal is not to find one universally “best” model. It is to define a policy that makes good trade-offs for each request.
At its simplest, the policy could be rule-based:
This is easy to understand and test. But it does not yet account for the state created by a longer conversation.
The hidden cost of switching models: KV cache
When a model processes a prompt or conversation history, it creates a KV cache. That cache stores attention keys and values so the model can continue generating without recomputing every prior token.
It is tempting to call this “the conversation cache.” But it is really a cache created for a particular model and serving setup.

If a conversation starts on Model A and the router sends the next turn to Model B, Model B can receive the visible conversation history—but it generally cannot reuse Model A’s KV cache. It has to process that history again and create its own cache.
A model switch can therefore mean:

A new prefill phase for the accumulated conversation
Higher time-to-first-token latency
More input-token processing cost
Loss of the benefit from an already warm cache
Potentially different model behaviour, tone, or tool-use patterns

Even moving the same model between replicas can lose cache locality unless the serving system can locate, transfer, or rebuild the cache. Switching to a different model makes the issue more fundamental.

Prefix caching is valuable when the same model sees the same token prefix again; systems such as vLLM use it to avoid redundant prompt computation. But it is not a generic cache that automatically follows a conversation across unrelated models.

links.text: Cross-Model KV Cache Transfer in LLM Families

blocks.text: Cross-model KV-cache transfer is an active research problem precisely because a model switch normally requires the receiving model to prefill the context again. A recent NVIDIA research preprint explores mapping cache between compatible models in a family, but that is specialised work—not something a typical model router can assume today. Cross-Model KV Cache Transfer in LLM Families
Conversation affinity matters
Now consider a longer conversation.

A user may begin by asking for a quick summary, move into a detailed technical question, ask for a code example, and then return to summarising a document. A stateless router might choose a different model for every turn.
That could be individually optimal for each prompt, but poor for the conversation as a whole.
The router has to decide whether it values the best model for the latest request more than it values continuity, cache reuse, and predictable behaviour.
There are three broad approaches:
Route every request independently
This gives the router the best chance to optimize each prompt for cost or capability.
The trade-off is more model switches, cold prefills, and potentially inconsistent behavior.
Keep one model for the full conversation
This provides better model affinity, cache locality, and consistency.
The trade-off is that a simple follow-up may remain on an unnecessarily expensive model.
Route by task or conversation branch
This lets a genuinely new task use a better-suited model.
The trade-off is that the application has to identify task boundaries well.
There are also two related forms of affinity to think about.
Model affinity means keeping a conversation on the same model. This preserves more consistent behavior and avoids a cross-model prefill restart.
Replica or cache affinity means keeping requests near the same serving replica. This can preserve access to the model’s already-computed KV cache.
Model affinity alone is not enough. If the same model is selected but the next request reaches a different replica without access to the cache state, prefill work may still be repeated.
This is where model routing and KV-cache-aware serving need to work together.
A good model router should not only ask, “What is this prompt?” It should also ask:

Is this still the same task?
Which model is already serving this session?
Is there a useful cache behind that model?
Is the expected gain from switching larger than the cache and affinity penalties?
Would a new task thread be better than switching models mid-conversation?
In other words, a strong router needs memory.
A useful mental model is:

routing score =
task fit
+ required capabilities
+ cache/affinity benefit
− cost
− latency
− switching penalty
That is not a literal formula every router uses, but it captures the real decision. The best route may sometimes be: do not switch models.
How products approach this

OpenRouter’s Auto Router is a managed example of model routing. It classifies prompts, considers task fit, model capabilities, and cost preferences, and then selects an eligible model. It can also apply allowed-model restrictions and cost tiers.

What is especially relevant here is its session stickiness. With a session identifier, OpenRouter can prefer the model already selected for a conversation while still reconsidering the choice if the task changes. That is a practical acknowledgement that completely independent per-turn routing is not always ideal.

LiteLLM’s Auto Routing takes a more configurable gateway-style approach. Its current Auto Routing feature is marked beta, but it supports heuristics, keyword rules, an LLM classifier, or a custom classifier. It also supports optional session affinity.

This makes LiteLLM particularly interesting for a hands-on experiment. Instead of accepting an opaque routing decision, I can define the model tiers, make the policy visible, record why a route was chosen, and compare different affinity strategies.
A managed router can be useful when I want to experiment quickly. A configurable gateway becomes more interesting when I want to understand and evaluate the routing policy itself.
Neither approach removes the need to define what “good routing” means for a specific application.
The router needs to be evaluated too
A router can look successful if it lowers average cost while quietly making the hardest requests worse.
For each routed request, I would want to capture:

The selected model and routing reason
The task category or complexity score
The number of model switches in a session
Input and output tokens
Time to first token and total latency
Cost per request
Cache-hit or cold-prefill signals, where available
Quality and consistency across the conversation
Retries, fallbacks, and failures
The real question is not:
Did the router choose the cheapest model?
It is:
Did the router preserve the quality users needed while improving cost, latency, or both?
The experiment I want to run next
For the next hands-on lab, I want to explore model routing with LiteLLM and compare three strategies across a small, multi-turn workload:

One fixed model for every request
Stateless, per-request routing based only on the latest prompt
Session-aware routing that keeps a model pinned unless there is a strong reason to switch
I would use three model tiers:

A fast, lower-cost model
A stronger general-purpose model
A reasoning-oriented model
The test set should not only contain isolated prompts. It should include conversations where the user changes direction midway through:

Summarization followed by a deeper technical question
RAG questions followed by a request for a structured action plan
A coding discussion that later becomes a simple extraction task
A conversation with repeated follow-ups about a long document
The goal is not to prove that one strategy wins everywhere.

Stateless routing may lower the average model cost. Session-aware routing may reduce cold-prefill events and create a smoother multi-turn experience. The interesting part will be making that trade-off visible.
Closing thought
Model routing changes the question from:
What is the best model for my application?
to:
What is the best model for this request, in the context of this conversation and this inference system?
That final part matters.

Choosing a different model may improve the answer to one prompt, but it can also discard valuable inference state built during the conversation. Good routing is not only about finding the cheapest or strongest model. It is about knowing when switching models is worth it—and when preserving affinity is the smarter route.

title: Model Routing: Choosing the Right LLM for Each Request

blocks.text: As I started looking at LLM inference benchmarks, I kept seeing results that said a certain CPU, GPU, model server, or engine was “better.”
Better at what?

That question matters more than the benchmark tool itself. A CPU can be the better choice for a low-volume, latency-sensitive workload at a given cost. A GPU can be the better choice for a high-concurrency workload. Both statements can be true, even for the same model, because they may describe completely different tests.
This is why GuideLLM, vllm bench serve, NVIDIA GenAI-Perf, llama-bench, and MLPerf Inference are not simply different ways to produce one score. They answer different questions.
The mental model I am carrying forward is this: a benchmark is not a score; it is a conditional statement about a system under a workload.
First, decide which layer is being measured
There are three very different kinds of benchmarking:

Local execution-path benchmarking: “How quickly does this model artifact execute on this machine with this runtime configuration?” llama-bench belongs here.
Serving-system benchmarking: “How does a deployed service behave when requests arrive at a particular rate or concurrency?” vllm bench serve, GuideLLM, and GenAI-Perf belong here.
Standardized system benchmarking: “How does one complete hardware-and-software system compare with another under common rules?” MLPerf Inference belongs here.

The phrase “under a workload” is the missing part of many benchmark conversations. Before reading any tokens-per-second number, I want to know the prompt shape, output shape, arrival pattern, cache condition, and latency target behind it.
If a CPU performs “better,” what did we actually test?
The answer should never be just “we ran the model.” At minimum, a benchmark needs to state:

The model artifact: model revision, quantization, tokenizer, context limit, and sampling settings. Changing the quantization or tokenizer can make two runs incomparable.
The input distribution: the actual prompt-token distribution, not only an average. Long inputs stress prefill and KV-cache capacity.
The output distribution: both target and actual generated-token distribution. Long outputs emphasize decode and inter-token latency.
The traffic model: closed-loop concurrency or open-loop request rate; steady, bursty, or trace replay. Queueing and batching behave differently under each.
The cache state: cold or warm cache, prefix reuse, session affinity, and cache-hit rate where available. A warm shared prefix can change both TTFT and capacity.
The success target: SLOs for TTFT, token cadence, end-to-end latency, errors, and cost. Peak throughput may be irrelevant if the user experience fails.
This is how I would make a CPU-versus-GPU claim honestly:

For this quantized model, at this low offered load, with this interactive prompt/output mix, the CPU met the P95 TTFT and token-cadence SLO at a lower cost per successful request. At higher offered load, the GPU delivered more goodput.
That is a useful engineering result because it explains the trade-off instead of hiding it.
Use a workload matrix, not one benchmark

One fixed test—such as a 512-token prompt and 128-token completion—can be useful for regression testing, but it is not a representation of every application. I would use a small workload matrix instead.

Interactive chat / decode-heavy: 128–512 input tokens and 256–1,024 output tokens; 1–8 concurrent users; streaming; mostly cold requests. This tells us about token cadence, P95 time per output token, and perceived responsiveness.
RAG / prefill-heavy: an input distribution such as P50 4K and P95 8K tokens, with 64–256 output tokens; run a rate sweep with cold and warm-prefix variants. This tells us about TTFT, prefill capacity, KV-cache pressure, and the effect of retrieval context.
General assistant / mixed: 512–2K input tokens and 128–512 output tokens, with Poisson or trace-like arrivals and realistic bursts. This exposes the balance of TTFT, decode speed, queueing, and goodput.
Offline batch: prompt and output sizes based on the batch job, run at high concurrency or maximum sustainable throughput. This is where total tokens/second, cost, power, and time to finish matter most.
Multi-turn / cache-aware: a shared system prompt or conversation history plus a small incremental turn; compare session affinity on and off, and cold versus reused-prefix requests. This tells us whether cache reuse and routing improve the end-to-end result.

These token values are examples, not a universal standard. The important thing is to use the distribution your application sees. A RAG system should not be represented by a tiny synthetic prompt simply because it produces a flattering throughput number. Likewise, a creative-writing application may need a longer output distribution than a retrieval question-answering workload.

This is where our earlier routing discussion becomes relevant again. A model router may look efficient when the test assumes a warm cache, but the benefit can disappear if related turns land on different replicas and must rebuild the KV cache. A cache-aware, multi-turn workload should make that assumption visible.
The tools are different because the questions are different

llama-bench: A local llama.cpp tool for testing prompt processing (pp), text generation (tg), or both. It is useful for CPU-thread, GGUF-quantization, and GPU-offload sweeps. It does not establish production API latency, queueing, routing, continuous batching, or multi-user capacity. Its documented measurements also exclude tokenization and sampling. llama-bench documentation
vllm bench serve: A client-side benchmark for a running endpoint. It can control input/output lengths, request rate, burstiness, concurrency, warmups, and SLO-aware goodput. This is where I would start when tuning a vLLM deployment. vLLM benchmark-serving documentation
GuideLLM: An endpoint benchmarker for production-like load profiles, especially rate, concurrency, and sweep tests. I would use it to compare capacity or regressions across configurations and endpoints. GuideLLM documentation
NVIDIA GenAI-Perf: A token-aware endpoint-testing tool that fits naturally into Triton or TensorRT-LLM environments. It supports synthetic, dataset, and JSONL inputs. NVIDIA GenAI-Perf documentation
MLPerf Inference: A standardized suite for comparing hardware-and-software systems under prescribed models, data, scenarios, accuracy checks, and rules. It is valuable for published system comparisons, but not a replacement for an application-specific load test. MLPerf Inference overview

For deployed inference experiments, I would begin with vllm bench serve or GuideLLM. For a local GGUF experiment, I would use llama-bench. I would use MLPerf to understand published system comparisons.
A shareable framework: use an MLPerf-inspired benchmark card

MLPerf is the formal framework for standardized published comparison. Its harness covers query scheduling, logging, latency tracking, accuracy validation, and final metric computation; it also requires a prescribed result structure. MLPerf’s submission guide explains why its results are comparable.

For an application-specific serving benchmark, I would adopt the same discipline in a lighter benchmark card. It is a transparent template that lets somebody else understand, challenge, or reproduce the result.
Every shared benchmark should contain four things:

A one-page benchmark card: the human-readable answer—what was tested, why, and what passed or failed.
A reproducibility manifest: model revision, image and engine versions, hardware, server configuration, exact command, and seed.
Raw result artifacts: JSON or CSV with request-level timings where practical; not just a screenshot of one number.
A small set of plots: offered load versus goodput, P95 TTFT versus offered load, and P95 token cadence versus offered load.
A single benchmark card could look like this:

Run ID and intent: rag-cold-4k-128-v1 — find the highest arrival rate that still meets the chat SLO.
System under test: exact model revision and quantization; server and engine versions; CPU, GPU, memory, driver/runtime; replica and parallelism settings.
Workload: RAG prompts with P50 4K and P95 8K input tokens; output capped at 128 tokens; streaming enabled; tokenizer named.
Arrival and cache: open-loop Poisson at 2, 4, 6, and 8 requests per second; maximum concurrency 16; cold cache, then a separate warm-prefix run.
SLO / pass rule: P95 TTFT at or below 1.5 seconds; P95 inter-token latency at or below 50 ms; error rate below 1%.
Results: offered and attained request rate; P50/P95/P99 TTFT; P95 inter-token latency; end-to-end latency; output-token throughput; errors; and goodput.
Reproduction: exact server and benchmark commands, configs, seed, duration and warmup, raw JSON/CSV, and chart links.
