GuideLLM produces JSON, CSV, and self-contained HTML reports. vLLM can save detailed result JSON and metadata. GenAI-Perf exports CSV/JSON and comparison plots. GuideLLM output formats, vLLM result options, and GenAI-Perf output options

The most important reporting habit is to separate offered load from attained throughput. If I offer 8 requests per second but the service queues, errors, or misses the SLO, reporting only the resulting tokens/second hides the actual behavior. Goodput is much more honest: it counts work that was completed within the latency requirements that matter.
What I want to test next
The next hands-on lab should not try to crown one tool the winner. It should use one deployed vLLM endpoint and a reproducible benchmark card to answer a real question.

I would keep the model and system fixed, then change one variable at a time: offered rate, cache condition, or serving configuration. The result would show exactly which workload, at what load, under what SLO, and with what cache behavior makes a setup the better choice.
That is the kind of benchmarking data I would trust—and want to share.

title: Benchmarking LLM Inference—What Are We Actually Measuring?

blocks.text: Understanding Cold Starts in LLM Inference
In the last few articles, I have been thinking about autoscaling, routing, KV cache, and distributed inference.
Autoscaling sounds straightforward:

Traffic increases
↓
Add another replica
↓
More capacity
But there is an important gap hidden inside this picture.

We decided that we need
another inference replica.

How long before that replica
can actually generate tokens?
That gap is the cold start.
And with LLM inference, starting a replica can mean much more than simply starting a container.
What exactly is a cold start?
A cold start is the work required to turn inactive capacity into a model that is actually ready to serve inference requests.
For an LLM server, that can look roughly like this:

Get a machine
↓
Start the container
↓
Start the inference runtime
↓
Find and load the model weights
↓
Move the weights onto the GPU
↓
Prepare GPU memory and execution
↓
Warm up the engine
↓
Start serving requests
I had seen diagrams like this before.
But terms such as initialize runtime or load model weights do not explain much by themselves.
So what is actually happening?
What does “get infrastructure” mean?
Suppose Kubernetes decides that another model-server pod is required.
If an existing node has enough free GPU capacity, Kubernetes can schedule the pod there.
But imagine every GPU is already occupied.
Now the new pod remains pending.
The cluster autoscaler may then ask the cloud provider for another GPU machine.
That means the cloud has to do things such as:

allocate the VM or bare-metal machine
↓
boot the operating system
↓
initialize networking
↓
attach required storage
↓
start Kubernetes components
↓
register the node with the cluster
Only after that can Kubernetes place the model-server pod on it.
So sometimes the biggest cold start has nothing to do with the model yet.
The machine itself did not exist.
What happens during a container cold start?
Now assume the machine exists.
Kubernetes wants to start something like a vLLM model-server container.
First it needs the container image.
If the image is already cached on that node, this can be relatively quick.
But if it is not cached:

Container Registry
↓
download image layers
↓
unpack them onto the node
↓
create the container
↓
start the inference process
A large inference image may contain Python, CUDA libraries, PyTorch, the inference engine, and many other dependencies.
So downloading and unpacking the image itself can take time.
This is why:
Pod created
does not mean:
Model ready
The application has only started its journey.
What does “initialize the runtime” actually mean?
Now the inference program starts.
For example, imagine we started vLLM.
Before it can generate anything, the program has to understand the environment it is running in.
It may need to:

Read the model configuration.
Load the tokenizer configuration.
Detect available GPUs.
Initialize CUDA.
Decide how the model will be split if multiple GPUs are used.
Create communication between GPU workers.
Work out how much memory can be used for KV cache.
Create internal schedulers and memory managers.
So when I say:
initialize inference runtime
I really mean:

Build all the machinery
that will run the model.
The weights are only one part of that machinery.
Why does CUDA initialization take time?
The GPU is physically present, but our process cannot simply start sending matrix multiplications to it.
The CUDA runtime first needs to establish the application's connection to the GPU.
Conceptually:

Inference process
↓
CUDA runtime / driver
↓
GPU
The process needs GPU contexts, memory management structures, streams, and other runtime resources.
If we are using several GPUs, the engine also has to make those workers aware of each other.
For tensor parallel inference, for example:
GPU 0 ←→ GPU 1 ←→ GPU 2 ←→ GPU 3
Parts of every layer may be distributed across those GPUs.
They therefore need communication channels before inference can work correctly.
This is one reason a distributed replica has more startup work than a simple single-GPU process.
What does “load the model weights” mean?
This was one phrase I wanted to understand more clearly.
A model is ultimately stored as files somewhere.
For example:

Model repository
Object Storage
Network filesystem
Local SSD
Those files contain billions of learned parameter values.
When we start the inference server, those parameters must become available to the inference process.
There are two very different situations.
The model is already stored locally
Then there may be no internet or object-storage download at all.
The engine reads the model files from local disk.

Local SSD
↓
Inference process
The model is not available locally
Now it may first need to come across the network.

Model repository / Object Storage
↓
Network
↓
Node storage or memory
So when someone says:
Model loading took 60 seconds.
I now want to ask:

Was the model already local?

Or did we spend most of that
time downloading it?
Those are very different problems.
What does “read model files” mean?
Suppose the model is already on an NVMe disk.
The model might still be tens or hundreds of gigabytes.
The storage device has to read all those bytes.
Very roughly:

100 GB model

Storage reads at 2 GB/s

Even perfect sequential reading
would take about 50 seconds.
Real systems are more complicated, but the intuition is useful.
Large-model startup is partly a data movement problem.
The GPU can be incredibly fast at matrix multiplication and still sit waiting for the model to arrive.
What does “deserialize the weights” mean?
The model file is just stored data.
Something like:
model.safetensors
contains parameter values plus information describing what those values represent.
The runtime needs to turn that stored representation into tensors that the model code can use.
Conceptually:

Bytes inside model file

↓ interpret them as

Tensor:
shape = 4096 × 4096
dtype = FP16
belongs to layer 12
That conversion from stored model representation into usable tensor structures is what people mean by deserialization.
It is not the model “learning” anything.
We are simply rebuilding the model from its saved representation.
What does “allocate memory” mean?
Before putting model weights onto a GPU, the runtime needs space to put them.
Imagine the GPU has:
80 GB HBM
The inference engine has to divide that memory among things such as:

Model weights
KV cache
Temporary computation buffers
Runtime overhead
So the engine reserves memory for these different purposes.
For example:

80 GB GPU

50 GB → model
24 GB → KV cache
6 GB  → runtime/workspace
The actual numbers vary significantly, but this is the idea.
This is another reason model startup is not simply:
copy file → GPU
The engine first has to construct the memory environment in which inference will happen.
What does “copy the weights to the GPU” mean?
Eventually those parameter values need to be accessible by the GPU.
A simplified path might be:

SSD
↓
CPU memory
↓
PCIe
↓
GPU HBM
Different runtimes can optimize this path, so it is not always exactly this sequence.
But something fundamental remains true:

Large amounts of data
have to move.
If 100 GB of weights need to cross a connection, the bandwidth of that connection matters.
This is why cold-start performance can depend on:

storage speed
network speed
PCIe bandwidth
model size
number of GPUs
model format
not simply GPU FLOPS.
What does “initialize tensors” mean?
Once the weight data is available, the framework has to associate it with the correct parts of the neural network.
For example:

Layer 0 attention weights
Layer 0 MLP weights

Layer 1 attention weights
Layer 1 MLP weights

...
If tensor parallelism is being used, the runtime may also need to determine which GPU owns which portion.
For example:

Weight matrix

GPU 0 → shard 1
GPU 1 → shard 2
GPU 2 → shard 3
GPU 3 → shard 4
The model is effectively being reconstructed in the form required for execution.
What does “prepare the inference engine” mean?
Now we have the model.
But the engine still needs infrastructure around it.
Take vLLM as an example.
It needs things such as:

Scheduler
KV Cache Manager
GPU Workers
Model Executor
PagedAttention structures
The scheduler needs to know how requests will be batched.
The KV Cache Manager needs memory blocks it can assign to requests.
GPU workers need to be initialized.
The model executor needs to know how computation will be launched.
So:
Weights loaded
still does not necessarily mean:
Inference engine completely ready
Why does the engine sometimes run a warm-up?
Suppose everything is loaded.
The engine may still execute one or more test requests before declaring itself fully ready.
Why?
Because the first execution may trigger additional setup.
Depending on the runtime, this can include things such as:

loading or compiling GPU kernels
building execution paths
capturing CUDA graphs
creating temporary buffers
testing memory usage
Think of it almost like starting a car.
The engine exists.
The fuel is there.
But we still start the engine before driving onto the highway.
A warm-up request lets the system exercise the important inference path before a real user does.
So where does cold-start time actually go?
Now the picture is much easier for me to understand.

Need capacity
↓
Maybe create a machine
        infrastructure time

↓
Maybe download the container
        image/network time

↓
Start inference application
        process/runtime time

↓
Maybe download model
        network/storage time

↓
Read model files
        storage time

↓
Build tensors and model structure
        CPU/runtime work

↓
Move model onto GPUs
        memory-transfer time

↓
Initialize GPU workers
        CUDA/distributed setup

↓
Reserve KV cache and workspaces
        memory setup

↓
Warm up execution
        kernels/graphs/runtime work

↓
Ready
Now “cold start” no longer feels like one mysterious number.
It is the sum of several different startup costs.
Is a cold KV cache the same thing?
No, and I think this distinction is especially important.
Suppose the server has finished everything above.
The model is loaded.
The engine is ready.
It can serve traffic.
But imagine a request arrives with a large system prompt the replica has never processed.
The model is warm.
The prefix cache is cold.
So the complete prefill still needs to happen.

Model warm
+
Prefix cache cold
Later, if another request uses the same reusable prefix:

Model warm
+
Prefix cache warm
The server may avoid repeating some of that prefill work.
So I now separate these two ideas:

Model cold start
=
How long until I can serve?

Cache coldness
=
How much useful inference state
have I already built?
What happens when autoscaling adds a new replica?
This connects cold starts directly with my previous articles on KV-cache-aware routing.
Imagine:

Replica A
Replica B
have been serving traffic for an hour.
They may already contain useful prefix-cache state.
Traffic increases.
Autoscaling creates:
Replica C
Replica C first pays its startup cost.
Then it becomes Ready.
But Replica C may still have almost no useful cached prefixes.
Now a request arrives.
Replica A might have:

longer queue
+
useful prefix already cached
Replica C might have:

empty queue
+
cold prefix cache
Which one should the router choose?
Now routing is no longer simply:

Send traffic to
the least busy replica.
The router may be balancing:

queue depth
+
cache locality
+
available memory
+
replica readiness
That is why inference-aware routing becomes so interesting.
How does this become even harder with model routing?
Now imagine the router is not just choosing between replicas of the same model.
It can choose between completely different models.
For example:

Small Model
→ already running

Large Model
→ currently scaled to zero
A complex request arrives.
Maybe the large model would produce the better result.
But choosing it could mean:

Start infrastructure
↓
Start container
↓
Load large model
↓
Initialize GPUs
↓
Warm engine
↓
Finally run request
So the routing decision is no longer only:
Which model is best?
It can become:

Which model is good enough?

Which model is already warm?

How much will starting another
model delay this request?

Is that extra quality
worth the startup latency?
And there is another issue.
Suppose a conversation started on Model A.
Then halfway through we route it to Model B.
Even if Model B is already running, Model B does not magically inherit Model A's KV cache.
It will usually need to process the conversation context itself.
So switching models can introduce another cost:

Model routing
↓
Different model
↓
Existing KV state cannot simply be reused
↓
Context needs prefill again
This makes model routing very different from ordinary HTTP load balancing.
A request carries useful computational history with it.
Why does this matter so much for autoscaling?
Because the autoscaler can make the correct decision and users can still experience poor latency.
For example:

10:00:00
Traffic spike begins

10:00:10
Autoscaler detects it

10:00:15
New replica requested

10:01:30
Replica finally becomes ready
The autoscaler worked.
But there was still more than a minute during which demand exceeded available serving capacity.
That leads to the metric I find most useful here:
Time to Usable Capacity
Not:

How quickly did Kubernetes
create a pod?
But:

How long after deciding
that I need more capacity

did I actually get a model
capable of generating tokens?
What is the key intuition?
Cold start is really about turning:
Potential capacity
into:
Usable inference capacity
And that requires much more than simply starting a process.

Infrastructure
↓
Software
↓
Model weights
↓
GPU memory
↓
Inference runtime
↓
Ready
Then, even after the model is Ready:
Cache state builds over time.
That gives me two different warm-up problems to think about:

Can this replica serve?

and

Can this replica serve efficiently
using the state it has already built?
Both matter for autoscaling and routing.
What comes next?
Understanding the cold-start path immediately creates the next question:

Which of these steps
can we eliminate,
hide,
or make faster?
For example:

Do we keep GPU nodes warm?

Do we pre-pull container images?

Can model weights already be
cached on local NVMe?

Should we keep minimum replicas?

Can models be loaded before
traffic arrives?

Can scaling be predictive
instead of reactive?

Can we stream weights differently?

Can warm pools help?

Should small and large models
use different scaling strategies?
So that is where I want to go next:
How Do We Reduce Cold Starts in LLM Inference?
Not just a list of optimizations, but understanding which part of the cold-start path each technique actually removes — and what we pay for it.

title: Understanding Cold Starts in LLM Inference

blocks.text: How Agentic AI Changes LLM Inference
Until now, I have mostly looked at inference through the lifecycle of a request: an application sends a prompt, the model processes it, generates tokens, and returns a response.
That is still the foundation. But once the application becomes an agent, one model request no longer maps neatly to one user interaction.
A chatbot may answer with one call. An agent investigating an issue, comparing options, or updating a record may plan, call tools, read results, make more decisions, retry an action, and then answer.
The user sees one task. The inference system sees a sequence of calls with different input sizes, output sizes, cache requirements, and latency expectations.
That is why agentic AI is not just more inference. It is a different inference workload.
What changes when an application becomes an agent?

Consider a support agent investigating a customer issue. It reads the request, decides which system to query, calls a CRM or searches documentation, interprets the returned information, possibly takes another action, then drafts a response.

Those calls do not look alike. Tool selection may have a short prompt and a tiny structured output. Reading account history, logs, or retrieved documents can be prefill-heavy. The final explanation may be decode-heavy.
One task can include:

short decision calls
long prefills after tool use
longer decodes for synthesis
retries after tool or validation failures
That is why requests per second does not describe agent demand very well. It misses the number, shape, and timing of the model calls created by each task.
Why can a fast model endpoint still produce a slow agent?

Single-call metrics—time to first token, token speed, total latency, queueing, and throughput—still matter. But an agent's end-to-end time also includes tool waits, orchestration, additional prefill, retries, and the queue for every next model call.

A GPU can serve other requests while an agent waits for a database or browser tool, but the user's task is still paused. When that tool returns, the agent may also have a much larger context to send back to the model.

Sequential stages amplify tail latency. If five required stages each meet a latency target 95% of the time, only about 77% of tasks will have all five stages meet it, assuming the stages are independent. That is not a prediction for every system, but it shows why individually healthy services can still create a poor end-to-end experience.

This is where goodput becomes more useful than raw throughput. The outcome is not simply that a server generated many tokens. It is that a useful task was completed at the expected quality, within an acceptable time and cost.
Why does context become such an important cost?

An agent needs enough state to understand the original goal, what it has learned, what tools it has called, and what it should do next. In many implementations, a meaningful part of that state is sent back to the model after every tool call.
The final answer may be short, yet the system may repeatedly prefill the original request, conversation history, tool decisions, search results, logs, or retrieved documents.

Keeping everything in the prompt increases token cost, prefill latency, and KV-cache pressure with every loop. Summarizing or dropping information too aggressively can cause the agent to lose an important detail or repeat work it has already done.

That makes choices such as limiting tool output, extracting relevant fields, keeping structured state outside the prompt, and retrieving only the evidence needed for the next step part of inference design as well as agent design.
Where do KV cache and session affinity fit in?
They become much more visible in an agent workflow.

If the next model call preserves the earlier prompt tokens, the serving system may reuse the KV cache for that prefix rather than compute it again. The system prompt, the user's goal, and earlier agent messages may stay unchanged while a new tool result is appended. Reuse does not remove the cost of processing the new result, but it can avoid redoing earlier prefill work.

That reuse is not automatic. The token sequence has to remain compatible, so reordering messages or rewriting an early section can cause a cache miss. The next request also has to reach the cache. In many serving systems, cached state is local to a worker or GPU, so moving the continuation to another replica can turn a potential cache hit into a full prefill.
Session affinity, cache-aware routing, and shared-cache designs can help keep related steps near that state. But affinity is not free: it can make load balancing, autoscaling, and recovery harder.

There is another important constraint when model routing enters the picture: a KV cache created for one model cannot simply be used by a different model. If an agent switches models, the new model has to build its own representation of the context.
Does model routing help agents, or make them harder to serve?
Both can be true.

Agents create useful routing opportunities. A small, fast model may be enough to classify a request, select a tool, extract a field, or validate a structured response. A stronger model may be needed for planning, complex reasoning, or the final answer.

That can reduce cost and improve latency for independent steps. But choosing a model only by the immediate subtask can hide the cost of the full workflow. Moving a long, context-heavy reasoning loop to a cheaper model may require a fresh prefill, lose the previous model's cache, and create more work if the result needs correction.

The routing question is therefore broader than, “Which model is best for this call?” It is, “What is the best decision for this task, given the context already built, the cache that may exist, the latency budget, and the cost of a retry?”

Affinity becomes a routing consideration, not only an infrastructure concern. The best destination may be the model that is capable enough for the step and can continue from state the system has already paid to build.
What should we benchmark and scale for?

Traditional inference benchmarks remain valuable. They tell us about prefill and decode performance, time to first token, queueing, tail latency, and how a serving engine behaves on particular hardware.

But a benchmark made of identical, independent prompts will not reveal how a real agent behaves. An agent-focused workload needs sequential calls, changing context, representative tool-result sizes, tool delays, retries, and the bursts created when many workflows resume together.
I would want to look at both the individual call and the full task:

How many model calls and tokens does a successful task require?
Which stages are prefill-heavy and which are decode-heavy?
How often does the system reuse a useful cache prefix?
How long do tools take, and how often do they trigger retries?
What are the end-to-end latency and cost per completed task?

Autoscaling changes for the same reason. User request rate is no longer a direct proxy for model demand. An agent waiting on an external tool is not using generation capacity, but hundreds of tool responses arriving together can create a sudden wave of prefill work. Average GPU utilization or incoming requests alone can miss that shape.

The right signals will differ by system, but queued tokens, time to first token, active sequences, cache pressure, the prefill-versus-decode mix, and tool-completion patterns are often more informative than one request-per-second number.
What does good agent inference look like?

It is not simply the fastest response from an individual endpoint. It is an agent that completes useful work reliably, within the expected latency and cost, while the system uses model capacity intelligently.

That means looking at both layers. At the inference layer, we still need model latency, token throughput, queueing, cache behavior, and utilization. At the workflow layer, we need to know how many steps the task took, where time was spent, whether a tool failed, which model was chosen, and whether the final result was useful.

Agents do not replace the inference questions I have been exploring. They connect them. Prefill and decode, KV-cache reuse, routing, batching, autoscaling, and observability now affect a chain of decisions rather than a single response.

The unit we are optimizing is no longer only a request. It is a workflow that carries state, pauses for external systems, resumes with new context, and still has to feel fast and reliable to the person waiting for the result.

title: When One Prompt Becomes a Workflow

blocks.text: Most of the inference concepts I have been exploring start with tokens.

How many tokens are coming in? 
How many need to be generated? 
Is the workload prefill-heavy or decode-heavy? 
Can the KV cache be reused? 
How should requests be batched?
Those questions still matter when we move from text to images, audio, and video. But multimodal inference adds a new one:
what has to happen before the LLM even receives its input?

Someone can send the text, “What is happening in this video?” That is only a few words. Yet the system may need to retrieve a file, decode frames, resize images, run a vision encoder, turn its output into the LLM’s input representation, and only then begin prefill and decode.
That is why multimodal inference is not just text inference with an image attached. The LLM may still generate text one token at a time, but the prompt is no longer just what the user typed.
Why does prompt length stop telling us the whole story?

With text-only inference, prompt length is relatively easy to reason about. A tokenizer converts text into token IDs, then the model processes them during prefill. Longer context means more prefill work and more KV-cache memory.
With multimodal input, the visible text can be misleading.

Imagine two users who both write, “Summarize this.” One attaches a single image. The other attaches a ten-minute video. The prompt text is identical, but the work required to serve those requests is not.

The image may be resized or split into tiles. The video may need decoding and frame selection before it reaches a vision encoder. Audio has its own decoding and chunking path. Those choices decide how much information becomes part of the LLM’s context.
So what does that mean for an inference service?

Image resolution, image count, video duration, sampled frames, and audio length become part of capacity planning. They affect latency, memory, and cost. In multimodal inference, the expensive part of the prompt can be hidden behind one attachment button.
Where does the time go before the first token?
For a text request, time to first token usually leads us to think about queueing and LLM prefill. That is still useful, but it is no longer enough.
A multimodal request often follows a path like this:
media retrieval → decode and preprocessing → modality encoder → LLM prefill → decode
The exact implementation varies by model, but there is now meaningful work before the LLM receives its effective prompt.
Why does that matter?

Because a faster decode path will not help if the request is waiting for video frames to be decoded. Likewise, optimizing LLM prefill only solves part of the problem if the vision encoder is the bottleneck.
Instead of asking only, “Why is the LLM slow?”, I would ask, “Which stage delayed the first token?”

Media retrieval, 
CPU-side decoding, 
mage preprocessing, 
the encoder, 
LLM prefill, 
or queueing behind another kind of request can all matter.
Does the LLM still do the same prefill and decode work?
At the LLM core, yes.

For the common architecture where a vision or audio encoder output is mapped into the language model’s embedding space, the LLM receives one combined sequence: text tokens plus media representations. It then performs prefill over that combined sequence, just as it would for a long text prompt.

The familiar transformer work is still there: Q, K, and V projections, attention, output projections, and MLP layers—the same matrix multiplications that make up text serving. Prefill builds KV-cache entries for the combined context. Decode then runs the same autoregressive loop: process the next token, attend to the KV cache, sample the next output, and repeat.
So is the only change before prefill?

That is the right first way to think about the pipeline, but it is not the whole performance story. Multimodality adds preparation and encoder work before LLM prefill. Then the media representation can make the LLM context larger, which increases prefill work and KV-cache pressure.

Some models use resamplers or cross-attention rather than simply placing every media representation into a decoder-only token sequence. But the serving conclusion stays the same: modality encoding is an additional workload, and its output changes how much context the language model has to process.
What do I mean by input shape?
I do not just mean file size in megabytes. I mean the normalized form of the request after the serving system has prepared it for the model.

For an image, that includes image count, original and processed resolution, whether it is tiled, and how many visual representations the processor produces. A 2,048 × 2,048 document page and a 512 × 512 screenshot can have very different encoder cost even if both are one image.

For video, I would track frames decoded, frames sampled or retained, and the processed resolution of each frame. Duration alone is not enough; a ten-minute video sampled at a few frames per minute is a very different request from a short clip where many frames are kept.

For audio, the useful shape includes duration, sample rate, chunk count, and the resulting audio representations. For every request, I would still keep text-input tokens and the requested output-token budget.
Why track the processed form rather than only the upload?

Because it determines encoder batching, LLM prefill length, KV-cache use, and eventually latency. Two similar files can create very different workloads once one is tiled, another is downsampled, or a video is sampled more aggressively.
If media becomes model input, what happens to the KV cache?
KV cache is already central to text inference. During prefill, the model stores attention keys and values so it does not have to recompute all prior context for every generated token.
When media representations are part of the LLM context, they contribute to prefill work and KV-cache memory. A user may send only a short sentence, yet the effective context can be large.
But there is another cache opportunity before the KV cache.
What if many requests use the same image, document page, or product asset?

A system may be able to reuse the processed media representation and avoid running the encoder again. That is different from reusing a text prefix or an existing KV-cache block. One avoids modality-encoding work; the other avoids downstream LLM prefill work.

This is why one generic cache-hit metric can be misleading. A media-embedding cache hit does not necessarily mean the LLM prefill was reused, and a prefix-cache hit does not necessarily mean the expensive image or video processing disappeared. vLLM supports stable media IDs so media work can be reused across requests without rehashing the raw content.
Can we simply use fewer visual tokens?
That will often be the first instinct.

For video, we can sample fewer frames. For images, we can resize more aggressively, reduce tiling, or prune visual tokens. These choices can lower encoder time, reduce LLM prefill work, and make the KV cache easier to manage.
So why not always make the media budget as small as possible?

Because the removed information may be exactly what the user needs. Lower frame density may work for a broad video summary, but fail when the task is to identify a brief moment, extract text from a document, or inspect a chart label.

Reducing visual or audio representations is not only an efficiency decision. It is also a decision about what evidence the model is allowed to lose. vLLM’s multimodal support makes that trade-off explicit: video-token pruning can reduce prefill time and KV-cache usage, but at some cost in accuracy.
Does batching work the same way?
Not quite.
Text batching already manages different prompt and generation lengths. Multimodal batching adds image resolutions, image counts, video frame counts, audio durations, and different encoder shapes.

That creates more uneven neighbors. A batch of small image questions may run efficiently. Put one long video request in that same batch, and it can demand much more media decoding, encoder work, and downstream context memory than the others.

If we batch every request together only to maximize utilization, a simple image question can wait behind video-heavy work. If we isolate every shape, hardware utilization can suffer. The real decision is how to group requests with similar expected work while keeping the system busy.
What should a multimodal inference dashboard show?
Tokens per second is still useful, but it will miss the most important part of some requests.

I would start with end-to-end time to first token, broken down into media acquisition, decode, preprocessing, encoder, LLM prefill, and queueing. Then I would break it down by input shape: image count and processed resolution, video frames decoded and retained, audio duration and chunks, text tokens, resulting multimodal tokens, and requested output tokens.

Media or embedding-cache metrics should stay separate from prefix- and KV-cache metrics. Finally, p95 and p99 latency should be shown by workload type and input-shape bucket, not only as one blended average. One image at a standard resolution is a different user experience from eight high-resolution document pages or a long sampled video.
So where does this leave the familiar inference model?
Prefill, decode, batching, routing, KV cache, and goodput are still the right concepts. Multimodal inference does not replace them. It asks us to apply them to a larger pipeline.
The system is no longer only scheduling tokens. It is also scheduling the work that creates them.
For images, audio, and video, that hidden work is often where the real performance story begins.

title: The Hidden Prompt: Why Multimodal Inference Is a Different Serving Problem

blocks.text: What Actually Happens Before Your Prompt Reaches an LLM
When I first started looking at model routers, the idea sounded straightforward: send simple requests to a smaller, cheaper model and difficult ones to a stronger model.
That is part of the story. But it also raises an important question:
Does every team now need to build its own router?

No. Most teams should not start by training a router or writing a large routing service. What they need first is a clear routing policy—and they can often implement that policy with a managed router or an LLM gateway.

The distinction matters because the most visible benefit of routing is cost reduction, but a useful router is not only a cost tool. It is an application-and-serving decision system. It decides what quality is acceptable, which capabilities are mandatory, how much latency is tolerable, whether a conversation should stay on the same model, and what to do when an endpoint fails.
That is why I now think of model routing as a
system problem, not a pricing spreadsheet.
So what can an existing router do, and when would I need my own policy?

Existing routers and gateways already solve a lot of the mechanics: model pools, retries, provider failover, health checks, rate limits, budget controls, and sometimes prompt classification or model-tier selection.

They are not limited to cost. For example, Microsoft Foundry’s model router lets a team choose a model subset and route in Cost, Quality, or Balanced modes, with automatic failover. LiteLLM’s Auto Routing supports heuristic, LLM, semantic, and custom classifiers, as well as optional session affinity. Provider-routing layers can also prioritize health, latency, throughput, parameter support, and data policy—not only price.
That gets many teams far enough.

But a general-purpose router cannot know what quality means in your application. It does not know that a support answer must cite a policy correctly, that an extraction workflow can tolerate an occasional review queue but not malformed JSON, or that an agent’s next tool call is more important than beautiful prose.
That is when a custom policy becomes valuable. And “custom” does not necessarily mean a custom-trained router model. It may be a small policy layer on top of a gateway:

Keep all ongoing customer conversations on the same approved model unless a high-risk task requires escalation.
Send document extraction to a smaller, validated model, but route any ambiguous field to a stronger model.
Allow only models and regions that meet a particular data policy.
Route agent steps that require reliable tool calls differently from ordinary chat.
The existing router can still execute the policy. Your application supplies the judgment it cannot infer on its own.
The word “router” hides four different decisions
Consider a customer-support assistant that receives this request:
“Read this 40-page contract, identify whether the cancellation clause conflicts with our policy, and return the issues as JSON.”
Several routers may be involved, but they are doing very different jobs.

Model routing decides which model should answer. A smaller model might handle ordinary FAQ responses, while this request may need a model with a long enough context window, strong document reasoning, and reliable structured output.

Provider or endpoint routing decides where the selected model should run. If the logical model is available from multiple providers, the router might avoid one endpoint because it is unhealthy, does not support the requested JSON mode, violates the data policy, or has poor p95 latency. The model choice may stay the same while the endpoint changes. OpenRouter’s provider-routing documentation is a useful public example of this layer.

Inference routing happens inside the serving fleet. If you self-host the selected model on several replicas, the system decides which replica should execute this request. For a follow-up turn, the best replica may be the one that already holds the conversation’s KV cache. Sending it elsewhere can mean prefill work all over again.

MoE routing happens inside the model itself. If the selected model is a Mixture-of-Experts model, an internal gate chooses experts while processing tokens. Imagine a model with eight feed-forward experts that activates the best two for a token at one MoE layer. The next token—or the next MoE layer—can choose a different pair, and their outputs are combined using the gate’s weights.

The application did not choose “expert 3 for this customer contract.” It chose the overall model before the request began. The MoE gate chooses computation paths inside that model, token by token. MoE routing has its own serving concerns: uneven expert load, token movement between GPUs, and expert-parallel communication can all affect latency and throughput. The Switch Transformers paper is a good reference if you want to go deeper into that internal layer.
The shared word routing is misleading. Model routing is an application decision. Provider and inference routing are serving decisions. MoE routing is part of the model’s forward pass.
What does a model router decide before it scores quality?
It should first remove candidates that cannot satisfy the request.

For the contract example, a model is not eligible if it cannot fit the context, produce the required JSON schema, comply with the data policy, or support any needed tools. These are hard gates, not trade-offs. A cheap model that cannot reliably meet the interface contract is not actually cheaper; it creates downstream repair work or failure.
Only after filtering does the router ask questions such as:

What task is this: extraction, summarization, reasoning, code, planning, or conversation?
How much input does it contain, and how long is the expected output?
How severe is a wrong answer?
Is this the start of a conversation or a continuation of one?
What are the user’s latency, cost, and quality expectations?

This is why “route by complexity” is too shallow. A short prompt can require difficult reasoning. A simple request can contain a huge document. A user might prefer a slightly slower answer if it is correct and correctly formatted.
Why token shape and cache affinity turn this into a system problem
The advertised price of a model does not tell us the cost or latency of a specific request.

For a long RAG or document-analysis prompt, prefill can dominate because the model must process all of the input before producing the first token. For a creative-writing request with a short prompt and a long response, decode work and output-token cost can dominate instead.
So a useful router estimates input and output separately. It asks, “What will this model cost and how long will it take for this token shape?” not simply, “Which model has the lower token price?”

Then there is conversation state. The KV cache created for one model cannot be reused by a different model. Even with the same model, moving to another replica can lose cache locality unless the serving layer can route cache-aware traffic or transfer the cache.

That creates real trade-offs. A model that looks slightly more expensive on a static price sheet may produce a faster and cheaper next turn if the relevant prefix is already cached. A less expensive model may require a full 40K-token prefill, change response style mid-conversation, and make the user feel as if the assistant has lost context.

Managed routers can help with this, but it is important to understand their limits. For example, Foundry documents session affinity as an attempt to keep related turns on the same eligible model; it can improve the opportunity for cache reuse, but it does not inspect cache state or guarantee a cache hit. The final cache-aware replica decision remains an inference-serving concern.
That connection—between model choice, request shape, conversation state, and live infrastructure—is exactly why routing is a system problem.
The same request can follow a direct route, a cascade, or a fallback
These three patterns are often discussed together, but they solve different problems.

Direct routing makes one decision before generation. The router sees that the contract request needs long context, policy reasoning, and JSON output, so it sends the request directly to a model that meets those requirements. This is often the best path when latency matters and the router already has enough confidence.

A cascade deliberately makes more than one decision. Think of a common support question such as “How do I reset my password?” A lower-cost model can generate a response first. If a task-specific evaluator considers it reliable enough, the system returns it. If not, it escalates to a stronger model. A cascade can save money when most requests are easy, but it pays for extra work and adds tail latency whenever the first answer is rejected. FrugalGPT is a useful reference for this pattern.

A fallback is an availability path, not a quality path. The system has already chosen the right model for the contract analysis, but its preferred provider times out. It can retry through another endpoint serving that model, or move to a compatible fallback model after checking the same context, JSON, tool, and policy constraints. The fallback is not saying, “This request is easier than we thought.” It is saying, “The preferred route is unavailable.”
The metrics must reflect that difference. A high cascade-escalation rate may reveal a weak first-stage quality policy. A high fallback rate may reveal endpoint health or capacity problems.
What is the router really optimizing?
After hard constraints are applied, the decision can be thought of as:
predicted quality − cost penalty − latency penalty − failure risk + cache and session-affinity benefit

The implementation might be a rules engine, a small classifier, an LLM classifier, a learned ranker, or a mix of all of them. RouteLLM, for example, frames routing as estimating whether a stronger model is likely to beat a weaker one for a prompt, then applying a quality-versus-cost threshold.

But that formula only becomes useful once the product has supplied the weights. Is a 1% quality improvement worth 3× the cost? Is it worth 500 ms more latency? Does the answer feed a human, a legal workflow, or an autonomous tool call? Does preserving the conversation’s cached state matter more than using the theoretically best model for one turn?
There is no universal answer. That is why a generic router is a strong starting point, but a mature system eventually needs workload-specific evaluation and policy.
How do we know the router is helping?
Average cost is not enough. A router can lower average cost simply by sending too many difficult requests to a small model.

I would measure quality by task slice, expensive-model call rate, actual cost including retries and cascades, time to first token and p95/p99 latency, tool and JSON failure rates, cache-hit behavior, session stickiness, and routing regret—cases where an eligible alternative was clearly better.

For offline evaluation, run representative prompts through several candidates and compare the results using ground truth, human review, or carefully designed LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. For online evaluation, log the route reason, model version, input/output shape, cache and endpoint state, fallback behavior, and user outcome together. Otherwise, the router becomes very hard to debug as models, pricing, and traffic patterns change.
My takeaway

Not everyone needs to build a model router from scratch. But everyone who uses more than one model eventually needs to decide what they are optimizing—and whether a generic router understands the constraints that matter to their application.

The moment we care about capability contracts, quality, latency, prefill and decode, KV-cache locality, endpoint health, agent behavior, and conversation continuity, model routing stops being “send easy prompts to a cheaper model.”
It becomes a system problem.
And that is the question I would ask before adopting any router: what decision is it making for me, and which decisions still need to come from my application and serving stack?

title: Inside a Model Router

blocks.text: As I have been exploring inference, model routing, and agentic workflows, I have started hearing more about Jev.

The timing felt relevant. In my recent article on agentic inference, I looked at how a workflow can contain both short decision calls and longer calls for reasoning or generation. Jev made me curious about that first category.

My first reaction was: Is this another small LLM? If it returns probabilities instead of sentences, where does its intelligence come from? And if I still have to provide the context and define the choices, what is it actually doing?
This article follows the questions that helped me understand it, with examples showing what goes in, what comes out, and what the surrounding application does next.
What exactly is Jev?
Jev is a model from TypeSafe AI that evaluates information and returns structured decisions rather than generating free-form text.

You provide the context, ask focused questions, and define the possible answers. Jev returns values your software can use directly: a choice, a score, or the estimated probability that the answer to a yes/no question is “yes.”
TypeSafe calls this a System One model—a model designed for fast, focused judgments inside software. TypeSafe AI
The basic interaction is:
State + questions → structured answers → application logic
So, is it just a small LLM that returns JSON?
That is a useful starting comparison, but it misses the intended distinction.

TypeSafe describes Jev as using a new model architecture, a parallel sampler, and training focused on calibrated decisions. It is not presenting Jev as a chat model with an instruction saying, “Only return JSON.” TypeSafe AI
However, structured output alone is not unique to Jev. Generative LLMs can also produce responses constrained to a defined schema. OpenAI Developers
The meaningful comparison is therefore not whether the response contains curly brackets. It is whether Jev produces useful judgments at the quality, calibration, latency, and cost our workflow needs.
Then where does the intelligence come from? Has it still learned from data?
Yes. The instructions we send are not its entire source of intelligence.

TypeSafe’s AI primer describes Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions, or RLCD, as a training path for adapting pretrained language models toward decisions and probabilities rather than conversational responses. So it would also be misleading to describe Jev as completely unrelated to language models. TypeSafe AI

For our application, we do not start by training Jev from scratch. TypeSafe currently says the same weights serve every account, without customer-specific fine-tuning or LoRA adaptation. We shape its behavior through the evidence, instructions, and criteria we provide. TypeSafe AI
But if I give it the choices and criteria, am I not giving it the answer?
We are defining what the answer should mean, not necessarily supplying the answer.
For example, we might define a complex coding task as one involving concurrency, data consistency, or architectural changes.
That definition does not tell Jev whether a particular user request belongs in that category. The model still has to interpret the request against those criteria.
That interpretation is the intended learned contribution. Our code decides what happens afterward.
What do I actually send? Is the “state” basically a system prompt?
Not exactly. State is the material Jev should evaluate.
It can include the incoming request, relevant records, conversation history, reference material, or a policy. Some information stays stable across calls; some changes with every request.
The question goes in instructions. The answer definitions go in criteria, where the question type requires them. Jev accepts state as a string or structured JSON. TypeSafe AI
The distinction is:
State: What information should the model inspect?
Instructions: What judgment should it make?
Criteria: What do the possible answers mean?
Can you show me what a typical call looks like?
Suppose we want to classify a request before choosing a model.

The request examples below follow TypeSafe’s documented API format. All output values are hypothetical—not results from live tests. Response excerpts show selected fields rather than the complete response. TypeSafe AI
Input to Jev:
Illustrative output excerpt:
Now the separation becomes visible.

We supplied the request and defined the categories. Jev supplied an estimated distribution across them. A Choice answer selects the highest-probability option and also includes a separate confidence field in the full response. TypeSafe AI
Our router would still need its own model inventory, capability checks, cost constraints, and routing policy. This answer does not prove which model will solve the task best.
Are all Jev answers choices like this?
No. Jev exposes three question types.
Choice selects from options we define, as in the example above.
Noul answers a yes/no question with the estimated probability of “yes.” For example, “Does this message explicitly request a refund?” might return noul: 0.95.

Score evaluates content against ordered levels. For example, we could define levels as “cosmetic issue,” “degraded feature,” and “blocking failure.” The result includes a score, probabilities across the levels, a legend, and confidence. A score can fall between levels; it is not an exact measurement of a physical quantity. TypeSafe AI
Several questions can share one state. They are evaluated independently: one answer does not automatically become evidence for another question in that same call. TypeSafe AI
Does a probability of 0.8 mean the answer is definitely trustworthy?
No. It is still a model estimate.

For a well-calibrated model, outcomes assigned roughly 80% probability should occur roughly 80% of the time across many comparable predictions. That is not a guarantee about one answer. We still need to test calibration on our own workload. TypeSafe AI

Jev’s separate confidence field for Choice and Score summarizes how concentrated the answer distribution is. It is not an independent verification of correctness. Noul does not have that additional confidence field. TypeSafe AI
A correctly structured answer can still be a wrong answer.
Okay, how would I use this around a web application firewall?
Consider an application that investigates suspicious login activity.

Cloudflare documents access to Jev through its AI interface. Here, we are designing a hypothetical application-level risk workflow—not describing Cloudflare’s internal WAF implementation. Cloudflare Docs
We would preserve existing security controls first. Cloudflare already has separate protections involving DDoS mitigation, custom rules, rate limiting, and managed rules. Cloudflare Docs
I would initially use Jev to evaluate selected events from that environment, rather than put a model call in the path of every request.
What would the state and questions look like?
Our application would collect a compact, sanitized evidence package.

Monitoring code would calculate request counts and baseline comparisons. Jev would interpret the resulting patterns alongside relevant operational context. TypeSafe specifically recommends keeping arithmetic in code. TypeSafe AI
Input to Jev:
We would not include passwords, session cookies, or other secrets in this evidence package.
Notice that we are not asking, “Should I block this IP?” We are asking two narrower questions about the available evidence.
What would come back?
Illustrative output excerpt:
These answers can coexist. The traffic pattern can look suspicious while an operational issue remains a plausible explanation.
The values do not need to add up to one: they answer different questions, not mutually exclusive alternatives.
Also, “a benign explanation is plausible” does not mean that explanation has been confirmed.
Would the application block the traffic because the first number is high?
Not automatically.
Our policy would combine those estimates with independent security signals, endpoint sensitivity, existing restrictions, and the consequences of a false positive.
For this example, the policy might produce:
Application output—not Jev output:
The reason code comes from our application’s policy. It is not an explanation generated by Jev.
Before enabling enforcement, I would run this in shadow mode: record the judgments without letting them change traffic handling, then compare them with reviewed outcomes.

That matters because TypeSafe warns that adversarial content can influence Jev’s answers. Separating trusted operational notes from attacker-controlled data helps organize the evidence, but does not turn the model into a trusted security boundary. TypeSafe AI
Does a larger LLM need to run after Jev?
No. Ordinary application code can finish this workflow.
Existing protections → selected events → evidence collection → Jev → policy checks → action or review → outcome logging
A generative LLM would be optional. We could use it to prepare an analyst-facing incident summary using the original evidence, Jev’s estimates, and the action taken.
Some cases might not need Jev either. In this design, I would keep a deterministic rule or specialist detector wherever it already solves the problem reliably.
How would the same idea work in a financial analysis application?
Let us build a research and scenario-analysis tool, rather than an autonomous financial adviser.
The user supplies a company and a time horizon. Our application retrieves the relevant filings, financial statements, market data, and guidance, preserving source identifiers and timestamps.
Then it selects the evidence needed for each judgment. We would not send only a ticker and expect that to substitute for current information.
For this example, the company, excerpts, and numbers are fictional.
What would the input look like?
Input to Jev:
This state is intentionally small. The application can retain a much larger research package without sending all of it to every judgment call.
TypeSafe’s guidance recommends retrieving relevant evidence, asking focused questions, and keeping the surrounding workflow in code. TypeSafe AI
What would Jev return, and what would those numbers mean?
Illustrative output excerpt:
Our application now has structured judgments about the disclosures.
The first could trigger a review of earnings assumptions. The other two could flag competing considerations: a growing backlog, but slower purchasing decisions.
These are interpretations of supplied evidence—not probabilities that the share price will reach a particular target.
Then how do we get from those judgments to price scenarios?
We need an explicit financial model and a review of its assumptions.
For a simplified example, we choose:
Scenario price = assumed future earnings per share × assumed price-to-earnings multiple
Jev’s output could trigger an analyst to review whether earnings include a non-recurring gain. But Jev’s 0.95 does not tell us what future earnings should be.
After that review, suppose the analyst approves these hypothetical assumptions.
Input to our valuation code—not to Jev:
Our code performs the multiplications.
Output from the valuation code:
For the base case, that is simply:
$4 earnings per share × 25 = $100
The calculation is exact under the assumptions. The assumptions themselves remain uncertain—a limitation that also applies to automated investment tools more broadly. Investor
Could Jev also give us the probabilities for those price scenarios?
We could formulate that question, but we should not assume its answer would be a validated financial forecast.
“Does this disclosure suggest improving demand?” and “Will this stock reach $150 in twelve months?” are different prediction problems.
For a basic scenario tool, we could instead use explicitly stated analyst weights.
Additional input to our calculation code:
The calculation becomes:
That is a weighted scenario value under those assumptions—not a validated expected future price.

For a more advanced design, we could test Jev’s signals as inputs to a separate forecasting model trained on historical outcomes. TypeSafe documents the general pattern of using its answers as features for a downstream statistical model, but that is not evidence of successful stock-price prediction. TypeSafe AI
Where would a generative LLM fit, and what would we send it?
We could use a generative LLM to explain the completed analysis.
It should receive the original evidence and the approved assumptions—not only Jev’s probabilities. Otherwise, it would be explaining numbers without the information behind them.
Example instruction to the generative LLM:

Write a research summary using the supplied filing excerpts, Jev estimates, analyst assumptions, and calculation results. Distinguish reported facts from model judgments and assumptions. Do not treat Jev’s disclosure estimates as probabilities of future stock prices. Do not invent an explanation of Jev’s internal reasoning.
Context supplied with that instruction:

The filing and guidance excerpts from the earlier state; Jev’s three estimates; the approved earnings and valuation assumptions; the $60, $100, and $150 scenario values; and the analyst-weighted value of $102.50.
Illustrative generated explanation:

Reported profit includes a non-recurring business-sale gain, so the earnings assumptions require review rather than simply carrying reported profit forward. Management describes a growing backlog alongside slower purchasing approvals.
The generative model is communicating the analysis. Our code performed the calculations. Jev supplied focused judgments about the disclosures.
What does the full financial workflow look like?
Company and horizon → sourced data → focused Jev judgments → assumption review → valuation code → optional LLM explanation → reviewed report
Different downstream components have different jobs.
A forecasting model would estimate outcomes. Valuation code applies formulas. A generative LLM can support broader analysis and communication.
None is automatically required just because Jev produced an answer.
What would I measure before adopting either design?
For the security workflow, I would measure missed attacks, false positives, added latency, and how often the system needs human review. I would also test misleading and adversarial inputs.

For the financial workflow, I would check whether Jev’s judgments agree with reviewed disclosures and improve the process beyond a simpler baseline. Any forecasting extension would need testing on later, unseen periods using only information available at the prediction time.

For both, I would define timeout behavior and record the model and question versions. The examples use jev-latest for readability, but TypeSafe notes that aliases can move. Once thresholds are tuned, pinning a model version makes changes easier to evaluate deliberately. TypeSafe AI
What changed in my understanding?
I started by thinking Jev might be an LLM that simply returns percentages.
The examples helped me separate the pieces:
The state supplies evidence. The question defines the judgment. Jev returns an estimate. The surrounding system decides how to use it.
Jev does not remove the need for data pipelines, domain knowledge, calculations, validation, or policy.
It gives us another component to evaluate at a specific point in that system.
Are there open and local alternatives to explore?

Projects such as Laya, OneJev, Decider, Winnow, and the Apache-licensed Nimble releases offer ways to explore Jev-like decisions locally, using different architectures and training approaches Hugging Face. Privatemode Decisions takes another route: adapting an existing model such as GLM-5.3-Flash at inference time, without additional training. GitHub
For me, that opens up the next question: Now that I understand the idea, which approach actually fits the system I want to build?

title: Understanding Jev: What Changes When AI Returns Decisions Instead of Text?

blocks.text: Your Inference Server Passes CI—but Is It Safe to Ship?
Imagine updating a dependency in your inference server. The container builds, the model loads, and the API tests pass. Streaming works. Everything looks ready.
Then real traffic arrives, and users wait longer for the first token. There is no crash or obvious error. The service still answers, but the experience has become worse.

Red Hat’s September 2026 report illustrates this class of problem with a GPT-OSS-120B serving regression on NVIDIA H100 associated with a Triton kernel update. Kernels are the low-level routines that execute computation on the GPU. A change underneath the serving engine can affect performance even when the API remains functional. Red Hat Developer
After exploring inference optimizations, benchmarking, and routing, this feels like the next question: how do we make acceptable performance and answer quality requirements for shipping a release?
If the server returns an answer, what else needs to pass?
I would separate the release decision into three questions.

Does it work? Check API behavior, streaming, cancellation, and error handling. If a client disconnects, does the server stop processing the request? If an input is invalid, does it return the expected error?
Are the answers still good? A successful response can contain an incorrect answer. A tool call can have valid JSON while selecting the wrong tool or supplying the wrong arguments.

Use a fixed set of representative tasks: extracting fields, answering questions from supplied documents, or completing a tool workflow. Define success for each task. For open-ended answers, use a consistent rubric rather than requiring identical wording.
Does it meet service targets? Measure how long users wait for the first output, how smoothly tokens arrive afterward, and how much work the system completes under load. vLLM

vLLM describes separate release gates for its full CI suite, performance benchmarks, and model accuracy evaluations. Its release process requires all three to pass. That separation makes sense: passing one does not establish the other two. vLLM Blog
So a throughput improvement could still fail the release?
Yes. Suppose a candidate serves more requests per second, but users wait substantially longer before responses begin.
That could be useful for a batch workload and unacceptable for an interactive assistant.

This is where goodput becomes useful again: the rate of completed requests that satisfy the defined service objectives. Raw throughput can remain high while goodput falls because too many requests miss their latency targets. Answer quality still needs its own evaluation. GuideLLM Docs
Why is comparing two inference releases so difficult?
Because “same model” does not mean “same experiment.”

For a comparison, I would record the model revision, tokenizer, chat template, precision, hardware, driver versions, serving configuration, and benchmark version. Keep those fixed except for the change being evaluated.
Then preserve the workload: prompt lengths, output limits, arrival rates, concurrency, and the mix of tasks.

A short classification prompt and a long document summarization request put different demands on the server. Testing one request at a time also tells us little about how the deployment behaves when requests compete for capacity. Tools such as GuideLLM support configurable workloads and concurrency or request-rate sweeps for this reason. GitHub

Cache state needs equal attention. Repeating prompts can reuse cached prefix computation and make a later run appear faster. vLLM’s benchmarking documentation explicitly warns about this. Control cache reuse, and test both cold and warm conditions where they reflect production. vLLM
I would compare a candidate against both a known-good baseline and the application’s absolute service targets. Matching the previous release is insufficient if both miss the target.
But benchmark results fluctuate. How do we avoid blocking every release?
A small change in a mean or percentile deserves investigation, but it does not automatically establish a regression.

Red Hat found that fixed percentage thresholds could produce false positives in short runs. It added Wasserstein distance as a secondary check alongside individual statistics. This measures how far two distributions are apart—think of moving one latency distribution until it matches the other. Red Hat Developer
The practical lesson is to examine the distribution and repeat questionable measurements.

A small overall distribution change can still hide a problem in the slowest requests. Keep explicit tail-latency checks, such as p95 or p99, and collect enough requests to make those estimates useful. GuideLLM’s metrics documentation explains both sample-size limits and why comparing runs requires repeated measurements. GuideLLM Docs
Does this also apply to model routers?
Yes. A routing change changes the workload reaching each model and serving pool.

Imagine a router sends more requests to a smaller model. Each attempt becomes cheaper, but that model struggles with some tasks. Retries and fallback calls increase. Its serving pool also becomes congested.
The routing decision looked economical in isolation. The complete task can now take longer and cost more.

I would replay a representative request mix through the complete routing path and measure task success, fallback frequency, attempts per task, tail latency, and cost per successful task. Include the cost and delay of failed attempts and fallbacks.
Keep two decisions distinct:

Model selection chooses which model handles the task. It changes the capability and cost tradeoff.
Replica selection chooses which instance of that model receives the request. It changes where the request encounters queues and potentially reusable cached context.
For multi-turn workloads, test complete conversations. A route that performs well on isolated prompts may behave differently when later turns depend on earlier outputs.
What would a practical testing workflow look like?
I would build a testing ladder, with depth matched to the change.

On pull requests, run fast functional checks and a small quality suite covering important application behaviors. Add targeted performance tests when the change touches kernels, scheduling, quantization, caching, or routing. A router update should exercise its decision path and fallback behavior.

Nightly, run broader benchmarks across the model and hardware combinations you actually operate. Sweep concurrency and arrival rates, repeat measurements, and include representative prompt and output lengths. Separate steady-state tests from startup tests so each answers a clear question.

For release candidates, test the exact image and configuration intended for deployment, including the gateway and router where applicable. Set acceptance criteria before inspecting results: required task success, latency targets at expected load, and an acceptable cost per successful task.

For example, an interactive service might require 95% of requests to receive their first output within one second at its planned request rate. That is an illustrative target; each application needs its own.
When a candidate fails, retain the workload, raw outputs, timing data, and configuration needed to investigate. After a fix, rerun the affected checks and the broader checks its scope warrants.

After deployment, begin with a canary: expose a small portion of traffic to the candidate and monitor the same quality, latency, error, and cost signals. Define rollback conditions before expanding traffic.
The principle I would carry forward is this: move useful feedback earlier, and match test depth to the change’s risk. Inference performance and answer quality belong in the release decision.

Next, I want to explore this hands-on on OCI. Getting an inference server running is the starting point. I also want to understand the DevOps work around it: checking answer quality, catching performance regressions, and managing releases as models and serving configurations change. The graphic below outlines the workflow I’ll be experimenting with, using OCI services and tools like GuideLLM to test, release, and monitor an inference service.
